finding: Revenue per installed (on-wing) engine delivery was £3.94m (2014), £2.90m (2015), £3.61m (2017), £3.84m (2019), £5.42m (2020), £5.56m (2022) and £5.10m (2024), or $94.7 per lb of thrust in 2024.

finding: On IFRS 15, OE was 40% of Civil revenue in 2019 (£3,246m OE vs £4,861m services) and 34% in 2024 (£3,105m vs £5,935m); in 1H25 it was 31% (£1,478m vs £3,308m).
implication: (inference) The business mix has shifted toward services. RR's value now rests mainly on the installed base and LTSAs rather than new-engine sales.

finding: Large (widebody) engine OE revenue was £2,089m in 2017, peaked at £2,568m in 2019, fell to £1,696m (2020) and £1,297m (2021), then recovered to £1,516m (2022), £2,039m (2023) and £2,154m (2024). The 2024 figure was still 16% below 2019; 1H25 was £993m.
Business jet OE revenue fell from £903m (2015) to £582m (2017), was £643m in 2019 and £574m in 2020, dropped to £310m in 2021, then rose to £657m (2023), £930m (2024) and £473m in 1H25.
The MS model's on-wing OE loss per widebody engine was £-1.6m in 2017, £-1.4m (2018), £-1.2m (2019), £-1.1m (2020), £-1.05m (2021), £-1.0m in 2022 and 2024, and £-0.85m in 1H25.
implication: (inference) RR has roughly halved the loss on each new widebody engine since 2017 through pricing and cost reduction. A new programme such as UltraFan would probably restart at a deeper loss per engine early in production.

finding: Defence revenue grew 3.2% to £3,355m in 2020 (organic +3.5%) and held at £3,368m in 2021 (organic +4.6%), while Civil Aerospace revenue fell from £8,107m in 2019 to £5,068m in 2020.

finding: Defence order intake was £5.2bn in 2023 and a record £13.3bn in 2024 (£11.6bn in 2H24), lifting the order book from £9.2bn to £17.4bn, a book-to-bill of 2.9 and 3.7 years of next-year revenue.
implication: (inference) A multi-year defence backlog (submarines and combat programmes) gives RR visible, low-risk earnings through at least the first game turns, supporting risk-taking in Civil.

implication: (inference) In the 2000s RR diversified: Civil fell from about 54% of revenue (2000) to about 44% (2009) as Marine and Nuclear grew, a hedge against the civil aerospace cycle.

finding: Defence was £1,403m of £5,864m group revenue in 2000 (24%) and £2,010m of £10,108m in 2009 (20%); in 2013 Defence (£2,591m) and Power Systems (£2,831m) together made up £5,422m of £15,505m (35%).
implication: (inference) RR has deliberately kept roughly a third or more of revenue outside civil aerospace since the 2013 Power Systems consolidation, a portfolio hedge against civil-cycle risk.

finding: On the old GAAP basis Civil revenue grew from £4,919m (2010) to £6,437m (2012), £6,837m (2014) and £6,933m (2015); the EBIT margin rose from 8.0% (2010) to a peak of 13.8% (£942m EBIT) in 2014, then slipped to 11.7% in 2015.
implication: (inference) The 2010-2015 growth era was when RR won the A350 (sole source) and 787 positions; reported margins peaked just before the loss-making Trent XWB ramp and the Trent 1000 problems hit.

finding: In 2013 revenue was Civil GBP 6,655m, Defence GBP 2,591m, Power Systems GBP 2,831m, Marine GBP 2,037m and Nuclear GBP 1,538m; by 2015 Civil was GBP 6,933m while Power Systems fell to GBP 2,385m and Marine to GBP 1,324m.
Civil Aerospace underlying EBIT margin was 10.5% (2000), 5.5% (2002), 4.9% (2003), 14.0% (2007), 8.0% (2010), 13.8% (2014) and 11.7% (2015); Civil EBIT peaked at GBP 942m in 2014.
implication: (inference) Civil margins fell in each launch or downturn phase (2002-03, 2010 during Trent 900/1000 ramp) and peaked around 14%, well below today's 20%+ levels.

finding: Under the 2017 new segment structure (IFRS 15) Defence 2017 revenue was restated from £2,275m to £3,180m and its order book from £3.4bn to £5.8bn, with margin moving from 16.4% to 14.3%.

finding: On the IFRS 15 basis Civil revenue grew from £6,598m (2017) to £7,378m (2018) and £8,107m (2019). Underlying EBIT was £-343m, £-162m and only £44m (0.5% margin) over those years, with a 7.7% gross margin in 2019.
implication: (inference) Peak deliveries of loss-making widebody OE and the Trent 1000 remediation left Civil barely profitable in 2017-2019 despite record revenue. More OE volume destroyed value in the near term.

finding: During the Trent 1000 years Civil Aerospace EBIT was -£343m (2017), -£162m (2018) and £44m (2019); in 2017 Defence (£454m) and Power Systems (£261m) earned £715m against group underlying profit of £306m, and in 2019 they earned £772m (£415m + £357m).
implication: (inference) Defence and Power Systems funded the Trent 1000 remediation years; a new Civil engine programme that goes wrong is cushioned by roughly £0.7bn a year of non-civil profit.

finding: On the 2017 IFRS 15 segment basis Civil revenue was GBP 6,598m and Defence GBP 3,180m; in 2019 revenue was Civil GBP 8,107m, Defence GBP 3,250m, Power Systems GBP 3,545m, ITP GBP 936m and non-core businesses GBP 189m, out of GBP 15,450m.

implication: (inference) The non-civil businesses offset only about a quarter of the 2020 Civil loss, which is why RR still needed a rights issue and disposals; they cushion but cannot absorb a full civil shock.

finding: Defence and Power Systems together were £6,795m of £15,450m group revenue in 2019 (44%) and £6,090m of £11,430m in 2020 (53%); group revenue fell further to £10,947m in 2021.

During COVID Civil revenue fell to £5,068m in 2020, with a £-1,987m gross loss and £-2,535m underlying EBIT (-50% margin; £-1,816m in 1H20 alone). Revenue fell again to £4,536m in 2021 (EBIT £-172m), and EBIT turned positive at £143m in 2022.
implication: (inference) Because Civil's revenue depends on flying hours, a demand shock turns the division deeply loss-making within months. The game's RR player should size new-programme commitments to survive a repeat.

finding: In 2021 Defence (£457m) and Power Systems (£242m) earned £699m against Civil Aerospace -£172m and group underlying profit of £414m; in 2022 they earned £713m (£432m + £281m) against Civil £143m and group £652m.
implication: (inference) In the 2021-22 recovery years Defence plus Power Systems produced more than 100% of group underlying profit, so RR's ability to keep funding Civil programmes depended on them.

response: Accepted the loss; kept supporting ANA's 83 Trent-powered 787s

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the U.S. Air Force is continuing to progress the reengineering of its fleet of B-52s with a new in-production commercial off-the-shelf engine. ... And we will compete with our F130 engine, a variant of the commercial BR725 engine.
finding: RR bid for the B-52 re-engine with a derivative of an existing commercial engine, reusing technology rather than developing a new engine.
trigger: US Air Force B-52 re-engine competition
response: Bid F130, a BR725 derivative

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: younger, more efficient and more versatile wide-body planes like the A350, where we are the sole engine supplier with our Trent XWB engines, and we're seeing much higher utilization levels there. Now we expect that these factors will continue to benefit our installed base, leading to accelerated market share gains with lower retirements of Rolls-Royce wide-body aircraft
finding: RR expected COVID retirements to hit older rival-powered widebodies more, so its young fleet would gain share of flying.
trigger: Airlines retiring older widebodies
response: Expects share gains in flying hours

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we'll do our best to maintain our flying hour rates. But where it's necessary to have a trade-off between offering temporary discounts on flying hour rates in order to keep our airplanes flying rather than somebody else's, then we'll work with airlines and with leasing companies to come up with sensible commercial win-win packages.
finding: RR will temporarily discount flight-hour rates when that keeps RR-powered aircraft flying instead of rival-powered ones during fleet resizing.
trigger: Airlines resizing fleets and choosing which aircraft to fly or retire
response: Temporary flight-hour discounts to keep RR-powered aircraft flying

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Now we're already exclusive on the A350-1000 variant of the aircraft, and we are extending our position, our exclusive position, on the A350-900 variant, and that accounts for the bulk of the A350 fleet, and that extension has agreed with Airbus out to 2030.
finding: RR secured sole-source status on the A350-900 until 2030, keeping its exclusive widebody franchise on Airbus rather than competing.
trigger: Speculation that GE was talking to Airbus about the A350
response: Extended exclusivity on the A350-900 to 2030

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: 12 months or so ago, there was a huge amount of speculation about our competitive position on A350 and GE having conversations with Airbus and so on. A huge amount of speculation and uncertainty in the community. And so we're delighted to put that speculation to bed for the remainder of this decade.
finding: RR treated a possible GE entry on the A350 as a threat and answered with a longer exclusivity deal with Airbus.
trigger: Reported GE-Airbus talks on an A350 engine
response: Exclusivity extended to 2030

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: in September, we were delighted to have been chosen for the B-52 replacement engine program, and that's an agreement to power the U.S. fleet of 76 8-engine aircraft for the next 30 years.
finding: RR won the B-52 re-engine competition, a long-dated defence engine franchise that diversifies it away from civil widebody cash flows.
trigger: US Air Force B-52 re-engine competition
response: Won the contract

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We also have more than half of the market share for new large engines with more than 1,500 on our order book. Our current order book includes 58 Trent XWB engines for Airbus' recently launched A350 freighter.
finding: RR uses Airbus's A350F launch to enter a freighter market it had not served.
trigger: Airbus launch of the A350F
response: Trent XWB-97 orders on the A350F

speaker: Chris Cholerton, President Civil Aerospace
quote: In our wide-body portfolio, we power 4 of the 5 of the new widebodies, all 4 of those, which are actually in service, with 3 sole-source positions with Airbus.
finding: RR's widebody franchise depends on sole-source Airbus positions.

speaker: Robert Watson, President Civil Aerospace
quote: In widebody, we had a 55% OE delivery share in 2022 and 36% market share of installed engines. We power 4 out of 5 new generation widebody aircraft, and we're sole source on 3 of those.
finding: RR's widebody strength rests on sole-source positions on three of five new-generation widebodies.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: If I give you a percentage, half of it market recovery, half of it actually installed engine growth.
finding: RR attributes half its flying-hour growth to installed-fleet share gains.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: sometimes people think because of our pricing actions, we are losing contracts, et cetera. That's not true, actually. So first of all, we are only thing -- we are remunerating our pricing actions is the investments we make and the risks we take. In the past, Rolls-Royce didn't actually price that fairly
finding: RR denies its higher prices lose engine campaigns and says it now charges for investment and risk that it historically under-priced.
trigger: British Airways choosing the GE engine for 787 aircraft
response: RR keeps its pricing discipline and relies on the Trent 1000 durability fix to win back share

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Over the past 2 years, we have captured more than 50% of total widebody deliveries. This means our market share of the widebody installed base has risen from 32% in 2022 to 36% last year.
finding: RR converted a majority share of widebody deliveries into a rising installed-base share, the base for future aftermarket revenue.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: In widebody, our installed fleet has grown at 10% per year since 2022 versus 5% for the market, as we have captured more than 50% of the deliveries. We continue to expect installed fleet growth of 7% to 9% per year to the mid-term
finding: RR frames widebody share capture (over half of deliveries) as the engine of installed-base and aftermarket growth, outgrowing the market two-to-one.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: The book includes orders for more than 1,600 XWBs, our best-selling Trent engine.
finding: By early 2014 RR's order book held more than 1,600 Trent XWB engines, its best-selling Trent.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: As you know, Trent 500, as a 4 engine aircraft is not doing as well given the high fuel price environment.
finding: RR acknowledged that high fuel prices hurt the four-engine aircraft powered by its Trent 500, which weighs on that programme's TotalCare economics.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: for the first time ever in civil large engines, we were 100% on-time all through the year. ... In fact, we won an award from Airbus, and Boeing have really been complimentary most recently about our quality, terrific improvement.
finding: RR reported 100% on-time civil large-engine delivery in 2013 and quality recognition from both Airbus and Boeing, which it uses to shift customer talks toward winning more business.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: The headline number that gets me is, in the last decade, about 2,000 deliveries; in the next decade, 4,000 deliveries, so a huge growth in this
finding: RR planned on widebody aircraft deliveries doubling from about 2,000 in the past decade to about 4,000 in the next.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: A380 is for us. We were more optimistic about sales, I think, of that, in terms of volumes, last year than we are at the moment.
finding: By mid-2014 RR had lowered its A380 volume expectations.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: XWB is unlinked because it's sole source or single source, should I say, and is done through Airbus. So we've got 2 separate contracts because we're negotiating with Airbus, we're doing the aftermarket contracts with the airlines.
finding: As sole source on the A350, RR sells Trent XWB engines to Airbus and signs TotalCare separately with airlines, so the contracts are unlinked, whereas dual-source Trent 1000 and 700 deals are mostly linked with airlines.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: And that reflects, obviously, the Trent 700, which will be retiring and slowing down as the 7000 starts to ramp-up.
finding: RR's 2018 OE plateau assumes the Trent 700 winds down as the Trent 7000 ramps on the A330neo, along with ageing business-jet and regional lines.
trigger: Analyst noted 787 rate increase to 14, A350 ramp and A330neo entry in 2017 contradict an OE plateau
response: Explained plateau by Trent 700 and older corporate and regional engines retiring

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: our 2015 numbers are completely aligned with where Airbus are. As they look out into the future between '16 and '17, we'll make sure we are aligned with them. But really, it's a question, I think, for Airbus, in terms of what do we think we can sell, or what do they think they can sell of those aircraft.
finding: RR set Trent 700 build rates to match Airbus's A330 schedule and treated A330ceo demand as Airbus's forecast; that view failed within months.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: On the Civil market, what we're dealing with actually, in a way, is the negative effects of a very successful outcome last year of the Trent 7000 win that we had for the A330neo. The unfortunate thing is, however, there's a bridge between that product launching in 2017 and the run-out for the A330ceos over the next 4 years
finding: Winning the A330neo created a costly bridge for RR: Airbus's decision to re-engine hollowed out demand for the competed A330ceo while the neo was still years away.
trigger: Airbus A330neo launch (2014) with exclusive Trent 7000

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: it does get down to a choice for individual airlines on their individual routes which they may have a mix of engines or very often, they may be more exposed to us or GE on those engines. So I haven't seen any evidence at all that it's guarantee or aftermarket pricing. I think it's much more down to operational factors.
finding: RR rejected the idea that airlines park RR-powered aircraft before GE-powered ones because of TotalCare pricing, attributing parking to route and operational factors.
trigger: Analyst suggestion that TotalCare pricing made RR-powered aircraft more likely to be parked than GE-powered ones

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Clearly, the highlight was probably the Trent 900 engine order from Emirates halfway through the year; but also, towards the back end of the year, with orders from the Chinese airlines.
finding: RR's 2015 order highlights were a large Emirates Trent 900 (A380) order and Chinese airline orders.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Near term, we absolutely hear about high shipments of wide-body airplanes, a little bit of softness in passenger kilometers, and that does certainly put out more risk there in terms of risk of deferrals ... But interestingly, we're not actually seeing any changes from the airlines, particularly in the routes that they're flying
finding: In mid-2016 RR saw widebody deferral risk from softer traffic but no change in airline flying, so its aftermarket stayed secure.

speaker: Eric Schulz, President Civil Aerospace
quote: For the first time since a long, long time, we have had less order than deliveries within a year on either airframe or engines as it goes together normally. ... We believe in terms of business that we are quite insulated from it because as you know, we have a very, very massive order book.
finding: In 2016 RR saw orders fall below deliveries for the first time in a long while but judged itself insulated by its large backlog.

speaker: Eric Schulz, President Civil Aerospace
quote: The world has changed a little bit, Boeing and Airbus, just to take these 2. I think they have been impacted and hit in their reputation, but also in their numbers -- financial numbers of delays for airplane. And the problem that they have now, they are asking for demonstration of technology. So it's no longer a world where you can show a nice PowerPoint. You need to show products.
finding: RR says that after costly aircraft delays Boeing and Airbus now require demonstrated engine technology before selection, so engine makers must invest in demonstrators (such as UltraFan) ahead of any launch.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: because Airbus had some other issues with, and so at no stage have we actually been the pacing item in terms of delivery of the airplane. And we don't intend to be a pacing item as we look forward.
finding: RR aims never to be the pacing item for Airbus's A350 deliveries and notes that Airbus's own issues masked its ramp difficulties.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Boeing, I'm sure, will make a decision based on sound business principles. And they understand that if we're going to put an engine on that plane, it has to make business sense for us as well.
finding: RR signals to Boeing that it will not power a new airframe at uneconomic engine terms, so its participation is conditional on its own returns.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: I sat here before and talked about small changes in the order book are inevitable after a period of such exuberant ordering. But now that the 97K is in service, then we don't actually see any issues as far as ramp-up is concerned.
finding: RR played down airlines switching from A350-1000 to A350-900 as normal after exuberant ordering, with volumes still dominated by the XWB-84.
trigger: United and Cathay shift A350-1000 orders to -900
response: no material change to 97K backlog

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: after the exuberant period of ordering, we would absolutely expect to see the absolute size of our backlog decline. But as we look at airline customers and their plans to modernize their fleet, then subject to what happens in the competitions, we don't see a problem with replenishing our order book
finding: RR expected its widebody backlog to shrink after the ordering boom but to be replenished by fleet modernisation, subject to campaigns.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the potential narrowbody encroachment on these long-range routes is pretty much balanced by the widebody adoption on much shorter routes in populous parts of the world.
finding: RR did not see long-range narrowbodies eroding widebody demand, citing widebodies used on short routes as an offset.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: It does appear to be a product cycle thing or orders did get ahead. And what we're seeing is activity in terms of rescheduling rather than ordering new airplanes.
finding: By mid-2018 RR saw a slowdown in widebody orders, with airlines rescheduling deliveries rather than placing new orders.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: If you are customer who has a large fleet of Rolls-Royce powered, 787s then there is -- there has been an unacceptable level of disruption. However, we are working very constructively with each and every one of those customers on a customer by customer almost engine-by-engine basis
finding: RR handled Trent 1000 disruption customer by customer and engine by engine, planning each airline's fleet 12-18 months ahead.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So the Rolls-Royce share of the underlying growth in the market will tend to increase because of our younger fleet. And of course, we are growing our fleet and compared with competitor, we're actually shipping more large engines
finding: RR expected its widebody aftermarket share to grow because airlines retire older aircraft first and RR's fleet is younger.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So we do sincerely regret the disruption caused to those customers, and that's why we're spending all this money on fixing it because we want those airplanes all flying as soon as we possibly can.
finding: RR explicitly spends to get customers' aircraft flying, accepting large disruption costs to protect relationships.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: they concluded they needed a different mix of airplanes. So they made 2 decisions: to cancel outstanding -- some of the outstanding A380s and order some more smaller airplanes. And the good news is that the more smaller airplanes that they ordered, a mix of A330neos and A350s, of course, they are Rolls-Royce-powered aircraft.
finding: RR was sole source on the aircraft Emirates chose instead of the A380 (A330neo and A350), so the switch still went to RR.
trigger: Emirates cancels A380s
response: welcomed switch to RR-powered A330neo/A350

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we are totally committed to supporting those customers and keeping those Rolls-Royce-powered A380s in service for the next 20, 25 years, as long as it takes.
finding: When Airbus ended the A380, RR committed to support the installed Trent 900 fleet for 20-25 years, protecting aftermarket revenue.
trigger: Airbus A380 programme cancellation
response: commit to long-term fleet support

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: But I can assure you that our relationship with Boeing is very rich and very healthy. ... it's been a great opportunity for some of the Boeing engineers to wander around in Derby and get a much better idea of how our UltraFan program is developing.
finding: RR kept up its Boeing relationship after withdrawing from NMA and was showing UltraFan to Boeing engineers, keeping future Boeing selections open.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: It's true that that's one of the tools that we've used to help our customers through this time, and that's one of the things that we're paying for in these extra costs.
finding: RR leased replacement aircraft for Trent 1000 customers as a form of compensation, a small number for months at a time.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: our main focus is our customers because these are the people who've bet the farm on choosing Rolls-Royce engines for their Dreamliners, and we are causing some disruption. ... The number of aircraft on the ground today is about half of what it was a year ago
finding: RR acknowledged that 787 customers who chose its engine bore the disruption, and it prioritised customer recovery; AOG halved year on year.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: That's primarily due to the absence of the material aftermarket deposits that we saw in the first half last year. We had one big customer that converted onto a TotalCare arrangement. There was a buying fee attached to that
finding: RR charges a buy-in fee when a customer moves onto TotalCare, so a single conversion can move cash materially.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: After a period of ordering above trend, then we're seeing actual shipments of airframes align more closely with the underlying rate of growth of demand in the market. And that looks like about 500 engines over the next several years.
finding: RR read the 2019 widebody slowdown as a return to underlying demand after above-trend ordering, rather than a collapse.
trigger: airframer widebody build-rate cuts
response: reset delivery planning to ~500 engines/yr

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We didn't have the capacity to build those spare engines since one of the benefits of the slightly softer wide-body market we're seeing today is that gives us that capacity now to build those spare engines
finding: RR observed a softening widebody market in late 2019 and used freed production capacity to build spare engines for its grounded Trent 1000 fleet.
trigger: softer widebody market
response: redeploy production capacity to spare engines

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Build rates from airframers were adjusted during 2019, and as a consequence, our forward-looking projections of build rates for large wide-body engines has changed. In some ways, I think this build rate adjustment from the airframers has alleviated somewhat the concerns which were growing
finding: RR welcomed airframers' 2019 widebody build-rate cuts as easing oversupply, and accepted lower OE volumes as healthy for the market.
trigger: Airbus and Boeing cut widebody build rates in 2019
response: Lowered widebody engine volume projections

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Chinese airline customers, it's about 10% of our backlog today. Flights touching China is about 20% of our engine flying hours.
finding: Chinese airlines were about 10% of RR's order backlog and flights touching China about 20% of its flying hours, so COVID hit RR through China first.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: 2016, though, was the first time that we materially got into invoice discounting, and that was largely around the time when the airframers changed their own settlement terms.
finding: Airframers lengthened payment terms to engine suppliers around 2016, and RR responded with about GBP 1bn of year-end invoice discounting.
trigger: Airframers changed settlement terms (2016)
response: Started material invoice discounting

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The underlying demand is going to carry on growing along with economic growth. And I think with the changes in sort of public opinion around flying, airlines are going to want to deploy cleaner, more efficient airplanes as and when they can afford to do so.
finding: Before COVID RR expected widebody build rates to rise again as airlines replaced aircraft with more efficient ones.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we must also take difficult but necessary decisions to ensure that the group emerges from this period with an appropriate cost base for what will be a smaller commercial aerospace market, which may take several years to recover.
finding: By May 2020 RR had concluded that commercial aerospace would be structurally smaller for years and sized its cost base for that.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: our airframer customers have reduced aircraft production rates. And as a result, we now expect to deliver about 250 engines in 2020, down from our previous guidance of 450 announced in February.
finding: RR's widebody OE deliveries follow airframer build rates; COVID cuts almost halved its 2020 engine delivery plan.
trigger: Airbus and Boeing widebody production cuts
response: Cut 2020 engine delivery guidance from 450 to 250

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we've been working closely with our airframe customers, particularly Airbus and Boeing, to reschedule engine deliveries to match their reductions in build rates. We expect to remain at lower levels until at least 2022.
finding: RR follows Airbus and Boeing build-rate cuts by rescheduling engine deliveries, and expected lower OE volumes until at least 2022.
trigger: Airbus and Boeing cut widebody build rates
response: Rescheduled engine deliveries to match

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Previously, we had used this to pull forward cash due from airframers who have fairly long payment terms. This provided us with short-term liquidity.
finding: Airframers impose long payment terms on RR for OE engines; RR had used invoice discounting to fund the gap and ended it in 2020.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We don't expect to see OE demand recover for several years, so a consolidation of our manufacturing facilities is inevitable.
finding: RR expected widebody OE demand to stay low for several years and consolidated factories on that view.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: in many of these contracts, we have minimum utilizations and so on. And so I don't think there's been any material impact whatsoever from actual renegotiations. We're trying to support our customers through this phase as much as we can, but we've also got our own business to run.
finding: RR relied on minimum-utilisation clauses in its service contracts and resisted material renegotiation despite airline distress in 2020.
trigger: Airlines seeking relief for low load factors
response: Held contract terms; limited support

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: there are some issues around OE concession payments, which depend on the timing of new aircraft deliveries to airlines and either outside of our control.
finding: RR's concession payments to airlines, which cut the effective OE price, are due when the airframer delivers and are outside RR's control.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: our flying hour rates are a portion of the costs, but they're by no means the only costs for an airline. There's the financing costs and many other operational costs. So hour rates are a very small part, actually, of airline operating costs
finding: RR argues its service rates are a small part of airline operating cost, which it uses to justify holding prices in a downturn.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We're seeing airlines saying that they are just not able to pay minimum flying hour per contractual terms right now, and we understand that. But we are building up a debtor's balance that you'll see at the year-end, therefore, of overdue debt.
finding: RR tolerated overdue minimum flight-hour payments from distressed airlines, taking on credit risk rather than enforcing terms.
trigger: Airline cash crisis
response: Allowed overdue debt to build; most customers still paying

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Now while the rollout of vaccines and testing gives us good reason to look forward to the recovery, the impact on our industry is severe, and OE demand is expected to remain low for several years.
finding: RR expected widebody OE demand to stay depressed for several years after COVID, which argues against near-term new-engine launches.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: A number of our customers have had challenges with their liquidity and financial stability. We have responded commercially with relaxations of certain terms and conditions, and we're keeping a close watch on the customer credit risk.
finding: RR supported distressed airline customers by relaxing contract terms, while booking an GBP 86m provision for customer credit risk.
trigger: Airline liquidity crisis
response: Relaxed terms and conditions; GBP 86m credit provision

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the newer, more efficient aircraft and engines are the ones that are recovering faster than the more mature ones. And that's, of course, driven by the economics for airlines as they look to minimize their operating costs.
finding: In the downturn airlines flew their newest, most efficient widebodies first, so RR's young Trent XWB fleet recovered first (about 60% by end-2020).

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: driven primarily by the OE concession payments that we talked about shortly before Christmas as a backlog of 787 aircraft are delivered by Boeing, and that triggers payments from us to airlines. The timing of this is completely outside of our control.
finding: RR pays OE concessions to airlines when Boeing delivers 787s, so Boeing's delivery backlog becomes RR's cash outflow at Boeing's pace.
trigger: Boeing 787 delivery backlog
response: Accepted concession outflow timing set by Boeing

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: on our OE volumes, we are completely dependent on the airframe build rates. And I think in 2020, we demonstrated a certain amount of ... flexibility being able to respond to that and manage our supply chain accordingly.
finding: RR sets its OE output by airframer build rates and adjusts its supply chain to match.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we have been working with customers to accommodate some of their short-term financial challenges ... that might manifest itself in terms of a period of lower per hour rate at given types of usage of an engine compensated by higher rates a little way down the road.
finding: When airlines were in distress, RR cut flight-hour rates in the short term only in exchange for higher rates later, protecting the lifetime value of the contract.
trigger: Airline restructurings and bankruptcies during COVID
response: Temporary lower $/hour rates traded for higher future rates

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: that announcement for Airbus has been a little welcoming, and we're delighted with that. It's a very welcome pull forward as far as we're concerned of growth in demand for our engines.
finding: RR welcomed the Airbus A350 freighter launch as extra demand for its sole-source Trent XWB, without needing new investment.
trigger: Airbus launched the A350 freighter (EIS 2025)
response: Welcomed it as extra XWB demand; no new capacity needed

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: around GBP 300 million of original equipment concession outflows are now expected to fall in 2022 rather than 2021 due to the delayed delivery of aircraft for which we have already supplied engines.
finding: RR's OE concession cash (payments to airlines on engine sales) is triggered by airframer deliveries, so airframer delivery delays shift RR's cash between years.
trigger: Boeing 787 delivery delays
response: Concession outflows of about GBP 300m slip from 2021 into 2022

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: most of the concessions are related to the 787 program. And we've had a bit of concession flow this year on the final deliveries for 380s. But apart from that, it's now going forward pretty much all related to Boeing 787 deliveries. And obviously, we're somewhat at the mercy of Boeing's production plans.
finding: RR's OE concession liabilities sit mainly on the Trent 1000/787, and it describes itself as dependent on Boeing's production decisions for their timing.
trigger: Boeing 787 delivery delays
response: Accepts timing risk; concession outflows follow Boeing deliveries

speaker: Dominic Horwood, Civil Aerospace services
quote: As our fleets mature, as we move decisively beyond the launch phases, as we reach the first renewals of some of those early contracts, we see opportunity to drive that together.
finding: RR uses the first renewals of launch-era service contracts to reprice.

speaker: Arvind Balan, CFO Civil Aerospace
quote: We see OE growth at mid-teens CAGR over the medium term. Most of that is driven by the Airbus programs and by some return of the 787 production.
finding: RR's OE growth depends mainly on Airbus rates and a 787 production recovery.

speaker: Unknown Executive (Civil Aerospace leadership)
quote: And clearly, our reputation took a knock on the statement on the 787. We've worked very closely with those customers through that period or for disruption.
finding: RR concedes the Trent 1000 durability crisis damaged its reputation with 787 customers.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: Since then, we've seen those further delays in 787 deliveries and the associated concession payments. Important to note though, that's largely offset by a reduction in concession receipts on new Trent 1000 deliveries as Boeing itself manages its own inventory.
finding: RR's OE cash flows are tied to Boeing 787 delivery timing, so a 787 delivery halt shifts concession payments and receipts.

quote: So I think when we look back to 2019, China was around -- China Airlines were about 17% of engine flying hours. They're around 11% at the moment, and they're at 40% of 2019 level.

quote: And I see huge demand for air travel in China on wide-body jets. And I don't actually see the Chinese getting those jets from anywhere else right now other than the Western suppliers.
finding: RR kept serving Chinese airlines, betting they depend on Western widebodies.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: In Civil Aerospace, for example, we set up a task force to review all the large engine LTSA contracts. We are also working to lower our product cost and drive up the margins in contracts to ensure we achieve the returns that are aligned with the risks that we take.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Our Airbus targets, they are in line with our production targets as well. So we are totally aligned.

quote: there are different rates depending on how it's flown. And maybe in the past, people were more forgiving on how it's flown. We're being much tougher on making sure the contractual terms are enforced within that.

quote: We have an onerous contract provision of GBP 1.4 billion. We must rebalance these contracts. A strong Rolls-Royce will be a much better partner to our customers and deliver superior service. I have personally spoken with each and every customer with which we have an onerous contract.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Our immediate focus has been on the 6 most onerous airline customers, who represent more than half of the onerous contract provision.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Thinking about what we do, we are a long-term partner, more than airframers are, right? Because you sell the plane, at least, for that transaction you are done. You sell the plane, our engagement is still another 15, 20 years on that plane, right?

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: We also have a new opportunity to grow in the freighter market due to the launch of Airbus A350 freighter.
finding: RR benefits from Airbus derivative launches on its sole-source platforms without having to launch a new engine.

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: the largest being an outflow associated with concessions, totaling around GBP 800 million across the period. There are 2 roughly equal parts to this. First, deferred Boeing concession payments

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: Second, an impact from historical agreements with customers to delay concession payments owed to them. These deals date back several years, in some cases, more than a decade.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Our plans are totally in line with Boeing and Airbus plans. They are totally aligned.

quote: Our competitiveness has been proven this year as we've won major orders, for example, from Air India and Air France, more recently with [ EVA ], Egyptair and Ethiopian Airlines.
finding: RR won widebody engine campaigns in 2023 with airlines including Air India and Air France.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: I actually met with Tim Clark last week. He's very happy where this is going to go. He cannot wait for that to come to the market.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: our pricing, one correction on that question, it's not an ambition. We are actually -- we have been implementing it. So it is an implementation for good 12 months. There is no new ambition, we will continuously implement that pricing framework that Airbus is well aware and well aligned.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO

response: RR says it was one engine behind and not holding up airframers

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO

finding: RR systematically reopened loss-making airline service contracts, finishing all significant ones by mid-2025.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: some of our customers have been disappointed with Trent 1000 time on wing issues. And we have a big task force dealing with it.

response: Task force and BoM B upgrade; RR says relationships improved through renegotiation

speaker: John Rose, CEO

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: there'll be a GBP 40 million to GBP 50 million negative effect year-on-year, partly for spend reasons and partly because of more R&D being expensed, particularly associated with the XWB engine Airbus A350.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director

quote: We continue to have net interest costs despite average net cash. And that's due to the low yield we have on cash balances compared to the funding costs on the debt. But we value the financial flexibility that, that gives us.
finding: RR knowingly carried a negative interest spread on gross cash and debt because it values financial flexibility.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: in terms of new customer finance improvement, it remains pretty modest. And that's basically because the wholesale markets and the ECAs have provided most of the capacity that the market has needed. And so there's been much less recourse to the manufacturers.
finding: RR's new customer-financing commitments stayed modest in 2010 because capital markets and export credit agencies funded aircraft, so airlines leaned less on engine makers.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: on a recurring basis, we can afford to spend what we need to spend to generate that growth. And we'll also be moderately cash positive on the way.
finding: RR's 2010 posture was to fund growth investment from internal cash while staying modestly cash positive.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: over the three years 2008, 2009, and '10, we've spent about GBP 3 billion on investment capital R&D and the like, IT, as well as GBP 700 million on dividends and payments to shareholders And along the way, we've also improved our average cash position by GBP 500 million.
finding: Over 2008-2010 RR invested about GBP 3bn, paid GBP 700m to shareholders and still raised average cash by GBP 500m, which shows its self-funded, cash-preserving posture through the recession.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: on the balance sheet, we've always made a feature of financial strength. And that continues to be the case. We have appetite to grow, in particular, our Energy and Marine businesses. In time we'll see what opportunities we identify, whether those are inorganic or organic.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: we're not incurring costs on our own dollar. I mean this is still a funded program... the engine, which is where we're 60-40 with GE.
finding: On the F136 alternate JSF engine, developed with GE on a 60-40 split, RR stressed that it was not self-funding: it takes part only while the customer pays.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: this level of investment will capitalize the business to be able to deliver a much higher number of Trent engines. So I think we're looking at sort of 2 to 3-year increase in CapEx that should tail off somewhat after that.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: we've got sufficient resources to pay for our share of the Tognum acquisition from our own internal resources. We don't need to raise any more money, and the credit rating is secure.
finding: RR funded its roughly GBP 1.5bn share of Tognum from cash without raising capital and protected its credit rating, preferring internally funded deals.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: the fact that we've had 3 new wide-bodied engines in very close succession, and the results in the cost increases as you said... which are inevitable when you are launching a significant new product.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO

finding: RR Civil Aerospace made GBP 499m underlying profit on GBP 5.6bn revenue in 2011, a margin of about 8.9%.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: we spend about GBP 1 billion on average on R&D growth. About 1/2 of that is what we fund privately. It’s somewhere in the order of 4% to 5% of turnover.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: we only capitalize between engine certification and entering into service. And you will recall, the T1000 went into service in September last year. So we've stopped capitalizing the Trent 1000.
finding: RR capitalises development only between certification and entry into service, so its R&D charge swings with the programme cycle (the Trent 1000 stopped being capitalised after its 2011 EIS).

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: CapEx and intangibles of GBP 775 million reflects continued investment as we tool up to meet the rising load... 80% cash conversion in 2011 demonstrates good cash conversion in the underlying business. But again, I expect this to be lower as we move into 2012
finding: RR spent GBP 775m on capex and intangibles in 2011 with 80% cash conversion, and expected conversion to fall in 2012 as it invested for the ramp.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: OE revenues growth is ahead of aftermarket, which is primarily due to the leveraging effect of large engine deliveries. You can see that engine deliveries were up 14%... Aftermarket revenues, up at 10%, slightly higher than where we guided at the half year and this is predominantly to a number of time and material contracts switching to TCA.
finding: In 2011 RR civil engine deliveries rose 14% and aftermarket revenue 10%, helped by airlines switching from time-and-material to TotalCare.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: Upon completion, and assuming we gain approval, the order book will reduce by about GBP 4 billion. We will receive GBP 1.5 billion as our share at closing. There will be a small reduction in 2012 revenues, and profits for the full year would rise by GBP 140 million.
finding: The IAE exit was to bring RR GBP 1.5bn at closing (as stated on the call) and about GBP 140m a year of extra profit, at the cost of about GBP 4bn of order book.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: we used to have 1/3 of all the revenue that came from IAE. We've monetized some of that by selling our equity stake. We continue to be a supplier... we continue to get a share of the aftermarket, which is effectively a royalty stream, which is obviously based on engine flying hours.
finding: After the IAE sale RR earned supplier margins on V2500 parts and assembly plus a flying-hour royalty on the fleet in place of its one-third equity share.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: some pull forward as part of the deal of what we've done in terms of how we structured over the 15-year period effectively... GBP 140 million in the first 12 month and then declining over a period of time
finding: RR confirmed that the IAE payment stream runs over about 15 years, pulled forward: GBP 140m in the first 12 months, then declining.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: 70% of our aftermarket now sort of captured in some form of long-term service agreements. You will see that on the newer programs, that's probably closer to around 90%. But on the older programs it may be around sort of 50% or even lower in some of them.
finding: RR captured about 70% of its aftermarket under long-term service agreements: about 90% on new programmes and 50% or less on older ones.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: We ended the year with GBP 869 million of net cash. speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: broadly about 2/3 of our aftermarket revenues are on some form of long-term services agreement with the remaining 1/3 on T&M... whereas, of course, in T&M, the ability for the operator to either defer or reduce the work scope means that you can see a bit more volatility.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: a significant higher proportion of new business tends to be on some form of LTSA, and of course, we get the usual effects, the TCA accounting providing services, the timing differences between recognition of income and costs and payments of -- cash payments and receipts.
finding: Because most new engines come with TotalCare, rising deliveries build a TotalCare receivable (revenue recognised ahead of cash). The analyst cited a GBP 168m H1 2012 rise, which RR accepted.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: it's not as if it's going to change overnight and next year all of a sudden we're just going to be looking at CapEx that's sort of in line with depreciation or something. We continue to invest in a growth cycle.
finding: RR signalled that capex would stay above depreciation for years through the growth cycle, softening its 2011 view that it would tail off after 2-3 years.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: the IAE transaction at the half-year, resulted in about a $1.5 billion of proceeds or GBP 940 million or so... the one-off profits at the time of about GBP 700 million... we ended up with about GBP 92 million, so slightly better than we thought, really reflecting higher part sales and more profitable part sales
finding: The IAE exit brought USD 1.5bn (about GBP 940m), a one-off gain of about GBP 700m, and GBP 92m of H2 2012 supplier profit, above the GBP 70m planned.

quote: we've seen some margin progression, better margins, up to 12.2%, so that's a 1.5 percentage point progression... Of that 1.5 percentage point progression, about 0.4% is from the underlying business and 1.1% is from the effects of -- trading effects from now Tognum and IAE.
finding: RR's 2012 group margin rose to 12.2%, but only 0.4 points came from the underlying business; 1.1 points came from the Tognum and IAE deals.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: underlying profit up 24% to GBP 1.4 billion with margins improving by 150 basis points to 12.2%. Payment to shareholders, up 11% to 19.5p.
finding: RR kept raising shareholder payments (up 11% to 19.5p for 2012) alongside a 150bp margin gain, even while investing heavily.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO

quote: the TCA net debtor, the increase of GBP 360 million... we're sort of getting about 85% to 90% penetration on TotalCare and sort of linked contracts. quote: the CapEx requirements of the business are significant. And they won't be going down rapidly anytime soon because we continue to invest for that growth... speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: We will continue to invest in R&D and CapEx to support the execution and growth of the business... the margins that we make on the OE equipment, the margins that we make on the aftercare, the way that the accounting works for that in terms of the profit versus the cash

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: CapEx in software was GBP 650 million, and included major projects such as new test beds in the U.S. and Germany, new blade and disc facilities in the U.K. and U.S. and a new test and assembly facility in Brazil.

quote: On the issue about launch costs, yes, of course, we know about them. They're contracted a number of years in advance. Lead times are typically sort of 18 months, 2 years, right out to sort of 5, 6, 7 as a set of delivery

doc: Special Call (sale of Energy business to Siemens)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: The total consideration is GBP 985 million paid in cash at closing. This is split GBP 785 million for the acquisition of the business and GBP 200 million in relation to a 25-year licensing agreement, granting Siemens access to relevant aero-derivative gas turbine technology
finding: RR sold its Energy business for GBP 985m in cash, including GBP 200m for a 25-year licence of its aero-derivative gas turbine technology, which shows it will monetise aero technology through licensing.

quote: First of all, we said in our RNS that we have no plans for any material M&A at present. Secondly, we said that we would return the proceeds from the sale of our Energy division by way of a share buyback

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: We've got to drive our CapEx down, and we're talking about 4% rather than the current 4.9% in the 3- to 5-year time period. speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: We commit to aircraft programs with people like Boeing and Airbus that will run for many, many years. We need to make sure they have the confidence in us that we will be around to fulfill our obligations

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: we have committed to a progressive dividend policy in line with underlying growth. We've returned over GBP 1.65 billion to shareholders over the last 5 years.
finding: RR had a progressive dividend policy and returned over GBP 1.65bn to shareholders in the five years to 2014.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: when I look at our organic investment opportunities, the human capital, that we just have not got enough people at the moment to go and spend some of that. ... So we've announced a GBP 1 billion share buyback.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: underpinned by the GBP 60 billion order book that we have in Aerospace -- Civil Aerospace, of which some GBP 30 billion is related to the Trent XWB.
finding: RR's civil aerospace order book was about GBP 60bn in mid-2014, about half of it Trent XWB.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: We do not take as much margin on a higher-risk transaction as on a lower-risk transaction. It's driven predominantly around the counterparty risk and the fleet fit, importantly, which is how essential are the aircraft that we are providing to the fleet.
