speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: the impact of adjustments to cost have been around plus or minus 4% on in-year civil profits. A 1% change on our portfolio in cost assumptions has an in-year impact of about GBP 30 million.
finding: TotalCare cost-estimate revisions have moved RR civil profits by about plus or minus 4% a year; a 1% change in portfolio cost assumptions is worth about GBP 30m in-year.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: the value that you -- generally was assumed by the market for our IAE business was a little lower than we actually realized.
finding: RR says the value it realised from its IAE exit was higher than the market had generally assumed.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: So if I break it down, our civil spend runs what, Mark, about 5% or so?
finding: RR's civil aerospace net R&D ran at about 5% of revenue, against about 2-2.5% in Marine and about 7% at Power Systems.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: a very mature program like an RB211, frankly, the estimation risk is very small and, of course, it's slightly larger that we allow for -- on a new program like -- whether it's XWB or 1000.
finding: RR holds back more margin as estimation risk on new engine programmes (XWB, Trent 1000) than on mature ones, a few percentage points, releasing it as experience builds.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: Cash outflow and CapEx was GBP 303 million ... Intangibles of GBP 239 million primarily includes GBP 40 million of software; GBP 28 million of contractual aftermarket rights ... GBP 91 million of participation payments on civil programs; and GBP 57 million of capitalized development costs.
finding: In H1 2014 RR spent GBP 303m on capex and GBP 239m on intangibles, including GBP 91m of participation payments to risk-sharing partners on civil programmes and GBP 28m of aftermarket rights, mainly Trent 1000.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: The TotalCare net debtor has increased GBP 165 million, reflecting the sale of engines we linked to aftermarket contracts, mainly Trent 700.
finding: Linked Trent 700 sales increased RR's TotalCare net debtor by GBP 165m in H1 2014, showing how linked OE sales absorb cash.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: we have seen better trading from V2500. And of course, it's got a big installed base. So we'll continue to see that coming.
finding: RR reported better V2500 trading than expected from the programme's large installed base, which supports its continuing V2500 income.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: our dividend policy is really a progressive policy that moves broadly in line with earnings growth, I mean mechanically from that, you could infer that we should have no increase on the grounds that we've guided no growth for this year. But again, we said this is temporary
finding: RR kept a progressive dividend policy, raising the interim payment 5% to 9p despite guiding flat earnings, to signal confidence.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: On profit, we are now expecting a 15% to 20% increase, which is driven mainly by an improvement in life cycle costs. ... This catch-up will flatter Civil's 2014 margins. Over the last 4 years, Civil's margins have averaged around 12%, and you should expect Civil margins in 2015 to return to this sort of level.
finding: RR's Civil profit rose 15-20% in 2014 mainly from lower TotalCare life-cycle cost estimates, including a one-off catch-up, with civil margins averaging about 12% and guided back to that level in 2015.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: On cash, we've guided around a GBP 780 million inflow similar to last year. We are now guiding at GBP 350 million inflow
finding: RR cut its 2014 group free cash flow guidance from about GBP 780m to GBP 350m in October 2014.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: The ramp-up in OE deliveries, where linked, will naturally increase to debtor as do shop visits, which reduce the creditor. So a key point to note is that the peak debtor will start declining as OE deliveries level off, and cash conversion will improve.
finding: Under RR's linked TotalCare accounting the net contract debtor grows with the OE ramp and shop visits, and only peaks once OE deliveries level off, so cash lags profit in growth phases.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: the reduction in '15 is a combination of the factors that have driven '14 higher and then all the other things that are going on, whether that's launch costs, launch pricing, unlinked, offset by cost reductions
finding: RR attributes the 2015 civil margin dip to new-engine launch costs, launch pricing and unlinked contracts, partly offset by cost reduction.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: What we said is that we are looking at additional restructuring as we seek to rationalize and control our costs.
finding: In October 2014 RR announced it was preparing additional restructuring, not included in guidance, as a response to the slowdown.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: In the Aerospace business, I'm spending billions of pounds employing brilliant people, and they are driving 1% fuel-efficient improvement in a year on average
finding: RR says it spends billions of pounds on aerospace engineering to achieve roughly 1% a year fuel-efficiency improvement, which shows how costly incremental engine gains are.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: It's versus EBIT. ... Free cash flow of EBIT, yes.
finding: RR's medium-term cash guidance was set as roughly 80% conversion of EBIT into free cash flow.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: when you start talking about 2015, again, things that you're familiar with would be the launch of the XWB, which is a lot of launch cost, lowish volumes and unlinked contracts.
finding: RR accepts that the Trent XWB entry into service carries heavy launch costs, low early volumes and unlinked contracts, which depress civil margins in the launch year.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: about GBP 200 million was due to low revenue, about GBP 100 million has come from lower deposits, just reflecting order intake after deferrals that we're seeing and people not ordering at the time. And then the other GBP 100 million again was inventory.
finding: The 2014 free cash flow guidance cut of about GBP 400m came from lower revenue (GBP 200m), lower customer deposits as orders were deferred (GBP 100m) and inventory (GBP 100m).

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: First of all, OE makes much lower margins and certainly, in launch phases will be -- can be and will be at a loss because you've got the learning curve. I'm talking cash.
finding: RR's CFO confirms that new-engine OE sales are cash loss-making in the launch phase because of the learning curve, with profits recovered later in the aftermarket.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: we talked about R&D being around about 5% and trending lower as we got the benefit of leveraging an increased volume. And on CapEx, we talk about driving it towards 4% of sale.
finding: RR's medium-term planning assumes R&D at about 5% of sales, trending lower with volume, and capex driven towards 4% of sales.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We've guided 2015 revenue to between GBP 13.4 billion and GBP 14.4 billion and profit to between GBP 1.4 billion and GBP 1.55 billion. We see free cash flow at around GBP 200 million... We expect both CapEx and net R&D will be lower in both absolute terms and over time as a percentage of revenue.
finding: RR's February 2015 guidance planned capex and net R&D to fall in absolute terms and as a share of revenue.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the growth that we will see during 2015 is primarily on products that have been launched, the XWB engine and the Trent 1000, and they are not cash-generative at the moment in terms of the initial OE sale. In fact, there will be cash losses on some of those engines.
finding: RR sold its new XWB and Trent 1000 engines at an OE cash loss during launch, so civil growth hurt near-term cash.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: These are important points. To build our installed base, we have to invest in higher levels of working capital. We're also trying to manage the customer deposits where possible to mitigate that.
finding: RR funds installed-base growth partly through working capital and uses customer deposits to offset it.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We also had increased Civil R&D investment, and it was actually our peak investment that we've ever made. So the investment in technology was at its highest level ever last year.
finding: RR's civil R&D reached an all-time peak in 2014 during the XWB and Trent 1000-TEN development.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: It's expected, as we've told you, to generate savings of GBP 50 million this year and GBP 80 million on an ongoing basis.
finding: RR's November 2014 aerospace restructuring targeted GBP 50m of savings in 2015 and GBP 80m a year after that.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: we saw low utilization and saw lower times and materials for older installed engines, primarily the RB2011, which was down 24%, but this is now actually less than -- around 10% of our revenue base. And it was largely offset by growth in our Trent fleet, which was up 6%, which is more than half of our revenue base.
finding: In 2014 RR's legacy RB211 aftermarket fell 24% while Trent fleet services grew 6%, showing the shift to the Trent installed base.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We also had a GBP 150 million retrospective benefit from better profitability in our TotalCare contracts. And that reflected a combination of factors: our cost improvements, changing operating patterns, which, by the way, are driven also by the same factors.
finding: RR booked GBP 150m of catch-up TotalCare profit in 2014 as lifecycle cost improvements raised contract profitability.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Second is the focus we have on life-cycle cost. This is hugely important as product life cost can be 3, 4x the OE cost of an engine.
finding: RR estimates an engine's lifecycle support cost at 3-4 times its OE cost, which is why its cost programme targets lifecycle cost.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Firstly, OE margins will improve as we exit the launch phase, which is higher cost and lower pricing. We'll also begin to generate growing amounts of cash from our aftermarket revenues as the OE curve begins to flatten out and the aftermarket becomes a bigger part of our business through increased engine flying hours.
finding: RR expects OE margins to recover after launch as costs fall and prices rise, with cash then driven by aftermarket flying hours.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: We have around 4,300 engines in service, predominantly operating in North America and Europe. Turn the clock forward 10 years, and you can see that our fleet is projected to grow to 7,500 engines... Over the lifetime of an engine, service revenue is around 4x higher than OE revenue.
finding: RR expected its large-engine fleet to grow from about 4,300 to 7,500 engines in 10 years, with lifetime service revenue about four times OE revenue.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: I think the average over the last 5 or 6 years is probably more in the 50 to 75 sort of range... looking at the cost of the spare parts, the costs particularly of the intervention of shop visits, and then all the good work on time on wing.
finding: RR's annual TotalCare catch-up gains normally run at GBP 50-75m, driven by lower spare-part and shop-visit costs and longer time on wing.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: this is where the business should be able to get to on a medium-term basis once we've met certain criteria... when we see the OE volumes flattening off and we've got the initial launch losses on the XWB and Trent 1000, in particular, were through that launch period. And the aftermarket service business begins to grow.
finding: RR's medium-term margin targets depended on OE volumes levelling off and the XWB and Trent 1000 launch losses ending.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: So our expectation is that we will complete the buyback during this year, yes... And our expectation is we will, provided nothing really happens in the market, that we'll continue on that rate.
finding: In February 2015 RR planned to complete the full buyback in 2015, a plan it dropped in July after the Trent 700 warning.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Yes. So on FX, we have a hedge book that is roughly 4 to 5 years cover. It's about GBP 25 billion roughly, with an average rate of about 161.
finding: RR hedges its dollar revenue exposure four to five years ahead (about GBP 25bn at ~1.61), smoothing transactional FX.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Given the weaker near-term cash outlook, we will discontinue the share buyback program having completed GBP 500 million of the planned GBP 1 billion program in the first half of the year.
finding: When the cash outlook weakened RR stopped its buyback halfway (GBP 500m of GBP 1bn) to protect liquidity, reversing its February plan to complete it in 2015.
trigger: Trent 700 and offshore headwinds
response: Buyback halted at GBP 500m

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Free cash flow for 2015 is now expected to be between negative GBP 150 million and a positive GBP 150 million.
finding: RR cut its 2015 free cash flow guidance to about breakeven (-/+ GBP 150m) from about GBP 200m in February.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: In total, we expect these changes to Trent 700 demand, which benefits from linked accounting that ties aftermarket margins to engine delivery, to reduce Civil Aerospace profits by around GBP 250 million compared to 2015. Now it's important to remember that there are still several open campaigns for Trent 700, and we don't yet know how many engines we'll win.
finding: The A330ceo run-out was expected to cost RR about GBP 250m of 2016 civil profit, with several Trent 700 campaigns still open against the rival engine.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the GBP 250 million, it is made up of 3 components: the volume effect which, as you know, is linked and, therefore, includes an element of OE and aftermarket; the pricing effect... both of those 2 effects are roughly the same size... and then the spare engines, which, although smaller, is essentially the loss of volume of relatively higher-profit engines.
finding: The GBP 250m Trent 700 hit split roughly equally between volume and price, plus a smaller loss of higher-margin spare-engine sales.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: it's still selling 20 years later and an OE and has at least another 20 years of aftermarket to give... the indications on XWB, on all of the work that we've done, all the analysis that we've done, is that the XWB will be twice as successful as the previously most successful engine.
finding: RR's reference lifecycle is the Trent 700: about 20 years of OE sales plus 20 more of aftermarket; it expected the XWB to be worth twice as much.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Our financial strength is really important to us, and we are very focused on maintaining investment-grade rating. One of the things that we did during the first half was to refinance, as many of you know, our revolving credit facility, and we increased our overall to GBP 1.5 billion.
finding: RR placed maintaining its investment-grade rating ahead of shareholder returns and enlarged its RCF to GBP 1.5bn.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: But we're impacted by quite a change in mix between more profitable linked deliveries on the Trent 700 and 900, which were replaced by Trent 1000 and XWB, which were unlinked and, therefore, on which we do not book in advance aftermarket profit.
finding: RR's reported profit fell as deliveries shifted from linked Trent 700/900 (aftermarket profit booked upfront) to unlinked Trent 1000/XWB.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: It will be generating cash through the next 40 or 50 years. And when we think about that, the cumulative cash flow that we expect from that program is actually twice as great as the best-ever program in Rolls-Royce's history, which is the Trent 700.
finding: RR expects the sole-source Trent XWB to generate cash for 40-50 years, with lifetime cumulative cash about twice the Trent 700's.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We have a robust balance sheet today, but we do need to be prudent, and we don't want to create any unnecessary uncertainty. And that's the main reason why we canceled our share buyback program... And so maintaining a progressive dividend policy is essential and an important building block in underpinning that confidence in the value in the future.
finding: In July 2015 RR cancelled its buyback to protect liquidity but called a progressive dividend essential; by November the dividend itself was under review.
trigger: July 2015 profit warning
response: Cancelled buyback; kept progressive dividend (later reviewed)

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Our aftermarket revenue increased by 7% in the first half, and that reflects good growth in wide-body aftermarket, which increased 9% even after we saw some lower revenue from the RB211 and Trent 500, but we also saw a weaker regional aftermarket as well.
finding: RR's wide-body aftermarket was still growing at 9% in H1 2015, before the legacy parking effects appeared.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: R&D was another headwind in the first half. R&D spend was higher for new programs, including the Trent 7000, the -- but also the Trent XWB and the -TEN on the Trent 1000.
finding: RR funded several concurrent derivative programmes (Trent 7000, XWB variants, Trent 1000-TEN), which pushed up R&D in 2015.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: And R&D spend is likely to be a little higher than the GBP 750 million, but that's factored into our profit guidance.
finding: RR's 2015 civil/group R&D spend guidance was slightly above GBP 750m.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: It will be years yet before the XWB actually overtakes the Trent 700 in cash flow generation... Now most of this cash flow is beyond 2025 on the XWB... So just to remind you that most of this cash flow is aftermarket.
finding: Most of the XWB's value is aftermarket cash beyond 2025, about 10 years after entry into service, showing how late RR's returns on a new engine arrive.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We actually see now that the long-term TotalCare net debt will peak much earlier at a lower level than we've previously indicated, so probably between GBP 2.1 billion and GBP 2.3 billion over the next 18 months or so.
finding: Because Trent 700 linked volumes fell, RR's TotalCare net debtor (profit booked ahead of cash) would peak earlier, at GBP 2.1-2.3bn.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: my view is actually that achieving those sort of levels on margins and certainly cash conversion of those levels is absolutely what we are aiming for and targeting. I'm not going to give a new time frame... That's clearly been interrupted and pushed back, as you said, by the Trent 700, 40% reduction in volumes basically.
finding: RR kept its medium-term margin and cash-conversion targets but withdrew the 2018 timing after the A330ceo rate cut.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: So I mean, the big drivers still, remember, of our aftermarket is installed thrust on Trent. And that's the key. It was up in double-digit terms in the first half of the year.
finding: Trent installed thrust, RR's main aftermarket driver, grew at double-digit rates in H1 2015.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: And I think we've talked about that number in the past at around GBP 200 million, I think, on an annualized basis... that royalty will remain a constant factor, that will obviously be constant in terms of pricing, but it'll be affected by engine flying hours.
finding: RR's V2500 royalty from IAE was about GBP 200m a year at fixed pricing, varying only with V2500 flying hours.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Remember, there's absolutely no difference between the cash flow between a linked and unlinked contract. The reason it has an effect on cash flow is simply the profit to cash flow movement. So in absolute terms, the cash income is really driven by the -- primarily by the engine flying hours
finding: RR's linked vs unlinked accounting changes profit timing, not cash; cash income depends on engine flying hours.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Now, our assessment of the profit headwinds for 2016, however, totaled some GBP 650 million in total, and that equates to a further GBP 350 million of headwinds compared with what we talked about in July.
finding: RR's second 2015 profit warning raised expected 2016 profit headwinds to GBP 650m, GBP 350m more than in July.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: No, not in general, overall. We still have sufficient cushion on those programs, but of course, as you know, we undertake actually a very detailed review and we will look at specific valuation reserves against individual airlines, that's a normal part of our process.
finding: RR did not expect a general TotalCare asset write-down from groundings, relying on programme cushions and airline-specific reserves.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: when we go out, 4 or 5 years looking at cash conversion, north of 80% and I've said before, some years that may well be north of 100% is absolutely right... as the aftermarket installed base grows on the XWB and Trent 1000
finding: RR targeted cash conversion above 80% (sometimes above 100%) within four to five years as the XWB and Trent 1000 aftermarket built up.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: it's just common sense to tell people that, of course, we're considering the strength of the balance sheet and we're considering the dividend in the light of changes that will be evident to dividend cover.
finding: After the November warning RR openly put the dividend under review to protect the balance sheet, reversing its July stance that a progressive dividend was essential.
trigger: GBP 650m 2016 profit headwinds
response: Dividend placed under board review

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Yes, I mean we view that by maintaining the credit rating at the kind of level that we're at, at the moment, is an important part of our financial policy.
finding: RR treated holding its credit rating as a core financial-policy objective when considering dividends and investment.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: we have given previously sort of guidance that CapEx and R&D over time may come down as a percentage of revenue. However, I don't think they are going to that change much in... We will continue to invest as we think we need to do in terms of new products.
finding: Under cash pressure RR protected absolute capex and R&D for new products and cut fixed costs instead, a change from February's guidance that both would fall in absolute terms.
trigger: Profit warnings and rating pressure
response: Protect new-product investment; target fixed costs

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So restructuring in a GBP 150 million to GBP 200 million per annum that we expect in terms of cost savings from this during 2017.
finding: RR's November 2015 restructuring aimed at GBP 150-200m a year of savings from 2017.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So in total, Rolls-Royce commanded about an 8% share of the market opportunity once upon a time... At the moment, we retain a cash-generative business, supplying modules for a while, and for many years into the future, to enjoy an aftermarket revenue.
finding: After exiting IAE, RR kept a cash-generative V2500 position (modules for a while, aftermarket for many years); its historic narrow-body share via the JV was only about 8%.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The OE costs are coming down with the learning curve effects. The prices are going up because we have gone beyond the launch pricing effects. And the aftermarket revenues are starting to exceed production losses. And this phase runs for quite a long time.
finding: RR's programme cash model: annual cash turns positive once learning-curve cost cuts and post-launch price rises combine with aftermarket revenue exceeding OE production losses.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And so we are cash-consuming at the moment. And the cash consuming nature of some of the newer engines is outweighing the cash-generating nature of some of the older engines that are in service.
finding: In 2015 RR's civil portfolio was net cash-consuming because several new engines were in their launch phase at once.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We recently raised around GBP 1 billion in new debt to replace maturing facilities and to provide the headroom needed, as well as increasing our revolving credit facility... I still feel comfortable targeting an investment grade rating in the medium to long-term, and we've been A rated since 2006.
finding: Facing profit warnings, RR raised about GBP 1bn of debt for headroom while keeping an investment-grade rating as a firm financial objective.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We clearly want to present the market with a sustainable policy that reflects the underlying strengths of the business and its long-term growth opportunity, but at the same time being mindful of the potential interplay with our rating.
finding: By November 2015 RR's dividend was explicitly subordinated to protecting its credit rating, a shift from the July commitment to a progressive dividend.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Unlinked engines are generally at 0 standard gross margin as we capitalize any cash losses or contractual aftermarket right so that grows over time as a proportion of our sales.
finding: RR sells new unlinked large engines at a cash loss, capitalising the loss as contractual aftermarket rights, so reported OE gross margin is about zero.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Corporate jet engines as Warren set out earlier are normally sold at a cash profit. And our remaining V2500 modules are sold under our agreement at a modest margin.
finding: RR's OE pricing differs by segment: business-jet engines are sold at a cash profit, unlike large wide-body engines sold at a loss.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Firstly, the impact of the Trent 700 rate reduction we outlined in July. At the time we talked about this being a significant volume and price effect of about GBP 100 million each as well as the loss of spare engines.
finding: The A330 rate cut hit Trent 700 profit through roughly equal volume and price effects of about GBP 100m each, plus lost spare-engine sales.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the GBP 100 to GBP 150 million we discussed on the 12th breaks down into 3 parts. Around GBP 50 million to GBP 80 million relates to aftermarket changes; GBP 25 million to GBP 35 million reflects lower JV profits... Overall, we expect something like a 15% to 20% decline in legacy engine revenue in 2016
finding: Parking of older wide-bodies was expected to cut RR's 2016 profit by GBP 100-150m and legacy engine revenue by 15-20%.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: For our corporate jet business, we are expecting a volume reduction impacting revenues by around 20%... Overall, our regional business is declining around 20% per annum, a little faster than we would have expected a year ago.
finding: RR's smaller civil businesses were shrinking fast: business-jet revenue down about 20% in 2016 and regional revenue down about 20% a year.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: At this stage, we've many uses for our cash resources over the next few years, and relatively few strong cash generators... But we will do this without also reducing our commitment to R&D, and the essential investments needed to complete our supply chain transformation... We'll therefore judge our dividend policy in the light of the priority uses of cash.
finding: In a cash squeeze RR ranked R&D and supply-chain investment ahead of the dividend, which would be set by what was left over.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Yes, so on the cash generation question, certainly, our cash is quite volatile. And so picking the exact moment when that transition happens is quite difficult, but it's certainly going to be comfortably before 2020.
finding: RR expected its civil portfolio to cross from net cash consumption to net cash generation comfortably before 2020.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: we, at the end of last year, had, I think, GBP 1.6 billion of cash, and we've now increased our revolving credit facility to GBP 1.5 billion. So that kind of GBP 3 billion at year-end is about what we think is the right number
finding: RR targets about GBP 3bn of year-end liquidity (cash plus undrawn RCF) as its buffer and aims not to draw the RCF.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: But -- so keeping within this sort of R&D level is absolutely what we intend to do. And it does assume that we continue with the programs on technology that Warren mentioned, in terms of simplifying that -- those technology programs as well as the wide-body and the BizJet product development programs as well.
finding: RR committed to fund its technology programmes and its wide-body and business-jet development within roughly 6% of sales in R&D.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Clearly we've got 3 sources of revenue: We've got the license fee, we've got spare parts, and both of those will be in aftermarket. And then we've got the modules, which are within OE at the moment, and that's the bit that will drop off over the next 2 to 3 years, as perhaps switched to the neo.
finding: After the IAE exit RR's V2500 income came from a licence fee, spares and modules; module income would end within 2-3 years as A320 output moved to the neo.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the snapshot of our portfolio of the moment is actually probably at its weakest point. We've got the RB211s as the 800, 500 are coming down, not generating all that cash. Trent 700, despite the fact it's been in production for 20 years, has only become cash positive in the last few years.
finding: RR's most successful engine, the Trent 700, took almost 20 years of production to become cash-positive, showing how long the payback on a new engine is.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Clearly, the Trent 700 for this last batch of engines over -- that we'll produce over the next 2, 3 years is going to be a lot less profitable than we saw there. And that's the reason why we're seeing this GBP 250 million headwind into 2016
finding: RR accepted much lower profitability on the final batches of Trent 700s for the A330ceo run-out, costing GBP 250m of 2016 profit.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We are taking the margin on the OE. It's not as profitable an engine as is the 900 -- as the 700 was, no. Part of that was because on the 900, certainly, is a volume effect. And on the 1000, it just isn't as profitable an engine as the 700 was.
finding: RR admitted its 787 engine (Trent 1000) and A380 engine (Trent 900) are less profitable than the Trent 700; the Trent 900 because of low volume.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We've got 4 or 5 engine programs now that are just going through the key investment phase. The Trent 7000 is the latest one. We've got the 2 versions of the XWB... So the weight of that is outweighing the benefits of the aftermarket on the installed base so far.
finding: RR was running four or five engine programmes through the investment phase at once (Trent 7000, two XWB versions and others), which kept civil profit low.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: I think it's clear that the profit that we get on the V2500, both from the license fee and sort of the engine flying hours fee and the module and spare parts profits is a significant chunk... So yes, if we strip all of that out, then we get quite a small number for civil profitability
finding: V2500 income from the former IAE stake was a large part of RR's 2015-16 civil profit; excluding it, civil profitability was small.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: I would love to maintain the rating exactly where it is, but I have to be a realist as well, that there are some competing pressures there and we have to take the right decision, I think, on balancing those pressures
finding: RR signalled it would accept a lower rating within investment grade rather than hold the A- rating at any cost.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: by investment, I count R&D, CapEx and OE engine losses because we're in the launch phase, is that at a peak this year or next year and then begins to moderate?... I think '15 and '16 are the peak period, yes.
finding: RR confirmed its combined investment (R&D, capex and OE launch losses) peaked in 2015-16.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: So I think in revenue terms, it's roughly GBP 600 million and in profit terms, I think it's in the GBP 250 million range, something like that.
finding: RR's residual IAE/V2500 contribution was about GBP 600m of revenue and GBP 250m of profit a year in 2015.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Firstly, we get escalation every year in pricing, so that's part of the contract. It doesn't stay the same, it goes up every year and inflation may increase, if you like. And then we continue to actually take cost out of that end of the legacy engines.
finding: RR's TotalCare contracts carry annual price escalation, so mature programmes keep improving margin through escalation plus cost-out even after deliveries stop.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: And we will be generating some fairly -- even though it's early on, some fairly significant aftermarket begins to get generated by then. So all of those things are positive and we will on that 84,000 [ph], we should be in positive territory on an OE basis. Absolutely.

trigger: Civil profit warnings and cash pressure in 2015
response: Halved final 2015 and interim 2016 shareholder payments

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: On R&D, we have -- we did invest further on R&D for the new Trent programs, plus the work that we're doing on the next-generation technologies across a number of our businesses. And that together increased the net R&D charge by GBP 83 million for the year.
finding: RR increased R&D in 2015 on new Trent programmes and next-generation technology despite falling profit.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Free cash flow for the year was GBP 179 million. ... So cash conversion was down year-over-year from 54% to 27%
finding: RR's 2015 free cash flow fell to GBP 179m, with cash conversion halving to 27% as new-engine OE losses and the TotalCare debtor grew.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We've maintained a strong investment-grade credit rating. We've worked very hard at this. Standard & Poor's updated their rating in January, We moved to an A/Negative outlook
finding: RR worked to keep its A-range rating through the 2015 profit warnings (S&P A/Negative, Moody's A3), with about GBP 5bn of liquidity.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: we can now, under our new policy, apply a 400% haircut to a specific contract value if we perceive a customer default is more likely. But we've reduced contingency rates for stronger credit airlines.
finding: RR prices airline credit risk into its long-term service contract values, adding contingency for weaker airlines.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the profit headwinds that we see for the Civil business, which, in aggregate, comes to a net GBP 550 million. This is unchanged from the expectation that we gave previously, and we don't see any reason to change that absent any external market conditions or rate changes from the airframers.
finding: RR guided to about GBP 550m of Civil profit headwinds for 2016 from its product transition and noted airframer rate changes as a key risk.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Our net R&D spend will continue on new development programs as we complete some significant new product launches, such as the 97K, XWB; and we expect net R&D spend should be broadly unchanged or slightly lower.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: For 2016, I believe that we'll be in line with our previous expectations of a modest overall outflow, somewhere in the GBP 100 million to GBP 300 million negative range.
finding: RR guided to negative group free cash flow of GBP 100-300m for 2016 during the new-engine ramp.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: You're right; it is over half of the Civil profit this year. ... But IAE is a significant part of the Civil profit because we're quite close to breakeven at Civil at the moment.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the CARs growth last year was a combination of Trent 1000, which is actually about half of it and a smaller number on XWB and some Trent 700, obviously, because of the lower pricing that we got on the ceos coming through.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: I think that that's going to peak probably around the sort of 2020, 2021 range. If I tried to give you an estimate now, I'd probably be where I think I might have mentioned numbers before in the sort of GBP 1 billion, GBP 1.1 billion sort of level.
finding: RR expected cumulative capitalised OE losses (CARs) to peak at about GBP 1.0-1.1bn around 2020-21, when unit-cost gains outpace volume.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: A large part of the rest of that is, essentially, the gross margin on our aftermarket business, whether it's in TCA or spare parts or T&M contracts. And we've talked before about margins there being in the 30% to 40% range across that range of businesses

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: because we've still got quite a negative cost position on the XWB and the Trent 1000 and we will have on the 7000 at the start in terms of unit cost, because we're not up the learning curve, the net effect of all that is negative to the business at the moment.
finding: RR's new engines start with negative unit-cost positions until they move down the learning curve, making the large-engine business marginal early in a programme.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We clearly have to get that up if we're going to get EBIT margins where they should be, which is sort of in the mid-teens long term.
finding: RR's long-term target was mid-teens EBIT margins, from gross margins then around 20-25%.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: we still do have a very robust balance sheet and with good liquidity that's been helped during the year by the additional GBP 500 million of revolving credit facility we raised in April. That's now up to GBP 2 billion. We continue to pursue a prudent financial policy.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: some forecast OE concession payments which slipped into the second half and a pull ahead for some of our second half cash actions.
finding: RR pays OE concessions to customers in cash after engine sales, and their timing makes cash flow lumpy.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We have been taking, in fact, since the beginning of the year both before and after the Brexit vote, advantage of the weaker pound in terms of adding to that hedge position. And we've now, at the end of June, increased that $29 billion up to $35 billion.

trigger: Sterling weakness before and after the June 2016 Brexit vote
response: Increased the hedge book from $29bn to $35bn at better forward rates

speaker: David Smith, CFO

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: we booked a GBP 31 million charge, which is for both incremental expenditure and expected expenditure around the whole improvement program on the A400M. speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We do expect higher net R&D spend to be closer to GBP 900 million as we support a very full program of delivery milestones, as Warren described, on the new projects.
finding: RR's net R&D rose towards GBP 900m in 2016 to fund several new-engine programmes at once.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: As you know, CARs additions represent the aggregate cash loss in the year from unlinked OE contracts. In 2015, our CARs additions were GBP 161 million.
finding: RR's contractual aftermarket rights (CARs) additions measure the aggregate OE cash loss on unlinked engine sales: GBP 161m in 2015, rising in 2016-17.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: In 2018, we have an upward arrow to show an improvement on 2017. Although we're still actually increasing our volumes at that point, we're managing down the average loss per engine
finding: RR expected total OE cash losses to peak in 2017 and fall from 2018 as unit losses dropped faster than volumes rose.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Our range of cash losses today on engine is typically and broadly a GBP 1 million to GBP 2 million range, but we expect this to reduce quite dramatically over the next few years as we execute on the program of cost reduction and benefits from pricing on some of our new programs.
finding: RR's OE cash loss per large engine was typically GBP 1-2m in 2016, expected to fall sharply through cost-down and better pricing.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: The new item is the change in timing of recognition of some of our performance guarantees, particularly on early Trent 1000s, where we now have to recognize the net present value of any expected payments or, for instance, the fuel guarantees.
finding: RR gave performance and fuel-burn guarantees on early Trent 1000s that carry expected payments to customers.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: The total effect on 2015 full year results would have been around GBP 700 million for OE.
finding: Under IFRS 15, RR's 2015 OE profit would have been about GBP 700m lower, showing how much new-engine losses its previous accounting deferred.

speaker: Chris Cholerton, President Defence Aerospace
quote: we continue to drive cost base production to sustain returns in the level of 15% to 17% return on sales.
finding: RR Defence targets 15-17% return on sales, a benchmark of the returns RR seeks where it has strong positions.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: The largest item is the GBP 370 million , which represents the aftermarket profit pulled ahead into OE contracts on linked contracts ... the GBP 150 million is a loss from linked and GBP 161 million from unlinked contracts
finding: In 2015 RR's OE cash losses on installed engines were about GBP 311m (GBP 150m linked plus GBP 161m unlinked), and it pulled GBP 370m of aftermarket profit forward into OE sales.

speaker: Andrew Dickinson, CFO Civil Aerospace
quote: we have a gross revenue of GBP 100 million, we have a concession of GBP 60 million at a net revenue of GBP 40 million with a cost base of GBP 50 million.

speaker: Andrew Dickinson, CFO Civil Aerospace
quote: it's reflective of what we've seen on the Trent 700 historically, when the program was at the level of maturity. So it's historically reflective of what we've achieved.

speaker: Unknown RR executive
quote: It's over the, whatever the contract period is, whatever the term of the contract is, so it will vary customer by customer. So on average, between 10 to 12 years.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: The GBP 500 million for 2018 that's in our LTIP, that still is the plan, in terms of what we're trying to get to, consistent with our own internal incentive targets, which will clearly imply further growth in '19 and '20, beyond that.
finding: RR's management incentive plan targeted about GBP 500m of free cash flow in 2018, with further growth in 2019-20.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: That begins to turn around once we've launched those engines, because we stopped capitalizing, roughly at the point maybe a little bit after the aircraft goes into service. finding: RR's development spending on derivative engines peaks just before entry into service and falls after.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: The 15 was -- in a way, a sort of conservative view on the lifetime of that engine. Clearly, we know the average is 25 years

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: by the time that we've eliminated the XWB losses, which will include the 97K within a year or 2, I think, of the 84k. Really, it's already going to be the Trent 1000 of any significance, I think, and probably Trent 7000s are, a bit -- that will have losses.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: XWB should -- we are planning on that breaking even by the end of the decade on a, just the OE nonspare engine bit.
finding: RR planned Trent XWB OE breakeven on installed (non-spare) engines by the end of the decade, about five years after entry into service.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the in-year savings for 2016 was GBP 60 million against our original estimate of GBP 30 million to GBP 50 million. ... we can deliver an annualized run rate at the very top end of those GBP 150 million to GBP 200 million expectations
finding: RR's 2016 transformation delivered GBP 60m of in-year savings, beating plan, with a GBP 150-200m annual run-rate expected by end-2017.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Our underlying profit before financing of GBP 915 million was 45% lower, largely driven by a reduction in Civil Aerospace profit to GBP 367 million, broadly reflecting the headwinds we've previously communicated.
finding: RR's 2016 underlying profit fell 45% to GBP 915m, driven by Civil Aerospace falling to GBP 367m as the shift to loss-making new engines hit.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: However, V2500 service revenues were actually 21% higher, and that reflected a combination of price escalation built into contracts on flying hour payments, together with some increased overhaul activity.
finding: RR's V2500 aftermarket kept growing strongly (21%) from escalating flying-hour prices, even as OE production wound down.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Overall, gross margins for Civil Aerospace were GBP 1.1 billion or about 16.8% of revenue, which was down GBP 397 million from 2015.
finding: RR Civil gross margin fell to about 16.8% of revenue in 2016, down GBP 397m, during the new-engine OE ramp.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Technical costs for large engines was GBP 74 million higher, at an absolute of GBP 98 million, and that included Trent 900 costs and upgrades to the Trent 700 engine management system.
finding: RR's technical costs for in-service large-engine issues rose to GBP 98m in 2016 (Trent 900, Trent 700 upgrades), before the Trent 1000 crisis.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: This was offset by a GBP 77 million higher contribution from the life-cycle cost improvements, an absolute of GBP 217 million for the year compared to GBP 140 million in 2015.
finding: RR earns margin by cutting lifecycle service costs under fixed-price service contracts (GBP 217m in 2016).

speaker: David Smith, CFO

finding: Because RR books expected TotalCare profit ahead of cash, its TotalCare net assets rose to GBP 2.44bn in 2016, with a peak of GBP 2.5-2.7bn expected.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: we recognized a GBP 671 million charge related to the agreements reached recently on the legacy investigations.
finding: RR took a GBP 671m charge in 2016 to settle legacy investigations (the SFO agreements), adding cash calls in 2017.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Our free cash flow of GBP 100 million was GBP 79 million lower than the prior year but well ahead of our original guided expectations
finding: RR's 2016 free cash flow was GBP 100m, beating guidance mainly through working capital.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We have GBP 570 million of CapEx, that included some payments against 2015 invoices; and GBP 631 million of intangibles, including the GBP 208 million that came from CARs.
finding: RR's 2016 group investment was about GBP 1.2bn (GBP 570m capex plus GBP 631m intangibles, including GBP 208m of contractual aftermarket rights paid to customers).

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Standard & Poor's did update their rating to BBB+ stable from A- negative outlook, although Moody's have maintained their rating at A3 stable
finding: After the SFO settlement S&P cut RR to BBB+, while Moody's kept A3.

speaker: David Smith, CFO

finding: RR put investment needs and balance-sheet flexibility ahead of shareholder payouts, holding payments flat after the 2016 halving.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: net R&D spend is expected to be at a similar level in 2016, although the charge to profits will come down because we'll have some higher capitalization by about GBP 60 million to GBP 100 million, close to GBP 800 million in total.

speaker: Warren East, CEO

So we're actually attacking the cash loss from both ends, from the cost reduction, which is 7% in '16
finding: RR's new-engine OE cash loss shrinks from both ends: launch-customer pricing expires after about 2-3 years of deliveries, and unit costs fell 7% in 2016.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the license income is about the same, and we saw a bit of an increase in aftermarket revenue, both from pricing and from volumes. So overall, I think we probably saw about the same level of total IAE, which I think is about 250
finding: RR still earned about GBP 250m a year from its IAE/V2500 earn-out (licence, modules and aftermarket) in 2016, a narrowbody income stream from a legacy engine.

speaker: Warren East, CEO

finding: RR accepts that long-term service contract margins swing with lifecycle cost improvements and individual durability issues, which it absorbs as they arise.

speaker: Warren East, CEO

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: there has been good progress, in particular on XWB around the economics there. And that is driven not just by the effect of launch pricing running out, as we said would happen during this year and during next year, but also there are cost-reduction initiatives
finding: RR's OE loss on a new engine narrows as discounted launch-customer pricing runs out and unit costs fall, showing launch pricing is deliberately aggressive for the first years.

finding: In 2016 RR's civil widebody economics were a GBP 500m OE cash outflow on 320 engines against a GBP 1bn aftermarket cash margin from 11m engine flying hours, about GBP 90 per engine flying hour.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: the cash flows for the business and regional engines of GBP 600 million, the V2500 royalty around GBP 300 million; gets us to a gross cash margin of GBP 1.6 billion.
finding: Besides widebody, RR's civil gross cash margin includes about GBP 300m a year from its V2500 royalty and GBP 600m from business and regional engines.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: GBP 300 million of commercial and admin costs takes us down to an operating cash margin of GBP 600 million. And then we're spending around GBP 600 million in R&D and CapEx in the civil business
finding: In 2016 RR Civil spent about GBP 600m a year on R&D and capex, consuming all of its GBP 600m operating cash margin, so civil was roughly cash breakeven.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we would hope that putting all of these three together will lead us to be secure as investment grade and ultimately delivering a pathway to a sustainable A rating.
finding: RR's balance-sheet goal is to secure its investment-grade rating and return to an A rating through free cash flow growth.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we receive about $6 billion a year to offset our sterling and euro costs. So to be sure about what we're going to be translating those dollars out, we sell those $6 billion forward over the next few years.
finding: RR is structurally long dollars (about $6bn a year against sterling and euro costs) and hedges them forward for several years.

finding: RR accepted that total OE cash losses would rise in 2017 because volume growth outpaced the fall in unit losses, with the inflection coming later.

speaker: Warren East, CEO

finding: RR's GBP 1bn free cash flow ambition for around 2020 was explicitly contingent on flying hours, fleet growth and in-service issues, so it avoided a hard dated target.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: It's in that the XWB production is significantly higher in '17 than it was in '16. And we know that, that carries an initial larger cash than the average of all the others, but again we expect that to come down. ... So GBP 1.6 million, I expect to be pretty much flat in '17

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: none of that really affects the rule of thumb that we talk about, which is a large engine is going to generate $1 million or so of flying hour revenue per annum.

quote: Timing and phasing of customer deposits, the timing of concession payments when they follow the original engine sale. There will be times where we -- contract payments get restructured with our customers as well.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: one of the things that struck me is a GBP 15 billion revenue business and a -- and a GBP 100 million cash flow.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
