quote: On the 2019 outlook, guidance is maintained, but we now expect the outcome towards the lower end of the range. ... underlying operating profits of GBP 700 million, plus or minus GBP 100 million; and core free cash flow is GBP 700 million, plus or minus GBP 100 million.
finding: RR held 2019 guidance but steered to the low end after the Trent 1000 update.

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: CapEx, that includes capitalized R&D, will remain steady at about GBP 1.4 billion or so, so recurring free cash flow will grow nicely. And then we're going to have around, in total, around GBP 700 million of costs on the Trent 1000
finding: RR kept group capex plus capitalised R&D flat at about GBP 1.4bn a year while absorbing about GBP 700m of Trent 1000 costs in 2020.

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: an extra GBP 200 million of cash costs there on spare engines to bring down the AOG levels from the levels that we're seeing today. And that investment has a very good payback, less within -- less than 12 months.
finding: RR justified GBP 200m of spare-engine investment on a sub-12-month payback, showing it treats customer-disruption costs as quickly recoverable.

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: So that margin, you should think about that as material decline. Using round numbers, one could go from around 20% or so to now sort of moving into single-digit territory or high single-digit, that sort of margin
finding: The aftermarket margin on Trent 1000 service contracts fell from about 20% to high single digits because of durability costs.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: It's the first time that we've seen profit in Civil Aerospace under IFRS 15. As a reminder, that came in at the start of 2018, we no longer capitalize the losses on the OE sales.
finding: Under IFRS 15 RR expenses OE engine losses up front, so civil aerospace reached accounting profit only in 2019 as unit losses fell.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Cash return on invested capital was stable at 12% and that's despite our R&D investment being at the highest levels of cash spend of GBP 1.1 billion per annum.
finding: RR's R&D cash spend peaked at about GBP 1.1bn a year in 2019 as it finished its widebody engine launches.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: First of all, reducing the loss on our OE wide-body deliveries. There was a further improvement in the year of around GBP 200,000 per engine in the reduction of the loss. The XWB-84 leads the average loss reduction. There's been a GBP 400,000 improvement per engine since 2017
finding: Cutting the loss per widebody OE engine is one of RR's three core cash levers; it improved by about GBP 0.4m per engine in two years, led by the mature XWB-84.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: The wide-body aftermarket cash margin delivered a further GBP 300 million improvement, moving from GBP 1.6 billion to GBP 1.9 billion aftermarket cash margin.
finding: RR's widebody aftermarket cash margin reached GBP 1.9bn in 2019, close to its GBP 2bn target for 2022; this is what pays back the OE losses.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Just calling out on the left-hand side here, the Trent XWB-84, we saw a 22% reduction in OE losses. And by the end of next year, we expect the XWB-84 to be a breakeven engine.
finding: RR expected its sole-source Trent XWB-84 to reach OE breakeven about six years after entry into service.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: That's just wide-body, 15.3 million engine flying hours, and then -- from the 5,000 installed engine base.
finding: RR's widebody aftermarket cash margin comes from about 15.3m engine flying hours a year across roughly 5,000 installed engines, with major overhauls about every 5 years.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we're guiding today that our R&D -- capitalized R&D will be between GBP 100 million to GBP 150 million lower in 2020 than in '19, and that will mostly be in Civil Aerospace.
finding: Even before COVID, RR was cutting capitalised civil R&D as its widebody programmes matured.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: The average loss per wide-body engine. We'd hope to get that to around GBP 1 million per engine.
finding: RR's average widebody OE loss was targeted at about GBP 1m per engine in 2020, with the XWB near GBP 0.2-0.3m.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the line that we are sticking to is just under GBP 500,000 across the portfolio by 2022. And the other data point that we're sticking with is breakeven on XWB 84k by the end of 2020.
finding: RR targeted an average widebody OE loss just under GBP 0.5m per engine by 2022, down from about GBP 1m in 2020.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: I'd hope for at least 20% pay at shop visit. Perhaps sort of the mid-high teens. And then the rest would be with flying hour.
finding: Most of RR's civil LTSA revenue is paid per flying hour, with roughly 15-20% paid at the shop visit.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: If you're looking for a metric, Standard & Poor's, in particular, are looking for a 14%, 15% EBITDA margin.
finding: RR's goal of returning to a single-A rating depended on reaching a 14-15% EBITDA margin and removing Trent 1000 risk.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: let's use a proxy of GBP 4 million, GBP 5 million per engine, that's about sort of 20 engines or so that we're building in addition, in 2020. In addition to the 20-or-so that we built in 2019
finding: RR builds Trent 1000 spare engines at about GBP 4-5m each, adding about 20 a year in 2019-2020, a cost of fixing its durability crisis.

speaker: Ian Davis, Chairman
quote: as half the revenues we make in civil aerospace comes from engine-flying hours, fewer flights means less cash coming into our business.
finding: About half of RR's civil aerospace revenue is paid per engine flying hour, so grounded fleets hit cash immediately.

speaker: Ian Davis, Chairman
quote: Given the rising level of uncertainty as to how the COVID situation will develop, your Board has decided not to recommend or make final payment to shareholders in respect of the 2019 final year.
finding: RR cut its shareholder payout at once to protect liquidity when COVID hit, putting the balance sheet ahead of dividends.
trigger: COVID grounding of fleets
response: Cancelled 2019 final payment (7.1p); pay cuts

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: these results include significant negative contract catch-ups, GBP 866 million in revenues and GBP 814 million in gross profit.
finding: Lower forecast flying hours cut the lifetime value of RR's LTSAs, forcing large negative catch-ups: flight-hour contracts carry utilisation risk.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we incurred a GBP 309 million charge for estimated future losses on a small number of contracts. Most of these related to Trent 900 engines.
finding: RR's Trent 900 (A380) service contracts turned loss-making when the A380 was parked, costing a GBP 309m onerous-contract charge in H1 2020.
trigger: A380 retirements
response: Onerous contract provision

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We took the necessary decision to reduce our hedge book because the industry downturn left us over-hedged by around $10 billion.
finding: RR's long-dated dollar hedge book, sized to expected civil dollar receipts, became a large liability when volumes fell.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: The benefit to profit from fewer loss-making large engine in-store deliveries is more than offset by lower business jet and large spare engine sales and under-recovery of fixed costs.
finding: RR's large engine OE deliveries are loss-making, so fewer deliveries helped profit, but lost spare engine sales and fixed-cost under-recovery outweighed that.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: In our Civil Aerospace business, it works with a negative working capital pattern. We're collecting the money owed to us from our customers ahead of carrying out the work. However, if business shrinks, we see an outflow of cash as the situation unwinds.
finding: Civil aerospace is funded by customers' advance payments under flight-hour contracts, so growth generates cash and shrinkage consumes it.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: that each percentage point movement in large engine flying hours are worth about GBP 30 million in flying hour cash receipts
finding: RR sizes its services cash sensitivity at about GBP 30m per percentage point of large engine flying hours.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: an important part of our TotalCare package for airline customers is the provision of spare engines, and we typically spend between GBP 50 million and GBP 100 million each year on spare engines
finding: RR's TotalCare model requires spending GBP 50-100m a year on spare engines, which it sought to take off its balance sheet.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We're going to see a modest benefit in Civil OE as average losses continue to recover, that's another part of the bridge.
finding: RR still expected average OE losses per engine to keep shrinking, a modest contributor to its cash recovery.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: very much a low single digit, so GBP 1 billion to GBP 2 billion or so of comfortable headroom. That's the sort of number that we've used in our modeling.
finding: RR's minimum comfortable liquidity is about GBP 1-2bn, a floor on how much cash it can commit.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: R&D cash spend, GBP 1.1 billion cash spend in 2019. I think you can expect to see that decline modestly as we get towards 2022. I think maybe declines, maybe GBP 100 million, GBP 200 million reduction in R&D cash spend.
finding: RR's R&D cash spend was GBP 1.1bn in 2019 and was guided down only modestly, while capex fell sharply.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We're commencing a GBP 2 billion rights issue and intend to launch a bond offering of at least GBP 1 billion in the near future. In addition, we have agreed commitments for a new GBP 1 billion 2-year term loan
finding: RR recapitalised with equity plus state-supported debt instead of cutting strategic programmes.
trigger: COVID cash burn and reasonable worst-case scenario
response: GBP 2bn rights issue, GBP 1bn+ bond, GBP 1bn term loan, UKEF-backed loan increase

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we expect an improvement of around GBP 2 billion in cash from Civil Aerospace business with engine flying hours expected to return in our base case to 90% of 2019 levels by the end of 2022 ... significantly lower Trent 1000 in-service costs and lower losses on installed wide-body OE deliveries.
finding: RR's civil cash recovery depends on flying hours, lower Trent 1000 costs and smaller losses on each widebody OE engine delivered.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Nonpermanent costs of approximately GBP 300 million related to reducing the size of our FX hedge book, and it includes GBP 200 million to GBP 300 million related to Trent 1000 disruption and in-service costs.
finding: RR's 2022 cash target still carried GBP 200-300m of Trent 1000 disruption costs and about GBP 300m of hedge costs.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: In October, we launched our GBP 5 billion refinancing package. That was necessary to increase resilience to see us through this crisis and strengthen our balance sheet as well as support our long-term strategy.
finding: RR raised GBP 5bn of equity and debt in the COVID crisis to protect liquidity and its long-term strategy.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: But no, the GBP 1.3 billion is structural.
finding: RR says its GBP 1.3bn of cost cuts are permanent even if revenue returns to 2019 levels, so unit costs fall.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: '21 and '22 will be the last 2 years of any material cash outflow on the Trent 1000.
finding: RR expected the Trent 1000 crisis cash costs to end after 2022, with about GBP 250m in the final year.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: I'm not going to go into specifics around it. They can be material. You have seen that in recent years, but I won't go beyond that.
finding: RR admits concession payables built up on delayed 787 deliveries can be material, a risk on top of its cash guidance.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We took mitigating actions that save more than GBP 1 billion in cash. We secured more than GBP 7 billion of additional liquidity and to secure the future. And we embarked on a very large restructuring, the largest restructuring in our history, to fundamentally change the economics
finding: RR's COVID response had three parts: cut cash costs, raise liquidity and restructure civil permanently, the largest restructuring in its history.
trigger: COVID collapse in widebody flying
response: GBP 1bn+ cash savings, GBP 7bn+ new liquidity, restructuring to save GBP 1.3bn a year

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: the impact of a GBP 1.1 billion negative catch-up charge ... on our Civil Aerospace long-term service agreements. This related to changes in the outlook on our long-term contracts as a result of COVID, which led to the derecognition of some of the revenue that has been booked in prior years.
finding: COVID's hit to expected flying hours forced RR to reverse GBP 1.1bn of LTSA revenue booked in earlier years, showing the model's exposure to flying assumptions.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we took a GBP 213 million charge related to onerous or loss-making contracts. Now we don't have many of these, and they are mostly related to the Trent 900 engines on the Airbus A380s.
finding: RR's Trent 900 A380 contracts became loss-making once the A380 fell out of use.
trigger: A380 grounded and retired early during COVID
response: Onerous contract charge

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we had a GBP 4.2 billion group free cash outflow in 2020 compared to a GBP 900 million inflow in 2019. This GBP 5.1 billion year-on-year movement can be divided into 3 broad categories. Firstly, compared to 2019, there was a GBP 3 billion impact from operational factors
finding: COVID swung RR's free cash flow by GBP 5.1bn in a year, mostly through lost engine flying hour receipts under LTSAs.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: In 2020, the cash impact of these combined was around GBP 700 million. Moving on to '21 and '22, they are expected to be around GBP 800 million and GBP 500 million, respectively. But beyond 2023, importantly, the headwind from Trent 1000 is expected to be de minimis.
finding: RR expected the Trent 1000 remediation cash drain, together with hedge close-out, to fall from about GBP 700-800m a year to minimal Trent 1000 cost after 2023.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We were supported by the U.K. credit export agency with an 80% guarantee on the 5-year term loan. In the fourth quarter, we added to this with a GBP 2 billion bond issue and a GBP 2 billion rights issue
finding: RR survived COVID with state-backed loans (80% UKEF guarantee), new bonds and a rights issue, showing it will dilute shareholders and lean on the state in a crisis.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: most of the planned group capital expenditure savings are also in Civil Aerospace. And there, we have a reduction of more than 50% versus the 2019 levels. And that's, of course, helped by the growing maturity of our newest engine program
finding: RR cut civil aerospace capex by more than half from 2019, helped by its engine programmes maturing.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: In 2020, large engine flying hours were 43% of 2019 levels, and we delivered around half as many of new large engines.
finding: In 2020 RR's large engine deliveries halved and flying hours fell to 43% of 2019; with costs slow to follow, civil trading cash outflow was GBP 4.6bn.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: our ambition to get back to at least GBP 750 million as early as 2022 includes up to GBP 500 million of temporary headwinds from the Trent 1000 fixes and the closure of our overhedged positions.
finding: RR's 2022 free cash flow target already absorbs up to GBP 500m of temporary Trent 1000 and hedge costs, so underlying cash generation is higher.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we're pivoting our midterm investments away from civil towards Power Systems and Defence because, as mentioned, the major investment cycle in civil is now largely complete. And in 2019 and 2020, we spent more than 70% on Civil Aerospace and ITP Aero. ... it will be more like 50%.
finding: RR planned to cut civil aerospace's share of group investment from over 70% to about 50%, a deliberate move away from civil.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The current investment in current technology falls from around 2/3 in 2019 to around 1/4 in several years' time.
finding: RR planned to move most investment into low-carbon and next-generation engines, cutting spend on current technology from about two-thirds to a quarter.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we're going to see around GBP 300 million lower Trent 1000 costs. We're about GBP 520 million this year. That will reduce to around GBP 200 million or so in 2022
finding: The Trent 1000 durability crisis still cost RR about GBP 520m of cash in 2020, falling to about GBP 200m by 2022.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: your interpretation is correct that one could see a route to free cash flows greater than GBP 1 billion in the absence of those 2 headwinds.
finding: RR confirmed underlying free cash flow above GBP 1bn once Trent 1000 and hedge costs end, at about 80% of 2019 flying hours.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we remain absolutely confident that we can maintain R&D within the sort of envelope that we've now established, which is significantly less than it has been over the last several years.
finding: RR cut its R&D envelope well below its peak, a structural reduction in capacity to fund new engines.
trigger: COVID and the end of the civil engine investment cycle
response: Cut R&D envelope below previous years

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: OE losses as we came into the year at full throttle, we had no chance whatsoever of being able to respond and scale down our operation quite as fast as the volume disappeared. So lots of under-recovery in 2020.
finding: The sudden OE volume collapse left RR with large unrecovered fixed costs, so its restructuring aimed to resize for lower OE and spares volumes.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: don't forget that this royalty stream is going to disappear in 2020 and -- or in 2027, anyway. So it's one to note, but it's not really the major driving factor of our business.
finding: RR's last narrowbody earnings, the IAE V2500 royalty, end in 2027, after which it has no narrowbody revenue without a new engine.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we're focusing our R&D investment on the necessary next-generation and lower carbon products. And we expect to spend 75% of our gross R&D in these areas by 2025, compared with approximately 50% in 2020.
finding: RR committed to shift its gross R&D towards next-generation and low-carbon products, which include UltraFan.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We committed to a reduction of at least 9,000 Rolls across the group. To date, we've removed around 8,000, and we remain confident of reaching our target. That will be a reduction in civil aero of about 1/3 of management roles
finding: RR's COVID response was a roughly one-third cut to the civil aerospace fixed cost base.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: With GBP 7.5 billion of liquidity and no maturities before 2024, we're confident our position is strong and not dependent on the pace of Civil Aerospace recovery.
finding: RR's crisis posture was to hold large liquidity so that it was not forced to act on civil recovery timing.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: Civil revenue is GBP 2.2 billion, some 13% lower than the comparative period. We've returned to operating profit at GBP 39 million.
finding: Civil aerospace returned to a thin operating profit in H1 2021 on sharply lower revenue, helped by cost cuts.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: Our concession balance fell by GBP 239 million, which was lower than we planned for due to third-party deliveries moving out. Our strong liquidity position means we are not sensitive to the precise timing of the unwinding of these delayed concessions.
finding: RR carries a balance of OE concessions owed to airlines that unwinds as airframers deliver aircraft, and it relies on liquidity to absorb the timing.
trigger: Airframer (787) delivery delays
response: Concession unwind slower than planned

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: Free cash flow of at least GBP 750 million is still achievable in a 12-month period when engine flying hours exceed 80% of 2019 levels. However, given the uncertain pace of recovery in international travel and looking at industry forecasts, it is unlikely that this will occur in 2022.
finding: RR ties its free cash flow target to a flying-hour threshold, and in mid-2021 it pushed back the date by which it expected to reach it.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: we have around GBP 3 billion of net debt today. That is too high. We will reduce it over the coming years.
finding: The new CFO put debt reduction first, which limits RR's appetite for new balance sheet risk such as launching a new engine.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: there's no big change to the absolute quantum that we've talked about before. I think what you are seeing in some of our commentary, though, is a tilt towards net zero and lower carbon, and an intention to push that up over the next several years to be 75% of our R&D investments and CapEx investments.
finding: RR held the total R&D budget flat and moved its mix towards low-carbon and next-generation work under disciplined five-year capital allocation.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: I'm a big believer in us being rewarded for the value that we bring, and we recognize that within the long-term contracts when we've got that value. So you can see some of that upward gain around those commercial negotiations coming through there.
finding: RR used COVID renegotiations to raise lifetime LTSA margins, booking positive contract catch-ups.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: that will, we believe, take us into a competitive zone in terms of profitability for our civil large engine business. And that would be certainly in the mid-teens.
finding: RR's ambition for its civil large engine business after restructuring is a mid-teens operating margin.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: On the OEM breakeven point, yes, you're right. Disruption caused last year made it very difficult for us to continue sort of reporting that because obviously, there were large chunks of unrecovered cost.
finding: COVID's under-recovery of fixed costs pushed back RR's OE unit-loss breakeven path; it says the target depends on volume and gains from restructuring.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Our restructuring program launched in May 2020 is now delivering sustainable savings. It's quicker than expected as we reduce costs and deliver a leaner and more efficient company. By the end of the full year this year, we expect to have removed more than 8,500 roles and saved more than GBP 1 billion.
finding: RR responded to COVID with a deep, fast fixed-cost cut rather than protecting capacity, running ahead of its own restructuring plan.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We're also firmly on course to complete our disposal program with proceeds totaling around GBP 2 billion, and these disposals include Civil Nuclear Instrumentation & Control ITP Aero, Bergen Engines and AirTanker Holdings. We plan to use the proceeds from these disposals, together with underlying free cash flow, to reduce net debt.
finding: After COVID RR sold non-core assets, including ITP Aero, to repair its balance sheet, putting debt reduction ahead of breadth.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: The rule of thumb, as you called it, that we talked about just over a year ago, it's an okay approximation, and it was done at a point in time given the engine programs and where they were at that particular point in time.
finding: RR confirms its rule of thumb that each 1% change in engine flying hours against 2019 moves cash by about GBP 30m, while warning it depends on programme maturity.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: if we've got lower engine flying hours, which means there's lower cash inflow from that, that means most likely, and it's what we saw this year, shop visits get pushed out. So that cash outflow from shop visits moves out in addition to the inflow from lower engine flying hours.
finding: Under RR's flight-hour contracts, lower flying cuts receipts but also defers shop visit costs, so the net cash impact of lower flying is partly self-hedging.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Last year, GBP 4.2 billion of cash outflow. This year, it's going to be better than GBP 2 billion. It's going to be better than GBP 1.7 billion. And next year, it's going to be a positive territory.
finding: RR framed its COVID recovery as a cash trajectory from a GBP 4.2bn outflow in 2020 back to positive free cash flow in 2022.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: material cost increases and supply chain challenges and all those sorts of things as well. And of course, those are baked in, but I'd remind people of the long-term nature of this business, the long-term nature of the contracts that we have with suppliers and the escalation clauses that we have in there.
finding: RR relies on escalation clauses in its long-term supplier contracts to limit how much material-cost inflation reaches its margins.
trigger: Material cost inflation and supply-chain pressure
response: Points to long-term supplier contracts with escalation clauses

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: The working capital outflow that you see, GBP 800 million, that was mostly driven by concession payments and lower OE deliveries in Civil Aerospace.
finding: Concession payments on OE deliveries are a big cash drain for RR.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: Services revenue was up 6% on the prior year and included GBP 214 million of positive long-term service agreement catch-ups compared with a negative catch-up of GBP 1 billion in 2020.
finding: LTSA profitability swings widely with expected flying and durability; COVID forced a GBP 1bn negative catch-up.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: We aim to spend around 75% of our investment on lower carbon growth opportunities in the medium term.
finding: In early 2022 RR aimed most investment at low-carbon and new markets rather than a new civil engine.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: We're into the newer engine programs. Those are the programs that are flying more frequently now than they were in the past. They are earlier stage. We recognize less margin on those as they are less mature.
finding: RR books low margins on young engine programmes and expects margin to rise as they mature.

speaker: Chris Cholerton, President Civil Aerospace
quote: making sure pricing truly reflects the value we bring. We're out of launch pricing phase. So frankly, we're also looking to operate with greater commercial edge.
finding: RR prices new programmes low at launch and raises prices once the programme matures.

speaker: Sebastian Resch, Civil Aerospace operations
quote: It's the OE margin of widebody engines, which we are building. And clearly, it's in our industry, one of our business models that we are losing money at the beginning and then generating cash and make money
finding: RR acknowledges the industry model of selling widebody engines at a loss and profiting in the aftermarket, and says it is changing that.

speaker: Sebastian Resch, Civil Aerospace operations
quote: despite the fact that the volumes on the OE side have been reduced by roughly 50% in the last 2 to 3 years, we have reduced the OE losses by more than 30%. ... If you add spare parts to that basket, we will breakeven even in this year.
finding: RR cut widebody OE losses by over 30% despite volumes halving, and said OE including spares would break even in 2022.

speaker: Sebastian Resch, Civil Aerospace operations
quote: The majority of our contracts have flat pricing -- of our top value contracts have flat pricing. Of the remaining contracts, we are using indices. And the majority of these indices are kept, and they are using the same indices we are using on the customer side
finding: RR matches capped supplier indexation to its customer indices, protecting margins from inflation.

speaker: Arvind Balan, CFO Civil Aerospace
quote: And then the last driver is lower R&D spend. R&D spend will be in the region of 5% of sales going forward.
finding: RR cut Civil R&D to about 5% of sales after its heavy product-development decade.

speaker: Arvind Balan, CFO Civil Aerospace
quote: One, always get your capital allocation right, but two, that's the hard one, don't spend money at the bottom of the ... we come off a peak of very large capital spend. And it's important that we're disciplined now and focused on getting the value from that capital.
finding: RR's Civil CFO ruled out heavy investment at the bottom of the cycle after a peak in capital spend and focused on returns from engines already developed.

speaker: Arvind Balan, CFO Civil Aerospace
quote: Back in 2019, more than half of our investments was on what we call NPI, new product introductions, new stuff, and maybe a quarter on time on wing. In the medium term, we're looking at more than 60% of our capital spent on time on wing.
finding: RR swung Civil investment from new products (over half in 2019) to durability of the installed fleet (over 60%).

speaker: Arvind Balan, CFO Civil Aerospace
quote: So what I've been telling you today as an outlook does not include concession slips, does not include deals, it doesn't include invoice discounting. This is good old clean cash.
finding: RR stopped relying on concession deferrals, customer deals and invoice discounting to flatter cash.

speaker: Chris Cholerton, President Civil Aerospace
quote: And I think our pricing escalation is always at least as good as the cost escalation. And perhaps Sebastian, do you want to say a little bit more about our hedging
finding: RR sets customer escalation at least equal to its cost escalation.

speaker: Arvind Balan, CFO Civil Aerospace
quote: We expect in the medium term for large widebody engines OE to be breakeven, including spare engines.
finding: RR's 2022 target was breakeven widebody OE including spares.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And the escalation clauses on OE and the timing. ... Obviously, it's good to be able to enforce escalation and then we have to manage the cost side of the equation. ... if we can tilt that balance so that the customer and the supplier piece is in our favor, and we can do that in a win-win way with our suppliers
finding: RR confirmed it has escalation clauses on OE contracts, said it is good to be able to enforce escalation, and aims to tilt the balance between what customers pay and what suppliers charge in its favour.
trigger: 2022 inflation
response: Enforce OE escalation; manage supplier costs

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: Going forward, we see sort of T&M being as we get to a more normalized level, it's still around about from the Civil Aerospace perspective, think of it as around 20% of the business.
finding: RR's CFO put time-and-materials work at about 20% of the Civil Aerospace business once activity normalises.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We're partnering with key suppliers, ensuring that we have contractual pricing protection in place through long-term contracts.
finding: RR relies on long-term supplier contracts to lock in input prices.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: Within those targets, we expect a low double-digit compound annual growth rate in total revenues based on 2021 as the start year, a high single-digit operating margin and trading cash flow to comfortably exceed operating profit.
finding: Before Erginbilgic, RR's Civil ambition was only a high-single-digit margin once flying recovered (later more than doubled).

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: In Civil Aerospace, we've been able to contractually pass on higher input prices on both OE and aftermarket through indexation clauses.
finding: RR's OE and aftermarket contracts include indexation clauses that pass inflation on to customers.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: It's our sort of 18,000 engineers ... we end up with what we call an R&D wedge ... those wedges are what we're filling out with potential new programs and which will, obviously, include narrow-body which, realistically, we sort of say middle of the next decade, would sort of start in terms of the sort of '18, '19 period.
finding: RR plans new programmes by filling a spare-engineering 'R&D wedge' from its 18,000 engineers; a narrowbody engine for the mid-2020s would start development around 2018-19.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: it's not incremental to our R&D plans. ... We're taking a lot of Trent 1000 architecture. And as you rightly said, we said that R&D will be around GBP 200 million to GBP 300 million between now and EIS and very little CapEx other than for tooling. So we're looking in the low tens of millions for that.
finding: RR costed the Trent 7000 derivative for the A330neo at GBP 200-300m of R&D to entry into service plus capex in the low tens of millions for tooling, within its existing R&D budget, by reusing Trent 1000 architecture.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: If you think about how R&D operates, it's predominantly people. And we have a finite number of people that are working to consume the bulk of what our R&D spend is. ... So this has been factored in within the balance of our affordable R&D.
finding: RR fits new engine commitments into a fixed engineering headcount, so taking on one programme uses capacity freed from others rather than adding to R&D.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: there is no sudden drop-off of the V2500 business. And as we look forward over our 10-year forecast, it will continue to contribute to part of the portfolio for many years to come.
finding: RR expects its V2500 income stream to continue for at least its 10-year forecast horizon, with no sudden drop-off.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: In our Civil business, we expect some softening in our Trent 700 sales as we move ahead with the launch of the new Trent 7000.
finding: RR expects the Trent 7000 launch (for the A330neo) to cannibalise sales of its incumbent Trent 700 on the A330 during the transition.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: In 2014, we filed 600 patents and invested GBP 1.2 billion in research and development... As you're all aware, we're progressing our next generation of aero engines, Advance and UltraFan. We have flown a test engine with carbon/titanium fan blades, and we're building a new test facility for power gearboxes in Dahlewitz.
finding: RR spent GBP 1.2bn on R&D in 2014, including early UltraFan hardware (composite fan test engine, power-gearbox test facility).

speaker: Ian Davis, Chairman
quote: In terms of what will be different about Warren, there are some unfinished businesses that we know we have to do. For example, getting into question about how we're going to deal with narrow-body. We would look to progress on that.
finding: In April 2015 RR's Chairman called the narrow-body question unfinished business for the new CEO; by November the CEO said RR did not need to be in narrow-body, a change of emphasis.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We will also only participate in that product if we see a business case, and by definition, therefore, they will probably only proceed if we see a business case. So this has to work for all parties here; ourselves, Airbus and the key customers... So we won't go ahead with it if there isn't a proper business case.
finding: As the probable sole engine supplier for an A380neo, RR saw itself as a gatekeeper and would not commit without a business case.
trigger: Airbus signalling A380neo launch; analyst suggestion of exclusive, zero-margin Trent engine
response: Participation only with business case

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: It would still be at a relatively good level in terms of coming off the 5.8% peak we saw last year... We've talked about our new technologies before. These are all really developing around the advanced and UltraFan concepts. Those will step up in spend within our total R&D spend over the next few years.
finding: As XWB development finished, RR shifted R&D (peak 5.8% of sales in 2014) towards Advance and UltraFan technology rather than new engine programmes.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: For the even longer term, we are undertaking an ambitious technology plan to focus on the next-generation Aerospace designs with our Advance and UltraFan projects.
finding: RR's long-term product plan in 2015 rested on the Advance and UltraFan technology programmes as the basis for its next-generation engines.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: So in terms of A380neo specifically, clearly, we are part, although a junior part, of that discussion that's going on... The amount of investment that's affordable is relatively low. So we have to find solutions here that are not high investment solutions.
finding: For a low-volume re-engine (A380neo) RR would only consider a low-investment engine solution, because volumes cannot support heavy development spending.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: If you ask me, have we provisioned for those investments in our future plans? Yes, we have, but not with a commitment to do them... We will not make a commitment until we are clear there's a business case. And I think the same would go for any further developments on the Trent 1000
finding: RR included possible re-engine and upgrade programmes (A380neo, further Trent 1000 work) in its plans but would commit only once a business case was clear.
response: Provision in plans; no commitment without business case

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: right now, there are no narrow-body aircraft shipping with Rolls-Royce engines nor will there be -- new aircraft shipping with Rolls-Royce engines nor will there be for some time to come. It's not a decision we have to make today, as you point out.
finding: In July 2015 RR's CEO put off any decision on re-entering narrow-body engines.
trigger: Analyst question on Boeing 757 replacement and competing with GE's scale

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the advance and UltraFan architectures, these are -- the technologies that sit behind there are equally applicable to lower-power variance suitable for narrow-body aircraft, such as any new design that might come out of Boeing to replace the 757 in due course. And obviously, they're are an important partner for us. That's an important opportunity.
finding: RR positioned UltraFan and Advance as scalable to a narrow-body or 757-replacement engine and saw Boeing as an important partner for such a bid.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Exactly how vital it is that Rolls-Royce wins that sort of design, exactly how much money we should spend on investing in that sector, is a bit more up for debate... In value terms, however, then of course these are lower-value engines... very successfully able to compete with GE in that space.
finding: RR questioned how much to spend on a narrow-body engine, noting their lower value and arguing its wide-body success lets it compete with GE without narrow-body scale.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we continue to invest in technology and we continue to invest in the product roadmap. And the opportunities that you talked about in the question, the A350 stretch, possible 757 successes and so on. Absolutely, these are on our radar and absolutely, these are taken into account when we talk about our forecast for the end of the decade.
finding: Even while restructuring, RR said its end-decade cash forecasts allowed for bidding on an A350 stretch (UltraFan) and a Boeing 757 replacement.
trigger: Analyst asked if forecasts included A350 stretch/UltraFan and Boeing middle-of-market/new narrow-body bids
response: Keep investing in technology and product roadmap; opportunities built into forecasts

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The big question, I think, and there's been a lot of debate that I've heard since joining the business, is so what about narrow-body in the future? And surely, you have to be in narrow-body in the future. I think the answer is, no, we don't. We don't have to be in narrow-body in the future.
finding: Rolls-Royce's new CEO explicitly rejected the idea that RR must re-enter the narrow-body engine market, treating it as optional rather than strategic necessity.
response: No narrow-body engine commitment; keep option open

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: But right now, there isn't an opportunity. There is no opportunity for us to enter this business for another until the early 2030s. There's maybe a little bit of discussion about a sort of quasi wide-body opportunity maybe 5 years ahead of that. So this is actually not something that we should be wasting our time on right now
finding: RR saw no narrow-body entry slot until the early 2030s (a middle-of-market 'quasi wide-body' slot perhaps five years earlier), so it deferred any narrow-body launch decision.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And in 10 years, the blue line is ever so much bigger than the white line. But the white line has grown again as well, because by that time, we're investing in the next generations of engines that are going to take us forward even more.
finding: RR's own 10-year cash picture (to ~2025) already assumed renewed heavy investment in next-generation engines, i.e. a new engine launch cycle in the mid-2020s.

speaker: Eric Schulz, President Civil Aerospace
quote: We sell fuel burn. We sell SFC. ... you all know about the advance program, you all know about the UltraFan, this is preparing the 2025 deliveries from Rolls Royce and it's absolutely important.
finding: In 2016 RR positioned Advance and UltraFan as its products for deliveries from about 2025, sold on fuel burn.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We're going through a little bit of a peak at the moment, but I think you will see in the 2017-2018 period a significant investment in the Advance and Ultrafan engines. And don't forget I said Civil is essentially the lion's share of our R&D expenditures
finding: RR committed to significant Advance/UltraFan technology investment in 2017-18 while R&D was at a peak, with Civil taking the lion's share of R&D.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: It's a paper airplane at the moment, and there is potentially an opportunity for about 5% of the traffic maybe to be taken by that sort of airplane, but we're a long way away from any sort of decision there. If it makes business sense and if that airplane goes ahead, then we'll be very keen to power it.
finding: RR sized Boeing's middle-of-the-market jet at about 5% of traffic and would be keen to power it only if it made business sense.
trigger: Boeing middle-of-the-market (MMA) concept
response: Keen to power it if the aircraft goes ahead and the business case works

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: if there's a sensible commercial opportunity around MMA, then of course, we're interested in going after it. ... If there's an opportunity to create from that architecture another engine variant that we can do economically and start having some return on all the investment that we're making in that architecture development a few years earlier
finding: RR would pursue Boeing's middle-market aircraft only as an economic derivative of its Advance/UltraFan architecture that brings forward returns on that technology investment.
trigger: Analyst question on whether Boeing will launch a middle-market aircraft (MMA)
response: Interested if a sensible business case exists, using Advance/UltraFan architecture

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: there's no committed program. We're in the business of selling engines, and so naturally, we would want to go after that opportunity. Now if it makes commercial sense as an individual opportunity to pursue that, strategically, it makes perfect sense for us to go after that, and that's what we're doing.
finding: In March 2018 RR was actively pursuing Boeing's NMA, subject to it making commercial sense; by end-2018 it had withdrawn, a change of position.
trigger: Boeing NMA discussions
response: pursue if commercially sensible (later withdrew)

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: if we're engaged in that program, it's likely to cost somewhere between GBP 1 billion and GBP 2 billion over a period of probably about 5 years. And what we will endeavor to do is make as much of that cost as possible overlap with the underlying architecture development, which is the UltraFan program.
finding: RR estimated an NMA engine at GBP 1-2bn over about 5 years and would pursue it only if it overlapped UltraFan development, to monetise UltraFan earlier.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We need to do that new architecture because we need to be competitive for larger engines in the back end of the next decade.
finding: RR saw UltraFan as necessary for large-engine competitiveness in the late 2020s, whether or not NMA went ahead.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We're probably going to be spending about GBP 50 million on transferring electrical capability into the Aerospace domain during 2018.
finding: RR spent only about GBP 50m in 2018 moving electrical capability into aerospace; electrification was a small bet relative to gas turbines.

speaker: Paul Stein, CTO
quote: Despite the incredible performance of the XWB engine, we can't rely on the Trent family forever. And so now we're developing UltraFan, a brand-new engine core, the first change since the RB211, will drive a huge composite fan via a gearbox
finding: RR saw UltraFan as the successor to the Trent family, a new core with a geared composite fan planned to fly as a demonstrator within a few years.

speaker: Paul Stein, CTO
quote: And the result is the UltraFan will be a 25% improvement compared with the first Trents.
finding: RR claimed UltraFan would be 25% more fuel-efficient than the first Trents (Trent 700); the XWB was 15% better.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We anticipate doing some new engine development. Whether it's NMA or whether it's larger engines based on our UltraFan architecture for widebody jets in the latter part of the decade ... specific NMA involvement will add GBP 1 billion to GBP 2 billion over a period of 6 to 7 years to the development.
finding: RR estimated a specific NMA engine would add GBP 1-2bn of development over 6-7 years, on top of UltraFan work, with large UltraFan widebody engines expected later in the 2020s.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We will be looking for about 15% cash return on invested capital from the program, so there will be rigor around this investment program. ... we've already spent around GBP 500 million developing the way we've got to the UltraFan so far
finding: Any NMA engine had to clear RR's 15% cash-return hurdle; RR had already spent about GBP 500m on UltraFan, which would underpin such an engine.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: I think where there is increased investment is in Civil Aerospace largely, the advanced-development programs, the UltraFan progress continues as Warren talked about.
finding: RR's rising civil R&D cash in 2018 went mostly to advanced development, including UltraFan, and the Pearl 15.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: It was all a matter of overlapping our UltraFan development program with the NMA requirements ... We have concluded that there is not sufficient overlap to create an engine out of the UltraFan architecture within the Boeing timescales
finding: RR bids for a new airframe only if the requirement overlaps its existing technology programme; with too little UltraFan/NMA overlap in time, it withdrew.
trigger: Boeing NMA engine requirements and schedule
response: withdraw from NMA

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And during the year, we have run the core up to full power. We've been demonstrating to ourselves and experimenting with the new composite materials around the fan and the fan case and also with the combustion system, the new lean burn combustion system.
finding: UltraFan component technologies (core, composite fan/case, lean-burn combustor) were being matured in 2018.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we chose to be completely open with Boeing and our customers and our investors that rather than get into a program and get towards the delivery dates and saying, sorry, we can't do this ... Once we've ascertained that we just couldn't make it fit in the timescale to get to that level of maturity, we had to withdraw.
finding: RR prefers to withdraw early rather than commit and miss an airframer's schedule by a year.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: As far as UltraFan is concerned then, it's a scalable architecture. And it's scoped to scale from by 2,500 pounds of thrust through to about 110,000 pounds of thrust. And that means we can go after widebody, we can go after single aisle. We expect the first opportunities will be in widebody
finding: UltraFan is a scalable architecture (up to about 110,000 lbf) that could serve single-aisle, but RR expected its first application to be a widebody, accepting the analyst's A350neo-type example.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And on NMA, would we partner with somebody else? Well, we'll have to see what happens and who gets selected. We've made our decision in terms of our proposed offering. If we can do something useful and it makes commercial good sense to partner in future, then, of course, we're open.
finding: RR left open joining a rival's NMA engine as a partner if it made commercial sense, a precedent for Joint Venture or partner roles.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And risk and revenue-sharing partners for UltraFan engines, probably the usual suspects. I couldn't be any more specific than that at the moment. I mean, it's a new architecture, but it's still a gas turbine
finding: RR planned to fund UltraFan with its usual risk and revenue-sharing partners, sharing development cost rather than going solo.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: This is the first serious architectural change that we've made to our gas turbines for about 60 years. So it's absolutely vital that we continue to invest in this technology to make sure we have a competitive solution, which just, as it says up there, 10% more efficient than Trent XWB.
finding: RR called continued UltraFan investment 'absolutely vital', aiming for 10% better efficiency than the Trent XWB.

speaker: Sir Frank Chapman, Non-Executive Director
quote: the new family of UltraFan mentioned earlier also by Warren, has the potential to make a step change in the emissions footprint of our products, we're working very hard to bring that forward in a whole family of products that can address a series of power ranges
finding: RR positioned UltraFan as a scalable family covering several thrust ranges, which leaves open a narrowbody version.

speaker: Paul Stein, CTO
quote: But we're now developing a new engine core, it's called the Advance 3, itself a 5% improvement, but for our next-generation engine, this will be mated to a large composite fan, driven through a gearbox to create UltraFan, an impressive 25% improvement over the Trent 700.
finding: RR claimed UltraFan would be 25% more efficient than the Trent 700, with the Advance 3 core adding 5% over the XWB (itself 15% better).

speaker: Paul Stein, CTO
quote: And then finally, in the much longer term, middle of the market aircraft up to widebodied, will eventually be equipped with electric fans to control the airflow around the aircraft. But this is not the next decade, this is more like 2035 to 2040
finding: RR expected electrified propulsion on mid-market and widebody aircraft only around 2035-2040, so gas turbines would power the next generation of large aircraft.

speaker: Paul Stein, CTO
quote: We're very pleased that in the regional hybrid area, we are ahead of the game with Airbus on the E-Fan X program, which we anticipate will be the world's first flying demonstrator of this hybrid electric technology.
finding: RR partnered with Airbus on the E-Fan X hybrid-electric demonstrator.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The core of the engine, the Advance 3 core, we tested during 2018. We tested it at full power. It's performing brilliantly. ... We also tested the gearbox which drives the large lightweight fan at the front of the engine. The gearbox is being run up to about 70,000 horsepower
finding: UltraFan technology was maturing in 2018-19, with the Advance 3 core tested at full power and the power gearbox tested to about 70,000 hp.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: at the end of last year, we made an important commercial decision about UltraFan which we announced in February when we decided not to take part in Boeing's new mid-market aircraft. And that was because we absolutely did not want to do anything that will jeopardize the success of this UltraFan program.
finding: RR declined to bid for Boeing's NMA rather than put UltraFan at risk, choosing technology maturity over a new airframe slot.
trigger: Boeing NMA engine competition
response: withdrew from NMA bid

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And so that's why we withdrew from that opportunity, but it doesn't in any way indicate a -- any dent in our appetite for making this an excellent product when it comes to market.
finding: Withdrawing from NMA did not mean dropping UltraFan: RR stayed committed to bringing it to market when it is mature.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We have a partnership activity with Airbus, a hybrid demonstrator aimed at regional transport, and so regional type -- size of aircraft.
finding: RR partnered with Airbus on a regional hybrid-electric demonstrator as part of three electric-flight programmes.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: As far as new technology is concerned, we're collaborating with the folks at ITP around some of our new technologies in UltraFan.
finding: RR was developing UltraFan technology with its ITP Aero subsidiary in 2019.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we see a very firm role for UltraFan and more efficient gas turbines, whether they used directly for the UltraFan propulsion or whether the core out of UltraFan, the more efficient core is used in a hybrid application in a smaller aircraft. The project is absolutely vital.
finding: RR called UltraFan vital before COVID and saw its core as usable in direct propulsion or hybrid applications for smaller aircraft.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: UltraFan, as many of you know, is a demonstrator program for a whole suite of new technologies. It's not simply one single new engine. Those individual technologies will give us competitive advantages as well as options. Exactly how we use them and when we use them is not something, for obvious competitive reasons, that I'm going to talk about today.
finding: RR treats UltraFan as a technology demonstrator that creates options, not a committed product; it keeps the deployment decision open for competitive reasons.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: CapEx on intangible assets was down by around GBP 100 million with lower capitalization of new civil engine programs as we reassessed our near-term investment priorities.
finding: RR cut spending on new civil engine programmes quickly in the crisis, showing development spend is its first discretionary lever.
trigger: COVID cash crisis
response: Cut capitalised development on new civil engines by about GBP 100m in H1

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Thirdly, we're looking to reduce the amounts that we need to invest to get new technology to market. We already have a number of risk- and revenue-sharing partners in manufacturing. But as technology develops, we need to think more broadly and work with more industrial partners to accelerate those developments and to share the upfront investments.
finding: RR wants more industrial partners to share the upfront cost of new engine technology, which fits a joint venture for a new engine better than going solo.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: these new products that we contemplate, things like UltraFan and beyond, have a greater range of new technologies within them. And developing those technologies ... is a lengthy exercise and it's a risky exercise. And so we'll be continuing to look for new partnerships, perhaps a little bit more at the development end
finding: RR plans to share UltraFan development risk with new partners at the technology development stage, a wider range of players than its past risk-and-revenue-sharing partners.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Engineering spend was also reduced as industry-wide delays have allowed us to slow down our R&D spend without jeopardizing our commercial objectives.
finding: RR slowed R&D when airframers delayed programmes, pacing its engine development to airframer launch timing rather than running ahead.
trigger: Industry-wide programme delays
response: Slowed R&D spending

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Now that's in line with the development time line for our next-generation UltraFan engine program. And just to remind you, by the way, that we're also the exclusive engine provider for the A330neo with the Trent 7000.
finding: RR matched the end of its A350 exclusivity to UltraFan's development timeline, suggesting UltraFan is meant for next-generation widebodies around 2030.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: technically, yes, when a period of exclusivity finishes at the end of 2030, then it could be dual-sourced at the end of 2031. But as I pointed out in the presentation a moment ago, the 2030 date does coincide pretty much with the timing of likely UltraFan and next-generation aircraft
finding: RR accepts that the A350 could be dual-sourced after 2030, and expects UltraFan and next-generation aircraft around then.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Firstly, UltraFan, our next-generation aero engine. As many of you will know, this new engine architecture is forming an exciting part of our sustainability journey. For starters, it's 25% more fuel-efficient than the first generation of Trent family engines. It's also 100% SAF compatible
finding: RR positions UltraFan as its next-generation engine, 25% more fuel-efficient than the first Trent engines.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We were very explicit about the reason why we withdrew from that proposed program a couple of years ago and that was around the timing of our UltraFan program.
finding: RR restates that it withdrew from Boeing's NMA in 2019 because the programme's timing did not suit UltraFan.
trigger: Boeing NMA engine competition
response: Withdrew in 2019 because the timing did not suit UltraFan

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we're sort of gearing up for a demonstration early next year. So then it will depend -- whether we go ahead with it at that stage or whether we pause at that stage, it will depend on the timing of new aircraft programs.
finding: RR's UltraFan launch rule: complete the demonstrator, then go ahead or pause depending on whether an airframer programme exists, so it will not launch without a platform.
trigger: Absence of a new airframe programme
response: Demonstrator in 2022, then go or pause

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the product will be scalable. It will go across single-aisle and dual-aisle applications. It will be applicable for new aircraft, compatible with 100% SAF and so on. So yes, it's quite applicable. But we'll have to see if programs actually materialize and when they do.
finding: RR describes UltraFan as scalable to single-aisle and widebody, keeping open a narrowbody entry if a programme appears.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: our UltraFan architecture will deliver a further step change in efficiency, making it easier for our customers to adopt the more expensive SAFs in the long run.
finding: RR presents UltraFan as its next efficiency step and justifies it partly by making costlier sustainable fuels affordable for airlines.

speaker: Chris Cholerton, President Civil Aerospace
quote: And the larger size, our UltraFan technology demonstrator, which is at the heart of our strategy for future widebody and indeed any future narrowbody opportunities.
finding: Even before Erginbilgic, UltraFan was RR's route to both future widebody and narrowbody bids.

speaker: Unknown Executive (Civil Aerospace leadership)
quote: So we intend to keep pushing and we know our share is low. We're not going to do anything silly, of course, on pricing to do so. But we think with the engine performing as it now does, we have opportunities still to have -- to make wins.
finding: RR will not cut prices to regain 787 share and relies on a fixed Trent 1000, a stance still held in 2024.
trigger: Low Trent 1000 share on the 787 after the durability crisis
response: Compete on durability and service, not price

speaker: Chris Cholerton, President Civil Aerospace
quote: So we're -- we've chosen to invest well ahead of a market need because you need to put demonstration of technology, showing you got a ticket to the game with customers is absolutely critical.
finding: RR funds demonstrators ahead of demand to earn a ticket to future engine competitions.

speaker: Chris Cholerton, President Civil Aerospace
quote: depending on the actual reality of any market opportunity, which is going to be well into the 2030s we'd anticipate on widebody and now it is 2030s on narrowbody too.
finding: In 2022 RR expected no new widebody or narrowbody engine competition until the 2030s and phased investment to match.

speaker: Chris Cholerton, President Civil Aerospace
quote: So our ambition would be enter into narrowbody to better utilize over a wider [indiscernible] technology.
finding: RR wants narrowbody to spread UltraFan's cost over a bigger market, and expects to do it in partnership as on all its Trent programmes.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We've also assembled the first UltraFan large engine demonstrator, which will go on test later this year with 100% sustainable aviation fuel.
finding: Under East RR kept funding the UltraFan demonstrator through the COVID recovery.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: hydrogen and the gas turbine together for wide-body aviation is a minimal investment today. And based on what we can see, revenue is not likely before the late 2030s.
finding: RR keeps hydrogen widebody propulsion as a minimal option, seeing no revenue before the late 2030s.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: it is a technology demonstrator. You need to think about that way, okay. And it has 2 purposes. One is to position us well for the next generation of engines, and it does exactly that.
finding: RR treats UltraFan as a technology demonstrator, not a committed product, until an airframer programme exists.
trigger: Analyst question on whether UltraFan is a must-do and on RR's history of failing to earn returns on technology
response: Demonstrator only; no payback period given

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: I'm not going to give you a payback period right now because next-generation aircraft is not going to happen before 2030, and we need airframers, obviously, to go there first. But I will say this. We won't do anything not profitable.
finding: RR will commit to a next-generation engine only after an airframer launches (not before 2030) and only if it is profitable, the launch-customer condition.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: that is a big engine, so -- intentionally, because we will scale down to wide body even to narrow body. It is scalable.
finding: RR built UltraFan at the top of the thrust range deliberately, to scale down to widebody or narrowbody.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: UltraFan is distinctive, developed to be competitive in the wide-body and narrow-body segments. It has scalable trust ranging from GBP 25,000 to GBP 110,000, enabled by a gearbox that delivered 64 megawatt on test
finding: RR designed UltraFan as one scalable geared core covering roughly 25,000-110,000 lb thrust, so the same investment can serve a narrowbody or a widebody.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: We can retrofit some of these technologies into today's engines, such as the Trent XWB to increase time on wing and fuel burn efficiency.
finding: RR spreads UltraFan R&D value into upgrades of today's engines, which cuts the stand-alone risk of the programme.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: In Civil Aerospace, we believe we are well positioned to reenter the narrow-body market. By choosing a partnership approach for the next program, our UltraFan technology is a vital step towards this. At the right time, with the right partner, we will decide the next steps.
finding: RR formally chose a partnership route back into narrowbody, with the timing and partner still open and UltraFan as its contribution.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Yes, we are seeing financially, I think sort of to derisk things a little bit, partnership approach will be a good approach for the next generation. Obviously, partnership needs to work. If it doesn't work, we can consider alternatives because we are actually bringing a technology into this.
finding: RR prefers a narrowbody partnership mainly to share financial risk, but keeps a solo option open if no partnership works.
trigger: Analyst noting RR had exited the geared turbofan with Pratt & Whitney and asking why it would not go alone
response: Partnership preferred to derisk; alternatives if it fails

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: To deliver these numbers and grow beyond that, we don't need to answer narrow body. It is an opportunity. ... I believe it can be a profitable place. And if it is not profitable, we won't do it because we don't need to do it.
finding: RR will enter narrowbody only if it is profitable, because its plan does not depend on it; this makes Do Nothing a credible default.

speaker: Robert Watson, President Civil Aerospace
quote: as the engine architecture is scalable, it can be considered for both widebody and narrow-body applications on future platforms. And while we expect this geared architecture will be 25% more efficient than the first Trent's engines
finding: RR keeps UltraFan platform-agnostic, ready for whichever next airframe (widebody or narrowbody) is launched.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: the UltraFan program successfully tested at full power in 2023 in trials that also showed the power gearbox handled accelerations and decelerations 20x faster than we had previously achieved.
finding: RR's UltraFan demonstrator, including its power gearbox, reached full power in 2023.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: all the orders coming into the industry, they will be only delivered '27, '28, '29, if you are lucky. So we are already -- sort of we will be ready when the new deliveries come
finding: RR times the Trent 1000 durability upgrade to be ready before new 787 orders deliver in 2027-29, aiming to compete for them.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: So I think -- do we believe we can regain market share? Absolutely. Otherwise, we wouldn't have invested in time on wing. That is the only thing holding us back.
finding: RR justifies its time-on-wing spending by the aim of regaining 787 share, which it says only durability is holding back.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: There's no change of strategy. We are pretty consistent company. ... Part of that, we said narrowbody is something attractive for us, and we will participate preferably with partnerships. Nothing has changed in that.
finding: RR says building a narrowbody demonstrator alone does not change its partnership preference.
trigger: Analyst question on whether RR is now going alone on narrowbody
response: Demonstrator proceeds; partnership still preferred

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Why are we going with the demonstrator? Because, frankly, that doesn't mean we don't want to partner, but that means we would like -- we don't want to wait and position ourselves well out there.
finding: RR self-funds a narrowbody UltraFan demonstrator to be ready and credible before any partner or airframer decision, rather than wait.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: UltraFan is 10% more efficient than that. And actually, at plane level, we believe you can get to 15% efficiency doing some other things on the plane combination.
finding: RR pitches UltraFan's efficiency gain at 10% engine-level and 15% aircraft-level.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: In civil aerospace, we successfully tested UltraFan in 2023, and we are further improving the design progressing the development for both narrow and widebody aircraft.
finding: After the 2023 demonstrator test RR kept developing UltraFan for both widebody and narrowbody rather than committing to one product launch, a dual-use stance it has held since 2022.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: We have switched our OE production to the new blade already and are aiming for certification in 2Q. We expect to be able to introduce the new HPT blade to all engines across the fleet over the next 2 years
finding: RR put the Trent 1000 durability fix straight into new production and planned a two-year retrofit of the installed fleet.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: The other one is only engine-level certification, we can quickly implement it. Yes, we are looking to increase the share on 787. Why not? Because this is going to be a highly competitive product.
finding: RR sees the Trent 1000 durability upgrade as a way to win back 787 share.
trigger: Analyst question on whether Trent 1000 fixes can regain 787 share
response: RR says it will seek a higher 787 share

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: We are very well positioned on narrowbody. Therefore, everybody is talking to us and we are talking to everybody. So I said it in CMD, our preference is partnership. We don't need partnership for capability, but our preference is that.
finding: RR says it could do a narrowbody engine alone but prefers a partner to share the risk; it repeated this from the 2023 CMD.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: The upgraded Trent 1000 HPT blade was certified in June, which will more than double the time on wing on these engines.
finding: RR delivered a Trent 1000 durability upgrade (new HPT blade) to fix the 787 engine's time-on-wing problem.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: We are doing further tests on wide-body UltraFan just to progress that, at the same time, working on the demonstrator for narrow-body, which may take 2 years to build a demonstrator.
finding: In 2025 RR was progressing both a widebody UltraFan test programme and a narrowbody UltraFan demonstrator about two years from build.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: The other angle is our preference continues to be partnerships. Therefore, we are in active dialogue with almost all the parties, I should say.
finding: RR prefers to re-enter narrowbody through a partnership rather than solo, and was talking to almost all potential partners.

speaker: Mike Terrett, COO
quote: Four years ago, it was an idea. We told Airbus it would run in June 2010... But we won't get any revenue for that engine until 2013
finding: The Trent XWB went from concept (about 2006) to first run in June 2010, on the date promised to Airbus, with no revenue until 2013: about 7 years from idea to revenue.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: we haven't seen much upturn in demand on the time and material side. And that continues to be the case. I mean, typically, we get two to three months of visibility of demand through the repair and overhaul network.
finding: Time-and-material aftermarket demand stayed flat in 2010, and RR has only 2-3 months' visibility of it, unlike its contracted TotalCare revenue.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: we have about 2/3 and what they put into an engine comes from the exceeding supply chain. So were also having to manage risk in the external supply chain
finding: About two thirds of RR engine content came from external suppliers in 2010, making supply-chain risk a constraint on the ramp and on inventory.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: We did incur some retrofit costs on the fleet of the delevers and the industrial trends to improve combust of life, and that caused the first half loss.
finding: RR paid to retrofit its installed industrial Trent fleet to fix combustor life, which pushed Energy to a first-half loss: the maker bore the cost of the fleet fix.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: record order book up 4% to GBP 61.4 billion. We won new orders of GBP 8.7 billion in the first half with around 75% coming from Civil Aerospace where we continue to take around half of the lucrative widebody market
finding: RR described widebody engines as 'lucrative' and claimed about half of that market; civil made up about 75% of H1 2011 orders.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: we have about GBP 140 million of installed thrust in a Trent fleet today. And if you look at the next 20 years and assume we get about 50% of the market, then we should deliver about another GBP 700 million of thrust over the next 20 years.
finding: RR used installed thrust as a proxy for aftermarket value: about 140m (units given as GBP in the transcript, presumably lbf) installed Trent thrust in 2011, and another 700m expected over 20 years at a 50% share.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: we will see a small effect from the nuclear disaster in Japan that has caused some disruption to our supply chains and delayed deliveries into the factories and also delayed some overhaul activity. And that's going to cost us about GBP 10 million
finding: The 2011 Japan disaster disrupted RR's supply chain and overhaul activity at a cost of about GBP 10m, which RR absorbed within its guidance.

speaker: Mike Terrett, COO
quote: The fan blade and the assembly of the engine is clearly make. We clearly make the turbine blades and we clearly make their rotating disks.
finding: RR keeps fan blades, turbine blades, discs and final assembly in house as core make items and outsources the rest.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: it's because there's a very large installed base of engines, about 30%, as you know, around time materials. And so there are some areas of the fleet that are looking better. For example, the 524 engines
finding: About 30% of RR's civil installed base was on time-and-material terms in 2011; ageing RB211-524s were generating more overhaul demand.

speaker: Mike Terrett, COO
quote: We've been planning this ramp-up in civil for some time. And rather sadly, we've had to wait a little bit on the 787 and the A380 delays, but we've had plenty visibility... and we've also hedged our materials probably far more extensively than we did back in 2004.
finding: Learning from the 2004 ramp, RR planned the Trent ramp with early supplier readiness and more materials hedging; 787 and A380 delays pushed it back.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: The Trent 900 incident, which you're all familiar with, which is a charge of GBP 56 million in 2010 and GBP 18 million in 2011. And finally, the Trent DLE, GBP 26 million charge, which we took in 2010
finding: The costs RR booked for quality events were small: GBP 56m (2010) and GBP 18m (2011) for the Trent 900 incident, and GBP 26m (2010) for the industrial Trent DLE.

speaker: Mike Terrett, COO
quote: That's both our internal supply chain and the 75% or so of the engines that are produced in the external supply chain.
finding: RR said about 75% of engine content is produced by external suppliers (two thirds in 2010), so partners and suppliers carry much of the ramp investment.

speaker: Mike Terrett, COO
quote: we are actually bringing on board the Seletar facility in Singapore this year, which will double our output of final assembly and double our output of wide-chord fan blades... near-term absorbers of cash, to later become tremendous generators of cash.
finding: The Seletar facility doubled RR's final assembly and wide-chord fan blade capacity in 2012; RR accepted near-term cash absorption for later cash generation.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: The order book increased 4%, adjusted for IAE, and now contains around 3,300 engines of which our Trent engines make up over 70%. Our share of the wide-body market continues to grow and we are on course to double our production of large civil engines by the middle of the decade.
finding: After the IAE exit RR's civil order book was dominated by widebody Trents (over 70% of about 3,300 engines), and it planned to double large-engine production by mid-decade.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: clearly, disappointing that we caused the ANA an issue, but we and they are primarily focused on safety... we found a component in the gearbox was wearing a little more quickly than we thought it should. So I think the summary is they put 5 aircraft on the ground, 4 of those aircraft are now back in the air
finding: An early Trent 1000 durability issue (premature gearbox component wear) briefly grounded 5 ANA 787s in 2012; RR said the financial consequences were not material.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: delivering 2,000 Trent engines over the next 5 years. And just to put that into perspective, it's taken us 15 years to deliver the last 2,000. So we're ramping up facilities to ensure we can meet the volume rise and deliver on our commitments to customers because that damages our reputation and gives us financial penalties if we don't
finding: RR planned to deliver 2,000 Trents in 5 years against 2,000 in the previous 15, and prioritised capacity because late delivery brings reputational damage and contractual penalties.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: we continue to grow our wide-body market share with Trent engines now making up 75% of the civil order book. Revenue rose by 16% in the year, driven by 31% increase in OE revenue off 23% more deliveries of higher thrust engines... Services grew by 5%. This was in line with the growth in the installed thrust base.
finding: In 2012 RR civil OE revenue rose 31% on 23% more deliveries, while services grew 5%, in line with installed thrust. Trents made up 75% of the civil order book.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: our older engines, we typically have a far lower level of TCA penetration, sort of 40% to 50%... you start to get some lumpy retirals, which we're starting to see in 524... You will get those engines being torn down and the service used material going back into the system and stopping some new spare sales.
finding: Retiring RB211-524s (40-50% TotalCare penetration on older engines) put used serviceable material back into the market and displaced new spare sales, holding back 2013 civil revenue.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: We've been up purchase order, 100%, all of this year on all the products... I think we've still got much more work to do in what I would call responsiveness to issues.
finding: RR delivered large civil engines 100% on time against purchase orders in 2013 but said its response to in-service issues needed to improve.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
