quote: Some of the cost benefits are associated with how can you get longer on-wing service to reduce servicing costs. Some of the benefits are around how do we drive repairs into our services business rather than replacement, which is something we are comparatively weaker relative to our competition.
finding: RR admitted it was weaker than competitors at repairing rather than replacing parts in overhauls and saw longer time on wing as a lever to cut TotalCare servicing costs.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: there is some transfers that are ongoing between us and UTC. And we've assumed the timeline for that. Some of those timelines have sort of moved a little bit to the right, so there is some stuff we're doing more that eventually we won't be doing.
finding: Following the IAE restructuring RR was transferring some V2500 work to UTC; delays in the transfer temporarily boosted RR's supplier income.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: you kind of see Trent 700 continuing to do well. You're seeing slow and good growth coming in Trent 1000; XWB, yet to come; and a slowdown in Trent 900s, which is exactly what you'd expect based on the aircraft sales... 90% of the order book related to Trent is yet to come.
finding: In 2013 RR's Trent volume still rested on the Trent 700 while Trent 900 volume fell with A380 sales; the Trent 1000 was ramping slowly and the XWB was still to come.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: In 3 years time, we will be producing twice as many Trent engines as we are today.
finding: RR planned to double Trent production within 3 years of 2014.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: The Aerospace industry is, quite rightly, strictly regulated. That means it takes both time and tenacity to drive cost out from the business. And you will not be surprised to hear me say that we are not where we need to be.
finding: RR's CEO admitted aerospace cost reduction was behind where it needed to be in early 2014, blaming regulatory recertification.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: Aftermarket revenue increased 3%, slightly lower than a 5% growth in the installed thrust. This reflects a 20% decline in RB211 revenue
finding: RR's civil aftermarket grew 3% in 2013 against 5% installed-thrust growth, held back by a 20% fall in RB211 revenue.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: In our Singapore facility last year, we produced 41 engines. In the next few years, production capacity will be over 200, so fixed cost absorption will improve.
finding: RR built its Singapore assembly plant well ahead of demand (41 engines in 2013 against 200+ capacity), accepting under-absorption during the ramp.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: About 1,100. Yes.
finding: RR cut about 1,100 indirect staff (11% of indirects) from October 2012 to early 2014, with similar cuts planned for 2014.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: We've got about 600 engineers focusing on cost reduction; about 400 on original equipment looking at our existing products, driving costs down in our existing products. ... We got a couple-of-hundred engineers working on the aftermarket, and they're actually driving costs down in absolute terms.
finding: RR deploys about 600 cost engineers (about 400 on OE, 200 on aftermarket); OE work only offsets supply-chain escalation while aftermarket work cuts costs in absolute terms.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: Low-cost country sourcing. We're about 20% at the moment on average, slightly higher in the Marine & Industrial Power Systems business than in the Aerospace business. We're targeting 40% by 2020
finding: RR planned to double low-cost-country sourcing from about 20% to 40% by 2020.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: So it's taken us 18 years in the company to deliver the first 2,000 Trent engines. We'll deliver the next 2,000 over the next 5 years.
finding: RR planned a steep Trent ramp: 2,000 engines in the next 5 years compared with 18 years for the first 2,000.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: some 8,000 people Rolls-Royce or joint venture employees ... some 22 million health -- engine health monitoring reports that we're dealing with every year, and around 5,000 overhauls
finding: RR's service network had about 8,000 RR or JV staff in overhaul centres and handled about 5,000 overhauls and 22 million engine health reports a year.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: the most powerful determinant of cost in a service and support contract under TotalCare, is time on wing. It is extending that time on wing, which delays the maintenance event and the cost to do the overhaul.
finding: RR sees time on wing as the main driver of TotalCare cost, so durability improvements go straight to its service margin.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: doubling the time on wing on engines like the Trent 700 and Trent 800 since they entered service is real ... some 92% of the engines that we deliver from new only being removed from wing at the point of which we expect it to be removed as a result of reaching a life-limited part
finding: RR doubled Trent 700/800 time on wing since entry into service, and 92% of new Trent 700s come off wing only at planned life-limited-part removals.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: an engine removal incident is somewhere between $0.5 million and $1 million every time it happens.
finding: RR puts the cost of an unplanned engine removal at $0.5-1m, which justifies its investment in predictive health monitoring.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: We found a mechanism, invested some GBP 14 million in a repair technique. ... It delivered a saving of some GBP 56 million by avoiding the need to replace that component at shop visit on some 350 engine overhauls.
finding: RR invests in repair technology when returns are high, e.g. GBP 14m spent to save GBP 56m across 350 overhauls.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: But the big things happen around 4 or 5 years, which is the first overhaul and then the second overhaul around 8 or 9 years, and these things can be quite lumpy anywhere between about $3 million and $5 million on a big engine.
finding: A big widebody engine's first overhaul comes at about 4-5 years and the second at about 8-9 years, each costing $3-5m.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: with RB-211 programs, generally, these guys are running -- together, they combine in there about sort of 35% to 40% on TCA. They're still very T&M-weighted, this part. And as we go across, these are much more on TCA. And again, as we go forward, sort of in the high 80s, 90% and across the fleet, about 70-odd percent.
finding: TotalCare coverage rose with each RR generation: 35-40% on RB211s, high 80s-90% on newer Trents, about 70% across the fleet.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: a large part of that was on the back of the revenue growth. But it was also on the back of the fact that we under invested, if I can be slightly critical, in the infrastructure of the business and we're having to catch that up now, which is one of the growing pains that we're going through.
finding: RR's CEO admits 2003-2013 margin gains partly came from under-investment in infrastructure, which it now has to catch up on as the Trent ramp brings growing pains.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: Go back in history, hundreds and hundreds of suppliers, XWB less than 100, that changes the negotiation dynamics significantly.
finding: RR cut the Trent XWB supply base to under 100 suppliers from hundreds on older programmes to increase its negotiating leverage.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: Rolls-Royce Aerospace today, 135 suppliers, is 80% of the value of equipment that we buy in our engines.
finding: RR Aerospace's supply base is concentrated, with 135 suppliers making up 80% of bought-in engine value.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: So we started with the top 50 suppliers with the 15%, 5% per year over 3 years. We've made good traction on some areas of that. We're still working on some of the more complex relationships
finding: RR asked its top 50 suppliers for 15% cost reductions (5% a year over 3 years), with mixed progress, especially with proprietary system suppliers.

speaker: Colin Smith, Engineering Director
quote: Well, we certified the engine late last year. We're in the middle of the endurance program to make sure that we got to maintain ability and the reliability that we're predicting, and it's looking very good in the line with prediction.
finding: The Trent XWB certified in late 2013 and was tracking reliability predictions in endurance and flight testing ahead of A350 entry into service.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: at the moment, I'm only delivering 25% to the internal plan and the rest is coming in over the course of this buffer
finding: RR's internal production was only about 25% on plan in mid-2014, so it relied on inventory buffers it was only slowly reducing.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: we delivered our first XWB engines to Airbus for Qatar Airlines, launch customer -- to launch later this year. We've run, for the first time, the large XWB engine, the XWB 97K that will power the A350-1000 aircraft and we'll also run the Trent 1000-TEN engine in the 787.
finding: In H1 2014 RR delivered first Trent XWB engines for the A350 launch customer and ran the XWB-97 for the A350-1000 and the Trent 1000-TEN upgrade for the 787.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: whilst the number of engine deliveries was down 1% in the period, OE revenue grew 5%, reflecting 16% higher Trent deliveries, partially offset by 10% lower business jet engine deliveries.
finding: H1 2014 civil OE revenue rose 5% on 16% more Trent widebody deliveries, offset by 10% fewer business-jet engines.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: On RB211s, we are seeing a combination of lower utilizations as aircraft are converted to freighters and more retirals. Revenue is down about GBP 70 million, and we expect an over-reduction RB211 revenue of about 25% for the full year.
finding: RR's legacy RB211 aftermarket was shrinking fast (revenue down about GBP 70m in H1 and about 25% for 2014) as aircraft were retired or converted to freighters.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: LLPs are high-value parts and many them are not covered by TotalCare. So we get this as incremental T&M revenue at the shop visits. As mentioned at the recent investor briefing, we continue to improve the reliability of our engines, which increases the time on wing and delays the overhaul. This improves overall margins, but delays the LLP sale
finding: Life-limited parts are sold time-and-material outside TotalCare, so better reliability improves RR margins but delays LLP revenue.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: This was particularly relevant to the Trent 700 in the period with the number of shop visits deferred. Importantly, our wide-body LTSA revenue continues to grow and is up 9%.
finding: Trent 700 shop visits were deferred in H1 2014, while RR's widebody long-term service agreement revenue grew 9%.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: reduce the flow of footprint by 20% by 2020 to make sure that we have the lean efficient machine ... that is the large part of the transformation that's going on at Rolls-Royce as we go from a low-volume engine manufacturer, bespoke tailors, as I've said to many of you, to a high-volume producer
finding: RR was moving from low-volume bespoke engine making to high-volume production, with a plan to cut its manufacturing footprint by 20% by 2020.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: in our model, we have the TotalCare model, which is driven by flying hours. Flying hours are fine at the moment. So my overview would be, no, we're not seeing any particular issues in terms of servicing associated with TotalCare
finding: RR's civil aftermarket is driven by flying hours under TotalCare, which held up in the 2014 slowdown while short-cycle businesses weakened.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: We've got about 600 engineers at the moment working purely on unit cost reductions. And generally, we know we have very good payback on those. Of course, while you have to make an investment upfront, on average, we see an IRR, in many cases, in excess of 40% in payback in sort of within 2 to 3 years.
finding: RR's unit-cost programme employs about 600 engineers and targets IRRs above 40% with a 2-3 year payback.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: when we talk about product cost, about half of it is unit cost and half of it is what we refer to as life cycle cost, which is aftermarket: improving reliability; being clever about the work scopes; sweating the asset; using serviceable use material
finding: RR splits product cost reduction roughly half OE unit cost and half aftermarket life-cycle cost (reliability, workscopes, serviceable material).

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: we're increasing the life of our engines on wing, which is saving us cost. So the example that Tony Wood gave in June was the life on wing of the Trent 700 has increased. That's a good thing for competition reasons, obviously, and also for cost reasons, financial reasons. But what that means is I need less spare parts
finding: Longer Trent 700 time on wing cuts RR's TotalCare costs and helps it compete, but reduces spare-parts load, so there is a trade-off between durability and aftermarket factory utilisation.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: we've got a significant amount of capacity that's been put in place, and you've all heard me give the example of Singapore in terms of the capacity that we've put in place there and the utilization of that capacity. Secondly, we've got load which is not increasing as much as we
finding: RR built capacity (e.g. Singapore) ahead of civil load that grew more slowly than expected, leaving under-utilised capacity that weighed on civil margins.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: In Civil aerospace, of 454 wide-body aircraft contested [ph] 2014, Rolls-Royce won 284. That's 62%; yes, 62%.
finding: RR won about 62% of contested wide-body engine orders in 2014, winning share where engines competed.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: The ramp-up in Trent XWB production is really only just beginning. We delivered 13 engines [ph], and we have over 1,500 orders in the pipeline last year. In December, we saw the XWB enter service with Qatar Airways.
finding: The Trent XWB entered service in December 2014 with over 1,500 engines on order.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: During the last few years, we've been investing in a major expansion in our manufacturing capacity, but that capacity build phase is now over. What we're really focused now is making those investments deliver
finding: By 2015 RR said its capacity build-out was complete and the priority was utilisation, not more capacity.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: Sunderland, as [ph] Singapore, has got a 250, 300 capability in terms of engine assembly... we did about 40... the delay in the programs, for example, the 787, impacts when that will be used... the delays that we've experienced from some of the programs means that we've got them -- gotten them a little bit too soon.
finding: RR built new assembly capacity ahead of demand; airframe delays such as the 787 left its Singapore line (capacity 250-300 engines) building only about 40 a year.
trigger: 787 programme delays
response: Capacity underutilised until volumes arrive

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: Aerospace turn is running at about 3.5 at the moment, still some opportunities to step that up... We've had some build rates moves with some of our major airframe partners that have caused some inventory to still be sitting on the book at the end of 2014.
finding: Airframers' build-rate changes left RR holding extra inventory, with aerospace inventory turns about 3.5.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: The fact that we delivered the XWB engine on time and to spec is very, very important for the future of this company.
finding: RR delivered the Trent XWB on time and to specification, unlike the troubled Trent 1000 launch.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We took a deliberate decision when we launched the Trent 1000 to actually take provisions against the launch programs there, so, essentially, the operating costs of those launch customers... as it's well known, the early versions of the aircraft and the engines had further engineering programs associated with them.
finding: RR provisioned upfront for the extra operating costs of Trent 1000 launch customers because early 787 engines needed further engineering, so RR bore the early-service shortfall.
trigger: Early Trent 1000/787 engineering and performance shortfalls
response: Provisioned launch customers' operating costs

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: So we don't believe that we need to continue to write down that asset, and we'll reverse that asset -- or that write-down in the second half of the year, which is about GBP 100 million. So this is purely being generated actually by improved technical performance.
finding: After Trent 1000 performance improved, RR released about GBP 100m of the launch-customer provision in 2015.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: 184, I think, was the number for 2014. I think we're likely to see that drop to around 140 level this year, maybe slightly higher than that... But we're likely to see it drop to sort of between 80 to 100, I would say, next year and a similar number for 2017.
finding: RR's Trent 700 deliveries were expected to fall from 184 (2014) to ~140 (2015) and 80-100 a year in 2016-17 as the A330ceo ran out.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: I think the number today is approximately 50% in terms of engine shipping, and that is set to grow with things like the new 900 order. And obviously, 200 engine is a very significant chunk... there are trickle of them of wins coming in from the campaigns that are out there at the moment.
finding: RR shipped about 50% of wide-body engines in 2015, helped by the ~200-engine Emirates Trent 900 order, and was winning a trickle of 787 Trent 1000 campaigns.
trigger: Emirates A380 re-order; Trent 1000 787 campaigns

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: So both on the Trent 1000, and interestingly, that's a project that we'll see fairly intense probably activity in the first few years as those engines are operated in relatively short segments intensively by the launch airlines.
finding: RR expected early, intense Trent 1000 shop-visit activity because 787 launch airlines fly the engines hard on short sectors.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And we're preparing for an increase in our wide-body engine production, an increase which doubles our production from around 300 to around 600 engines per year. And that is a reflection of a very strong order book and a growing market share.
finding: RR planned to double wide-body engine output from about 300 to about 600 a year on the back of its order book.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: I think we're carrying far too much fixed cost and we're not sufficiently flexible in managing the cost base in response to the changing market conditions. And actually, that's just unacceptable for a world-class business and particularly, where we're operating in a very competitive environment.
finding: RR's CEO diagnosed excess fixed cost and slow response to markets as the reason small revenue changes caused large profit swings.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Firstly, clearly, one of the things that we're doing is continuing to increase reliability, which does perversely, unfortunately, push out shop visits.
finding: Reliability improvements push out shop visits, which reduces RR's time-and-materials revenue in the short run.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: So I don't think this is a pricing/margin issue. This is absolutely about volume or flying hours utilization of the fleet for those legacy programs... It's going to require a bigger degree of change, I think, on the legacy than we expected.
finding: RR raised its expected fall in flying hours on legacy wide-body programmes during the new-aircraft transition; it saw this as a volume, not a pricing, problem.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: with our TotalCare programs, we take on the risk of maintaining these engines for our customers and we charge them by the hour... Well, the first thing we can do is make sure that we don't have to service the engine quite as often as we used to.
finding: Under TotalCare RR bears maintenance risk for a per-hour fee, so improving time to first shop visit directly lifts its services margin.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We are spending today about GBP 4 billion on sales -- on being a sales and engineering organization... we're talking about over the next 5 years reducing our footprint by 20%, and improving our output by about -- or increasing our output rather by about 80%.
finding: RR's cure for high operating gearing was fixed-cost reduction: a 20% smaller footprint producing about 80% more output over five years.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Our inventory turns are just over 3 at the moment. We believe a competitive benchmark is much more in the 4 to 5 range.
finding: RR's inventory turns (about 3) lagged its 4-5 benchmark, making inventory the main working-capital lever.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: In terms of the goals around the simplifying the -- or sorry, changing the network of external MRO shops, this is about our costs of handling our TotalCare, this is about reducing the cost. So it's introducing competition into the network there so that people can more effectively and we can more effectively shop around the network.
finding: RR restructured its MRO network (e.g. licensing Delta TechOps for XWB/7000) to create competition among overhaul shops and cut its own TotalCare costs.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We're transitioning from around about 70% outsourced value to around about 80% as we ramp up our XWB production. And the main change is the location of some of these suppliers which is a reflection of the where the market is and where our activity is.
finding: RR was raising outsourced content from about 70% to 80% of value as XWB production ramped, while moving suppliers towards Asia.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The Trent XWB is the fastest selling engine that we've had... I think I'm right that the order book at the moment is for XWB is roughly the same quantity as the installed base on Trent 700 at the moment.
finding: The sole-source A350 engine (Trent XWB) is RR's fastest-selling engine, with an order book about the size of the whole Trent 700 installed base.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: overall, we delivered just over 300 large civil engines, and we took orders for nearly 500 large civil engines during the year. The backlog is, therefore, up; and it's up about 4%
finding: In 2015 RR's large-engine orders (nearly 500) exceeded deliveries (just over 300), growing the backlog 4%.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: an GBP 84 million year-over-year movement on the Trent 1000, and that follows some detailed and positive engine analysis on the first service. This was recorded as a GBP 65 million in-year benefit from -- by reversing a balance sheet provision that we'd taken to previously impair contractual aftermarket rights.
finding: In 2015, before its durability crisis, RR judged the Trent 1000's first shop visits positive enough to reverse a GBP 65m impairment, which it later had to revisit.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: from 2000, we've moved to well over 10% improvement on the 2000 original carbon emissions with Trent XWB.
finding: RR markets fuel-burn gains by engine generation: the Trent XWB is more than 10% better than 2000-era engines.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: in 2015, in our Aerospace products, we achieved a product cost reduction overall of nearly 2%.
finding: RR's aerospace unit costs fell by only about 2% in 2015.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: If you take from, say, 2005 to 2025, then we are more than doubling the number of large engines in our installed base. ... we're increasing by a factor of 100, more than 100, the number of engines that are over 10 years old.
finding: RR's large-engine installed base more than doubles between 2005 and 2025, and engines over 10 years old grow more than 100-fold, shifting its service model.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So we have made changes in our repair and overhaul network, and we've made changes to increase that capacity, to increase that flexibility and actually, as a consequence as well, to increase the competition within the network and so provide better value.
finding: RR expanded its MRO network and added competition within it to handle a larger, older fleet.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: it's clear our priority has to be to make sure that we can deliver to schedule as we go at this ramp, and we are doing that and we'll continue to really focus on that.
finding: During the ramp RR put on-time delivery to airframers ahead of inventory and cost savings.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: this is, in the round, between 2010 and 2020, one program of industrial transformation that is changing the nature of our facilities.
finding: RR describes 2010-2020 as one decade-long programme of industrial transformation to reshape its facilities for competitiveness from 2020 (an analyst put the 10-year capex at over GBP 4bn).

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: in 2015, as a reminder, we supplied just over 300 large engines in total ... This year, we expect to deliver 400 large civil engines, and we're on track for that, having delivered 164 in the first half. ... We're moving the volume run rates from around about 30 a month to around about 40 a month.
finding: RR ramped large civil engine deliveries from just over 300 in 2015 to about 400 in 2016 by raising the run-rate from about 30 to 40 a month.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the concern is simply are in terms of our resource and the significant demands that we are currently placing on our engineering teams as they seek to help with this ramp up of volume at the same time as bringing some very sophisticated new engines into production.
finding: RR's main constraint in 2016 was engineering capacity, stretched between the volume ramp and several new-engine introductions.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we will be able to reduce the time it takes to develop a new product by the order of about 20%. And we'll have completed that project -- it's going to take several years. We'll have completed that project by around about 2020.
finding: RR aimed to cut new-product development time by about 20% through digital product definition, to be completed around 2020.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: after about 4 months, so far, we've taken about 25%, a little bit under 25%, away from the lead time that it takes us to assemble a Trent 1000 in Singapore. The good news is that we think we can take this quite a bit further, an additional 15% to 20% coming out on that particular engine.
finding: RR cut Trent 1000 assembly lead time by nearly 25% in four months and planned to apply the same methods to the XWB to add capacity.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: in 2010, we only had about 200 of these that were 8 years or older. Today, we've got about 500 that are 8 years or older, and in 2020, we'll have about 900 that are 8 years or older.
finding: RR's Trent fleet aged 8 years or more grew from about 200 in 2010 to 500 in 2016 and 900 by 2020, raising transition risk to its aftermarket.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: looking to the, say, Trent 1000 and XWB, we can see an increase in -- of more than 10% in the value that we will now consolidate in aftermarket revenues coming in.
finding: Taking full control of ITP raised the aftermarket value RR consolidates on the Trent 1000 and XWB by more than 10%.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we have teams embedded in these suppliers that work with them on a day-to-day basis and solve the problems as and when they arise. I'm not pretending that there are no issues
finding: RR manages forging and casting supplier risk, shared with GE and P&W, by embedding its own teams at suppliers.
trigger: Analyst concern that RR, GE and P&W rely on the same forging and casting suppliers during their ramps
response: Embedded supplier teams

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: XWB is new engine. Airlines are taking this engine for the first time. We need to put more spare engines around so that we can satisfy that.
finding: With a new engine type RR must seed more spare engines around the network to support airlines, which also adds profitable spare-engine sales.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: T&M was down a lot. I think, in roughly revenue terms, it was around GBP 100 million, something like that.
finding: RR's legacy time-and-materials aftermarket revenue fell by about GBP 100m in H1 2016 as older fleets retired.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: around about 13 airplanes have been placed in the first half. And we have a further 28 where owners have been identified. And that's a big improvement compared with where we were a year ago.
finding: RR actively found new operators for parked Trent 800 777s (13 placed in H1 2016, 28 more identified) to restore aftermarket flying hours.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we have to come up with a replacement program that doesn't interfere with our airlines' operations ... the team worked out an alternative way of changing these blades that resulted in an 80% reduction in the time that it took.
finding: RR reacted to the Trent 1000 blade crisis by cutting blade-change time 80% to limit airline disruption and its own costs.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: if an aircraft is on the ground for 12 months instead of 3 months, then we're clearly going to forgo a lot of aftermarket revenue.
finding: Because RR is paid per flying hour, it acts to shorten aircraft transitions and downtime between owners.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Based on current projections by 2020, broadly, we're expecting to deliver the same number of XWBs as our total large engine deliveries last year.
finding: RR projected Trent XWB deliveries by 2020 to equal its total large-engine deliveries of 2015 (A350 ramp).

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: deliveries of the V2500 modules dropping off quite sharply after 2017, although we are currently enjoying a bit of an uplift to revenues because of issues elsewhere in the A320 supply chain.
finding: RR got a temporary V2500 revenue boost from problems elsewhere in the A320 supply chain, before V2500 module deliveries fell away after 2017.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: we have relatively -- have a relatively small and young fleet today as the average age of our Trents is only around 7 to 8 years. ... The significant growth in our market share over the next few years means it's going to take some significant time for our average age to mature
finding: RR's Trent fleet averaged only 7-8 years old in 2016, so its aftermarket payoff from share gains lags for many years.

speaker: Eric Schulz, President Civil Aerospace
quote: One was Malaysia that started to stop 13 777s with the Trent powered ... I look at 2016, we've done 24 Trent-powered transitions as compared to 10 last year at the same period. So clearly, we have accelerated.
finding: After Trent-powered 777 parkings in 2015, RR set up dedicated transition teams and more than doubled Trent transitions in 2016.
trigger: Malaysia Airlines parked 13 Trent-powered 777s and an airline bankruptcy parked aircraft (2015)
response: Created dedicated transition teams and accelerated Trent-powered aircraft transitions

speaker: Eric Schulz, President Civil Aerospace
quote: in 2015, we had about 3,500 engines in the world flying. And within 10 years, we will barely double that number.
finding: RR expected its large-engine fleet of about 3,500 in 2015 to roughly double within 10 years.

speaker: Eric Schulz, President Civil Aerospace
quote: We have to grow our capacity, especially on the large engines. And it's growth of about 20% year-over-year. We've done 20% last year. We are doing 20% this year. We'll have to do 20% next year. Until a point where we reach a peak of about 600 large engines a year.
finding: RR planned about 20% annual large-engine capacity growth to a peak of about 600 large engines a year.

speaker: Eric Schulz, President Civil Aerospace
quote: we have 3 programs in parallel that are -- that is unprecedented in Rolls-Royce, with 3 big programs, which are very, very close to each other, the Trent 7000, the Trent 1000-TEN and the Trent XWB 97k.
finding: RR ran three large-engine development programmes in parallel in 2016-17, which it called unprecedented.

speaker: Andrew Dickinson, CFO Civil Aerospace
quote: Approximately about 20% of our costs occur outside of the shop visits ... we see the cost of the second shop visit, about 1.2x the cost of the first shop visit. ... So we expect second shop visits to occur between years 8 and years 12
finding: RR's service-contract cost model has about 20% of costs outside shop visits, a second shop visit costing 1.2 times the first, and second visits in years 8-12.

speaker: Andrew Dickinson, CFO Civil Aerospace
quote: as we go on market share from the 30% today to the 50% on wide-body over the course of the next 5 to 6 years.
finding: RR expected its widebody engine market share to rise from about 30% in 2016 to 50% within 5-6 years.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: It will grow with the XWB delivery profile, because as I think everybody knows, XWB actually has, yes, quite a high proportion of RRSPs.
finding: RR shares risk on the Trent XWB with a high proportion of risk-and-revenue-sharing partners, who also take part of the aftermarket.

speaker: Andrew Dickinson, CFO Civil Aerospace
quote: if we think the first shop visit is between years 4 and years 6, and under today's accounting, we are -- we're collecting revenue from day 1.
finding: Under TotalCare, RR collects flying-hour cash from day one while the first shop visit comes in years 4-6, so young fleets are cash-generative before costs arrive.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We are readying during this year now 3 large engines for our Civil business for entry into service very, very soon.
finding: In 2017 RR was bringing three new large engines into service at once (Trent XWB-97, Trent 1000 TEN, Trent 7000), a heavy concurrent development load.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the aftermarket revenue from those new engines not really coming through and completely dominating but being held back a little by the older engines with high-margin spares-type activity falling off.
finding: During the transition to new engines, RR's aftermarket was squeezed as high-margin spares on older engines fell before new-engine service revenue built up.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So the 2 key drivers of cash over the next 10 years are probably the XWB and the Trent 700.
finding: RR expected its cash over the next decade to come mainly from the Trent XWB (A350) and the ageing Trent 700 (A330) fleets, both Airbus platforms.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the 6x increase in installed base by the time we get to 2020. And if we look at the backlog of future orders, we've got 8x the current installed base out there in the backlog.
finding: RR expected the Trent XWB installed base to grow sixfold by 2020, with a backlog of eight times the current fleet.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Of this, sales of spare engines to joint ventures generated a revenue of about GBP 277 million.
finding: RR earned about GBP 277m in 2016 from selling spare engines to its leasing joint ventures.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the V2500 module revenues did decline by about 10% as production slowed, obviously, again, as Airbus transitions to the A320neo.
finding: RR's V2500 OE module revenue fell as Airbus moved to the A320neo.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: in absolute numbers, actually, the numbers weren't that different in '16 and '15. And I don't think we expect it to be that different in '17, maybe a modest increase in '17. But we're clearly seeing less activity on the -- on some of the legacy programs.
finding: RR's civil shop visit numbers were roughly flat in 2015-17, with legacy-programme activity declining and new-engine activity growing.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the first engine has been in service for over 2 years now, and the early signs from XWB are very good. Yes, we have had a few maintenance issues that are sort of perfectly normal, but we haven't had any serious issues.
finding: In early 2017 RR reported that the Trent XWB had had no serious in-service issues after two years, in contrast to the Trent 1000.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: volume production's up 37%, deliveries up 27%, so I think we're addressing that question. Importantly, behind that, and we've been fairly open, the new engines are still -- or from an OE perspective, we lose cash every time we ship one of those engines out of the door
finding: RR prioritised ramping large-engine volumes even though every new engine shipped loses cash at OE.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we are continuing to concentrate on engineering delivery and delivering important milestones on our future programs around Ultrafan, the big gearbox. And later this month, yes, it's August 1, so later this month, we'll be testing our Advance 3, which is the engine that sits behind Ultrafan.
finding: In 2017 RR kept funding UltraFan technology milestones (power gearbox, Advance3 core test) while ramping current production.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: a big issue for us right now is the in-service challenges that we are facing in our Civil Aerospace business. Now this is a scheduled program of maintenance, particularly around our Trent 1000 engine which is powering the Dreamliner, causing some problems for us and for our customers
finding: By mid-2017 RR acknowledged Trent 1000 in-service problems on the 787 were disrupting customers and required a scheduled maintenance programme.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: The growth in the installed engine base, right now just over around 3,000 or so wide-body jet engines, we'd hope to push that beyond that over the next few years as we increase our production ramp-up and deliver around 500 engines or so a year.
finding: RR's widebody installed base was about 3,000 engines in 2017, with production heading to about 500 a year.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: 85 Trent XWB engines were produced -- sorry, was -- were invoiced in the first half of the year, 41 in the prior year. Aftermarket growth, led by flying hours were -- which were up 15% for the in-production Trent fleet
finding: RR more than doubled Trent XWB deliveries to 85 in H1 2017, and in-production Trent flying hours rose 15%.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: there are a handful of issues with the current Trent 1000. There are about 400 to 500 engines affected. And basically, some parts of the engine are turning out not to last as long in service as their original design lives.
finding: RR disclosed that about 400-500 Trent 1000 engines had parts wearing out before their design lives, forcing early replacement.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we believe that, with the Trent 1000 TEN, the one that is coming into service at the end of this year, then -- we have addressed all the issues that have been identified. But if you look across our fleet of large gas turbines, there are issues with pretty much all of them.
finding: RR's fix for Trent 1000 durability was to build it into the next variant (TEN) while retrofitting the existing fleet, and it treats durability issues as normal for large engines.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So instead of having to have engines that typically would return every sort of 2,000 cycles, now it's sort of 5,000 cycles or even 7,000 cycles.
finding: RR says large-engine time on wing has risen over the years from about 2,000 to 5,000-7,000 cycles between shop visits.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: improvement in the economics of the XWB engines, which we are reducing the loss on the sale, the cash loss on the sale of those engines. And we are, as again, we confirmed a couple of days ago, expecting that number to get to the breakeven position by 2020.
finding: RR targets cutting the Trent XWB OE cash loss per engine to breakeven by 2020, so a new engine's OE loss is expected to close over roughly 5-6 years from entry into service.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Civil Aerospace delivered a record 483 engines, up 35%, and also achieved a 37% reduction in the cash deficit on the XWB-84
finding: RR delivered a record 483 widebody engines in 2017 and cut the XWB-84 cash deficit by 37%.

doc: FY 2017 Results Fixed Income Call, Mar 2018
speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: the 900 intermediate pressure turbine blade, and in the 1000, the ITP high-pressure blade and also the compressor rotor 1 and 2. ... The cumulative cash costs of that -- those 2 engine issues in 2017 was GBP 170 million. And we guided today that that's going to double to around GBP 340 million in 2018.
finding: In March 2018 RR put Trent 900/1000 durability costs at GBP 170m (2017) doubling to GBP 340m (2018); these estimates were later raised several times.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: I'm particularly encouraged with our over 35% in actual engines delivered, to nearly 500 engines; over 500 engines produced
finding: RR raised large-engine production over 35% in 2017, with XWB at about 40% of large engines.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We've almost tripled our repair and overhaul capacity to deal with the Trent 1000. We've tripled our capacity to provide the vital components that are necessary. And it obviously takes some time for that capacity to come on stream and be effective, which is why we've seen this issue escalate.
finding: RR responded to the Trent 1000 crisis by tripling MRO and component capacity, but the lag in adding capacity let the disruption escalate.
trigger: Trent 1000 premature wear
response: triple MRO and component capacity; redesign parts
lag: capacity takes time to come on stream

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We're guiding today to around 550 engines delivered. And these are engines delivered, that's invoiced. We build -- we built just over 500 engines in 2017. And I think, in 2018, we'll be heading towards building around 600 engines or so to deliver those 550.
finding: RR guided about 550 widebody deliveries for 2018 (about 600 built), up from 483.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: 2,500 engines on order, so good visibility, going back to that point about the visibility of revenues. And 1,400 of that 2,500 is the XWB.
finding: RR's order book was 2,500 widebody engines, 1,400 of them Trent XWB (sole source on A350).

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Cash deficit per engine, currently an average of GBP 1.6 million. We're aiming to get towards GBP 0.4 million cash deficit per engine by 2022 or over the next 5 years or so. The in-service fleet, 4,400, we think, is going to be growing at around 8% on a compound annual growth rate
finding: RR's 5-year plan (2017-22): OE cash deficit down to GBP 0.4m per engine, fleet growing about 8% a year, flying hours about 10%, deliveries about 5% CAGR, R&D and capex stable.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: yes, the A330neo will be delayed in terms of its entry into service versus the original time plan. And that was actually the case with 97K and the A350-1000 as well. ... We have undoubtedly played our part in the delay for A330neo.
finding: RR admitted its Trent 7000 contributed to the A330neo entry-into-service delay, as the XWB-97 had on the A350-1000.
trigger: A330neo EIS
response: accept share of delay

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the Trent 900 was designed around 2001, and the Trent 1000 was derived -- designed around 2005. And yes, we use different design tools as we move forward
finding: RR argued newer design tools make newer engines (XWB) less prone to Trent 900/1000-type durability problems, while not guaranteeing it.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: moving from just over 300 large engines per annum, to this year, where we hope to deliver more than 600 large engines per annum. ... And about 40% of those large engines were XWBs
finding: RR doubled large-engine output to over 600 a year for 2018, with XWBs about 40% of volume.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So our Trent 1000 engine powers the 787 and we have about a 40% share of the 787 market today and that's about 11% of the total Rolls-Royce fleet for large wide body aircraft.
finding: In 2018 RR held about 40% of the 787 engine market (in-service), about 11% of its widebody fleet.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: There are about 380 engines that are affected in this way and gradually we will replace them. At the moment, we don't have all of those new designs fully certified and available.
finding: About 380 Trent 1000 engines needed component replacements over several years, with fixes still being certified in 2018.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we have implemented this much more regular inspection. ... that will cause an incremental cost in 2018 and probably a little bit of an incremental cost in 2019 as well. And it's causing additional disruption to our customers, for which of course we are sorry. But we absolutely prioritize issues like safety
finding: RR put safety first by accepting more frequent Trent 1000 inspections, with more customer disruption and cost, while keeping its cash guidance.
trigger: regulator-agreed increased Trent 1000 inspections
response: accept cost; maintain guidance

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: since the beginning of this year, we now have approximately 50% more turbine blade capacity than we had at the start of the year.
finding: RR raised turbine blade capacity by about 50% in H1 2018 to deal with Trent 1000 turbine durability.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: A crucial question a few years ago was, could we deal with the volume ramp-up from approximately 300 engines to approximately 600 large engines per year, okay? So that's getting there, well over 500 engines last year, nudging towards 600 this year.
finding: RR doubled large-engine output from about 300 to about 600 a year, while bringing 4 new civil engines into service in 3 years.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: 15 years or so ago, we had about 1 in 7 of the large jet engines flying around. Today, we have about 1 in 3. And we have an order book that will take us to about 1 in 2 in a few years' time.
finding: RR's share of large (widebody) engines in service rose from about 1 in 7 to 1 in 3, with an order book pointing to about 1 in 2.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: So the Trent 7000, for example, we've transferred the pipe supply from Spain into Mexico. We get about a GBP 50,000 benefit per engine from that.
finding: RR cuts OE cost in small steps, such as moving sourcing to low-cost countries (GBP 50k per Trent 7000) and saving 2 tonnes of forging material per fan case (GBP 50k).

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: So the installed base will grow from 4,400 to around 6,500. Here are the assumptions that we've taken, around 550 to 600 deliveries per annum, and this won't be linear completely over the years but it's pretty -- that's a good guide. And we have about 100 to 150 retirements per annum
finding: RR's 2018 plan assumed 550-600 widebody deliveries and 100-150 retirements a year, taking the installed base from 4,400 to 6,500 by 2022, with 2,400 engines on order.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: The major shop visits are when the engine reaches the point of its regular service interval, whether that be 5, 6, 7 years. In 2017, we had 240 of those. In 2022, we're going to have around 650.
finding: RR expected major shop visits to rise from 240 (2017) to about 650 (2022) as the installed base matures.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So this isn't -- we haven't suddenly tripled our overall MRO capacity, what we've tripled is the ability to deal with Trent 1000.
finding: RR's crisis response added temporary, dedicated Trent 1000 MRO lines rather than tripling overall MRO capacity, and brought forward blade capacity it needed anyway.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we cannot be sure about XWB and its sort of -- and the durability of all the components until 20 to 30 engines or so get to the first shop visit. And it's simply too new.
finding: RR does not claim an engine's durability until 20-30 engines reach first shop visit, showing awareness of durability risk before scale.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: On Trent 7000, then, as you know, it is derived from Trent 1000. And so what we will be doing is making very certain, when we start making volumes of Trent 7000, which we haven't started yet, that any modifications that -- and design improvements that we can take from the Trent 1000 will be incorporated
finding: RR carried Trent 1000 fixes into the derivative Trent 7000 before volume production to contain the risk.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We are now sitting a well below that peak of just under 50 aircraft on the ground and increased MRO capacity is absolutely keeping pace.
finding: Trent 1000 AOG peaked at just under 50 aircraft around mid-2018; RR expanded MRO capacity to keep pace.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We've been on this journey of 300, 400, 500 and hopefully, this year about 600 engines being -- large engines being produced.
finding: RR ramped large-engine output from 300 to about 600 a year by 2018.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Engine deliveries grew by 24% to 259, wide-body engines in the first half of the year. And again, with reinforcing Warren's comments there, looking at a number there in the high 500s, if not getting towards 600
finding: RR delivered 259 widebody engines in H1 2018 (up 24%) and expected high 500s for the year, about 45% XWB and 28% Trent 1000.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Engine flying hour growth grew at 20% over the period, one of the standout numbers in today's results, I think. We have a growing fleet, but we also have a growing flying hour growth as well
finding: RR's large-engine flying hours grew 20% in H1 2018 on a fleet of just under 4,600, helped by a younger fleet.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: the XWB-84, now entering its fourth year over 2 million flying hours now, 99.9% dispatch reliability and the 1 or 2 engines that we have brought in for routine inspection or to carry something out are performing very well
finding: The Trent XWB-84, most of RR's order book, was proving durable in its fourth year of service.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: As a precautionary measure, then we are changing the design, we're taking the lessons out of the Pack Bs and the Pack Cs around the compressor that we're dealing with at the moment. And rather than wait for potentially those issues to arise on the TEN, we are redesigning the corresponding blades on the TEN as well.
finding: RR redesigned TEN compressor blades as a precaution rather than waiting for failures, and included the cost in its estimates.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The identified issues, it came to light back end of 2016 through '17, and it was described as a dynamic situation because we were learning about what those issues are.

lag: issues surfaced late 2016; compressor redesign need understood Q1 2018

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: But as far as these issues are concerned, that we're dealing with at the moment, we think we have them fully scoped.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The 84k version of the XWB continues with excellent performance in service, over 99.9% dispatch reliability. We hit the 3 million flying hours milestone a little while ago.
finding: The Trent XWB-84, RR's sole-source A350 engine, was performing well with over 99.9% dispatch reliability.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We've dealt with the Pack C first because most of the 600 Trent 1000s that are in service are Pack C. So clearly, to minimize disruption, we had to deal with that one first.
finding: RR ordered its Trent 1000 fixes by fleet exposure, Pack C (most of the ~600 in-service engines) first, then TEN, then the small Pack B fleet.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Just to put that in perspective, the number in the second half of 2018 oscillated between 40 and 45 engines. And as we speak in Q1, it's around 35 engines. Today, it happens to be 31.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We're expected to deliver approximately 500 engines. We actually only made 480 -- or we made 480 deliveries. We made more than that, but we didn't get them all tested and out the door.
finding: RR missed its 2018 large-engine delivery target (480 against about 500), mainly because of Trent 7000 industrialisation problems.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And indeed, we did run into issues, particularly around the Trent 7000, where we had some initial learning curve, basically, poor yield on final test.
finding: New-engine production ramps are a recurring RR execution risk: the Trent 7000 suffered poor final-test yield during industrialisation (32 engines in 2018, 11 in January 2019).

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: This cash outflow from the major shop visits, which is up from 240 to 286, and also from the check and repair shop visits growing from 356 to 569.
finding: RR's major shop visits rose to 286 in 2018 and check-and-repair visits jumped to 569, partly driven by Trent 1000 maintenance.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Widebody sales went to 469. We did ship 11 further. We're guiding to 520 for 2019. Bottom left-hand corner, a reminder that around 2,300 widebody engines that are on order
finding: RR delivered 469 widebody engines in 2018, guided to 520 for 2019, and had about 2,300 widebody engines on order.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Where we are now with Trent 1000 TEN, we are confident that we have solved the fundamental turbomachinery issues that have caused all the hiatus in 2018.
finding: In Feb 2019 RR said it had solved the Trent 1000 TEN's fundamental issues; within months the TEN HPT blade proved worse than expected, showing over-optimism.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: I think we're in the zone of 500 to 600. We know we have the capacity and the run rate to deliver at over 600 per annum if we need to because we've done that. We've done 160-plus in a quarter over the last couple of years.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: So spare engines, 50 spare engines delivered in 2018. And spare engines are an important part of the whole ecosystem for the airlines and ourselves, particularly important in 2018, of course, for the Trent 1000 issues
finding: RR delivered 50 spare engines in 2018 (about 60 expected in 2019), which it uses to limit customer disruption.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: These things are consumable parts in a jet engine. And what's happening is that they're actually being consumed a little bit faster than we anticipated when we introduced the limited life on those parts. ... It's been observed with some airlines, notably Singapore because they have large -- larger fleet of these engines.
finding: RR first described the Trent 1000 TEN HPT blade problem as parts being 'consumed a little bit faster' than expected, notably on Singapore Airlines' arduous operations.
trigger: accelerated TEN HPT blade cracking at Singapore Airlines
response: replace blades early, continue redesign

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We expect to be able to manage this problem with the normal service operations within the cost limits that we talked about a few weeks ago and within the timescales that we talked about a few weeks ago.
finding: In April 2019 RR said the TEN HPT problem was containable within existing cost and time guidance. It later reversed this, adding GBP 400m and delaying the fix to H1 2021 (Nov 2019).
trigger: TEN HPT blade early cracking
response: claimed containable within existing guidance

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And the new design of turbine blade is in progress, it's being tested at the moment, it's being live tested. It's making good progress through that live test. And it will be available towards the back end of this year
finding: In April 2019 RR promised the TEN HPT blade redesign by late 2019; the date later slipped to H1 2021, a pattern of optimistic fix timelines.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: I was referring to almost 0.5 million passengers in Japan alone that had been affected or had their journeys affected by the Trent 1000. So this was a big deal and it's a big deal for our customers and our customers' customers
finding: RR's CEO acknowledged the scale of Trent 1000 disruption to airline customers, with about 0.5 million passengers affected in Japan alone.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We had between 40 and 50 airplanes on the ground for most of the second half of last year. In the first quarter of this year, to a roundabout, now that number's between 30 and 40. Actually, it's in the lower 30s for -- at the moment. And we expect to be in single digits
finding: Trent 1000 AOG peaked at 40-50 aircraft in H2 2018 and was in the low 30s by May 2019, with a target of single digits by end-2019.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: as of the end of 2018, 4,700 large engines in store. That's 25% greater than the number 5 years ago. They're more efficient engines so airlines tend to use them more
finding: RR's large-engine installed base reached about 4,700 at end-2018, up 25% in five years, with flying hours up 14% in 2018.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: That rate improved in the first quarter of the year and sustained in the second quarter of the year. And so by the halfway through the year, we've delivered over 50 of these engines and we're comfortable that, that is now in production.
finding: After a delivery crisis around the turn of 2019, RR recovered Trent 7000 output to over 50 engines in the first half.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So the life limit of 1,000 cycles, let's be clear, is completely unacceptable for a typical customer. And so we were redesigning the turbine blades. However, we found that some of these blades come off a couple of hundred cycles before then and need replacing sooner. So even more unacceptable for our customers.
finding: The Trent 1000 TEN HPT blade durability fell short even of an interim 1,000-cycle life limit, affecting about one third of the TEN fleet.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: That is putting an additional load on our repair and overhaul facilities. ... this additional load is extending the turnaround times in those shops. And that means that for the Pack Bs and Pack Cs ... we are going to take a little bit longer to return those fleets to a position of single-digit aircraft on ground.
finding: RR's MRO capacity was the binding constraint: new TEN problems delayed its single-digit AOG target, showing how installed-base problems spread across variants.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: And you can see the wide-body deliveries, 257 delivered. We've put 14 in there, that's made up of 239 installed and 18 spare engines
finding: RR delivered 257 widebody engines in H1 2019 (239 installed, 18 spares).

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we invoiced 41 Trent 700s pretty much coming to the end of its OE life. But starting its OE life, the Trent 7000s, 61 -- sorry, 54 Trent 7000s and just 7 Trent 700s. So a very successful transition to that new engine.
finding: RR moved from the Trent 700 to the Trent 7000 on the A330 family: 54 Trent 7000s and 7 Trent 700s in H1 2019, against 41 Trent 700s a year earlier.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And if I'd been standing here a few years ago, you might have seen about 600 in that box. And you're looking at 500 today. That is where we are in terms of build rates.
finding: RR cut its expected annual large-engine deliveries from about 600 to about 500 as widebody build rates fell.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we can see going through the 6,500 mark in a few years' time. The 257-or-so engines invoiced in the first half of the year, offset by about 36 retirements in the first half of this year
finding: RR's large-engine installed base was heading past 6,500, with about 36 retirements against about 257 deliveries per half.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the fleet leaders are getting to the time when it's due, but actually the engines are performing very well. And so they're not actually -- we haven't had as many shop visits as we would have expected so far.
finding: Early Trent XWB engines needed fewer shop visits than expected, showing good durability on RR's A350 engine.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The large fleet is about 1,000 engines at the moment. So out of around 5,000, we've got roughly 4,000 Trents and roughly 1,000 older engines. They are time and materials.
finding: RR's installed base was about 5,000 large engines (4,000 Trents, 1,000 older engines on time and materials).

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Most of Rolls-Royce production facilities are used to create components. And a lot of those components are going into servicing the 5,000 engines rather than assembling the 500 or 600 engines.
finding: RR's fixed capacity sits mainly in component manufacturing that serves the installed base, so lower OE rates do not strand much overhead.

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Simon Burr, Director of Engineering & Technology - Civil Aerospace
quote: The issue at hand is not the blade's materials or how it's made, it's the cooling. ... We're increasing the amount of cooling air and making a slight redistribution of some of those holes that create the film
finding: RR traced the Trent 1000 TEN HPT blade problem to cooling, not materials, and its fix adds cooling air and redistributes the film-cooling holes.

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Simon Burr, Director of Engineering & Technology - Civil Aerospace
quote: So it's designed to operate up to 76,000 pounds of thrust, back seat, from 74,000. The vantage point is in the take-off on climb, that's what we've -- that's the design point we have to worry about.
finding: Explaining the TEN HPT blade problem, RR's engineering head noted the engine is designed to operate up to 76,000 lb of thrust, up from 74,000 lb, with take-off and climb as the critical design point for the blade.

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Simon Burr, Director of Engineering & Technology - Civil Aerospace
quote: the turbine blades fell off, deteriorating faster than anticipated from the original design. ... we have to do a series of arduous tests by, first of all, ourselves and then Boeing and then our regulators that we've got satisfactory life.
finding: The TEN blades wore faster than designed, and any redesigned blade must pass RR's tests, then Boeing's, then the regulators', which sets the lead time for a Trent 1000 fix or upgrade.

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Simon Burr, Director of Engineering & Technology - Civil Aerospace
quote: It's a recurring inspection regime to make sure the engine performs in the air, take-off and in the air [ in common ] as expected. ... that's led to our strategy in terms of overall management of the fleet until the new blade is in-service.
finding: Until the redesigned blade was certified, RR managed the TEN fleet with a recurring inspection regime guided by an in-service model of blade wear.

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we discovered cracking in compressors that we worked out would have a potential safety issue. And therefore, we had to instigate a regime of inspections with removals of defective components and replacement of defective components to ensure safety of the fleet. And all of those inspections and the removals led to effectively overwhelming our repair and overhaul network
finding: RR framed the Trent 1000 crisis as a durability problem that turned into a capacity problem: mandated inspections overwhelmed its MRO network, grounding aircraft and generating customer costs.

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We now have one issue, the high-pressure turbine blade on the TEN version of the engine. ... we expected to introduce -- to have a tick in that box ... and be installing that in the early part of next year, but recent testing has shown that we can't achieve the durability that we want to achieve
finding: RR admitted a further slip in the Trent 1000 TEN HPT blade fix after testing missed durability targets, showing repeated schedule over-optimism on fixes.
trigger: TEN HPT blade redesign failed durability testing
response: delay fix, take bigger charge

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So you should look for the trajectory from where we are now to single-digit aircraft on ground by halfway through next year.
finding: RR publicly committed to reducing Trent 1000 aircraft-on-ground to single digits by mid-2020.

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we only do this when the engine is in for an overhaul, when it's actually needed. This isn't like a sort of consumer world where you sort of have a product recall
finding: RR rolls durability fixes into the fleet only at natural overhauls rather than a recall, so retrofit takes several years (e.g. 25% of Package C refitted).

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We've also carried out a detailed financial review of the Trent 7000 of customer contracts undertaken. I don't expect any material impact on profit or cash on the Trent 7000.
finding: RR ring-fenced the Trent 7000 (A330neo) from the Trent 1000 TEN problems, stating no material profit or cash impact.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we are confident that, that GBP 578 million of cash cost in 2019 is the peak year of cash costs for Trent 1000. So we are beyond that peak. As we look forward in 2020 to single-digit position around the midyear, then we'll be underpinning that with more spare engines
finding: Trent 1000 remediation peaked at GBP 578m of cash cost in 2019 (before GBP 173m insurance); RR's fix was to extend MRO capacity and add spare engines.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: It's today just over 10% of our installed fleet, but it's approximately half of our wide-body deliveries. And it's on a journey to be around 1/3 of our fleet in the mid-term.
finding: The sole-source Trent XWB made up about half of RR's widebody deliveries and was set to become a third of its fleet.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the Trent 7000 powers the A30 -- A330neo. And we're putting all the lessons we've learned from the Trent 1000 into that engine. It is based on the same architecture as the Trent 1000 TEN.
finding: RR carries durability lessons from the Trent 1000 into derivative engines on the same architecture (Trent 7000 on the sole-source A330neo).

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we will still be at north of 6,000 wide-body engines in a few years. Because the size of the installed base is about the retirements and the rate of retirement as well as the rate of new aeroplanes going into the market.
finding: RR judges its business by installed base, which it expected to exceed 6,000 widebody engines, rather than by annual deliveries.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Capacity and capital. Simple as that. I mean, we -- it's a new engine. It's obviously had issues.
finding: RR admits its Trent 1000 spare engine pool was too small because of capacity and capital limits, a cause of the grounding crisis; it tripled the pool once it could.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: sometimes, we end up with a great idea to extend the life or reduce the cost. And then 2 years later, in in-service, we find some issue. And those are the sorts of issues that I'm talking about that crop up regularly.
finding: RR expects in-service problems as a normal cost of pushing time on wing and cutting cost, but calls the Trent 1000 unprecedented in its history.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The Trent 1000 has been absolutely unprecedented in our history. That's what everybody tells me.
finding: RR treats the Trent 1000 crisis (estimated by analysts at about GBP 2.5bn) as a one-off, not its normal in-service cost, which it had put at about four issues and GBP 200m at a time.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: 2019 was a pivotal year for the resolution of our Trent 1000 engine durability challenges. We have made significant progress and have now achieved fixes for 8 out of the 9 issues.
finding: RR worked through the Trent 1000 durability crisis issue by issue, taking a GBP 1.36bn net exceptional charge in 2019 that led to a reported loss.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Civil Aerospace widebody engine-flying hours were approximately 40% lower in the first 4 months of the year. This reflected a fall of 90% in April
finding: COVID cut RR's widebody flying hours by about 90% in April 2020.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: In May, we announced the largest restructuring of Civil Aerospace we've ever undertaken, fundamentally resizing to align our capacity with expected future demand and save at least GBP 1.3 billion of ongoing costs across the group.
finding: RR resized civil capacity to lower expected demand within about two months of the COVID collapse.
trigger: COVID grounding of fleets (March-April 2020)
response: Restructuring announced May 2020

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We've put in place a process now to check all engines, over 2,300 cycles, on a regular basis. And until a permanent solution is found, we'll now replace this part as standard at the first shop visit.
finding: RR dealt with the Trent XWB-84 IPC blade issue by inspecting early and replacing the part at the first shop visit, avoiding customer disruption.

response: Regular checks and standard part replacement; financial impact not material

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Notwithstanding this matter, the Trent XWB remains the most successful engine launch we have ever had. And the early performance of this program has been successful both operationally and financially.
finding: RR sees the Trent XWB (sole source on the A350) as its best engine launch, operationally and financially, and a model for new programmes.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: The lower flying hours this year and in our forecast means that more of our Trent 1000 engines will be able to have the final fix installed at the next shop visit, reducing forecast shop visits and customer disruption costs and saving around GBP 300 million.
finding: Lower flying let RR fit the final Trent 1000 fix at scheduled shop visits, cutting remediation and compensation costs.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we expect our large engine flying hours in the full year 2020 to be 45% of the 2019 levels, and you can see that in the table there up at the top, before recovering to approximately 70% of 2019 levels in 2021 and 90% of 2019 levels in 2022. We don't expect a full recovery until 2024.
finding: In August 2020 RR's base case had widebody flying back to 2019 levels only in 2024.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Net-net, we're shrinking our capacity by about 1/3. We remain committed to retaining our expertise and our capability, and we will continue to focus on the high-value manufacturing and services that differentiate us.
finding: RR cut civil capacity by about a third but kept core engineering and high-value manufacturing, protecting its ability to develop future engines.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We have a growing fleet of young engines. So despite the near-term shock to flying, we will actually need to grow our MRO capacity over the coming years. And we plan to maintain that capability consolidated into fewer locations and meet the future growth by enlarging our external network.
finding: RR planned to meet future overhaul demand from its young fleet by growing partner MRO networks instead of its own shops.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: China in itself is around 20% of our coverage and around 6% of that. So in other words, 6% out of the 20%, that is, is domestic China.
finding: About 20% of RR's widebody flying hours come from China (6% domestic), which shaped its recovery; its top markets are China, Japan, South Korea, the US and the UK.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Our reasonable worst-case scenario assumes a significant delay in recovery with engine flying hours in 2021 at only about 45% of 2019 levels.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We've got 4 wide-body engine programs that have been launched since 2010, which have taken our market share of in-service wide-body passenger planes up from 26% 10 years ago to 38% by December '19. Our share of the order book is even stronger at 55% in December 2019.
finding: RR's decade of launching four new widebody engines raised its in-service widebody share from 26% to 38% and gave it 55% of the widebody order book.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we've got over 7,000 engines installed on business jets, and our strong product positions mean that, that gives us 30% -- more than 30% of the market by value.
finding: Business aviation, where RR holds over 30% share by value, was its more resilient civil segment in COVID.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: our year-to-date large engine invoiced flying hours were at 42% of 2019 levels. We've been seeing a gradual tick-up in flying activity every month since April. October and November combined were at 33% of 2019 levels
finding: RR's widebody flying hours, the base of its services revenue, bottomed at about a quarter of 2019 in Q2 2020 and recovered only slowly.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We've completed our inspections of all high-cycle Trent XWB engines. We found early signs of wear on the first stage of the IPC blade in around 20% of cases, which is exactly the same as we reported in August. Most of these were already being refurbished, returned to the customers, and we have ample spares in place.
finding: RR handled early Trent XWB IPC blade wear by inspecting the whole fleet and holding enough spares to avoid disruption, applying Trent 1000 lessons.

response: Fleet-wide inspections, refurbishment, spare engines

quote: During the year, we have built sufficient spare engine capacity such that even if all those Dreamliners took to the air again tomorrow, we would be fine to maintain that 0 aircraft on ground position.

response: Built spare engine pool; final HPT blade fix due mid-2021

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We've had to make some very tough proposals after the last few months, but we can't afford to retain capacity where demand in the medium term has been so dramatically reduced.
finding: RR cut civil manufacturing capacity to match lower expected medium-term demand, bringing widebody assembly and test back to the UK and moving fan blades to Singapore.
trigger: COVID demand collapse
response: Footprint consolidation and site closures

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: when we agreed a compensation payment for disruption on Trent 1000, instead of actually paying over pound notes to an airline, we gave them a credit note that they could then cash in at some stage in the future.
finding: RR compensated Trent 1000 customers mainly with credit notes against future services rather than cash, spreading crisis costs over time and tying customers in.
trigger: Trent 1000 durability groundings
response: Customer compensation paid as credit notes against future flight-hour charges

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We've achieved our target of eliminating aircraft on ground due to the Trent 1000 durability fixes. And we've now got enough parts and MRO capacity there on Trent 1000 to avoid a recurrence of any customer inconvenience, even if miraculously all travel restrictions were lifted today.
finding: RR closed out the Trent 1000 grounding crisis by building spare parts and MRO capacity, reaching zero aircraft on ground by early 2021.
trigger: Trent 1000 durability crisis (787 AOGs)
response: Durability fixes plus extra spare parts and MRO capacity; zero AOG reached

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: About 2/3 of our savings were in Civil Aerospace, where earlier plans to increase capacity were shelved as we now expect to meet the forecast load within our existing facilities. We've reduced the pace of investment in spare engines

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We're now expecting around 80% average flying hours in 2022 compared to 2019, and that's different from the 90% we talked about previously.

quote: we're also looking to keep our capital expenditure low, and we're aiming to be at the better end of our peer group range of 3% to 4% of revenues in that respect.

quote: In 2020, we had 278 -- sorry, 272 large engine major shop visits, as you described in those -- major refurbs. In 2021, that number is going to be closer to 240.

quote: we're pledging to have proven all our in production, commercial and business jet aero engines to be compatible with 100% SAFs by 2023. And that will mean that 2/3 of our Trent engine fleet and 3/5 of our business jet fleet currently in service will be SAF ready.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: industry forecasts are not very different from our own expectations of getting back to 2019 levels. And I think we've been fairly consistent that, that is some way off probably in the sort of 2024, maybe even 2025 time frame

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we have -- essentially have capacity for about 500 new large engines per annum, and that's the rate that we were delivering at in 2019.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we were coming into the pandemic, the sort of de facto market leader in terms of share. And that had been a relatively recent, i.e., sort of last 5 to 8 years phenomenon, and therefore, our engines are significantly newer.

speaker: Warren East, CEO

quote: think around about 30% more load going through that business. And when we look at it from an operating cash cost perspective, it's around about 6%.

speaker: Sebastian Resch, Civil Aerospace operations
quote: So hedging is, for us, important because roughly 30% of our spend is raw material.

quote: You know about the situation we've had on the Trent 1000, that would obviously be an example of an engine that hasn't managed to achieve the time on wing we initially wanted.

finding: RR says the Trent XWB performs well in service and, because its LTSAs make it pay for overhauls, has been extending XWB-84 service intervals to defer shop visits.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
