finding: RR diverted engines into spares in 2022 to protect fleet availability as shop visits rose.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: As in all our businesses, supply chain management and wage inflation were more challenging in 2022. We manage this through commodity hedging, long-term supply contracts and pricing.
finding: RR manages input inflation with hedging, long-term supply contracts and price pass-through.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: that GBP 1.3 billion cost reduction was mainly in Civil Aerospace. It didn't actually include other divisions or the group to a great extent. And second thing is that was activity driven
finding: Erginbilgic says the COVID cost cuts were activity-driven and are returning with volume.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: But the supply chain remains challenging, particularly in Civil Aerospace, where we have also been impacted by the 2 supplier fires.
finding: Two supplier fires hit RR's civil supply chain in 2022-23.

speaker: Panos Kakoullis, CFO
quote: We delivered 188 engines, including 115 large engines, of which 18 were spare engines.
finding: RR's H1 2023 large engine output was 115, including 18 spares.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: But supply chain, frankly, unfortunately, because of this V-shape, supply chain issues, I don't think Civil Aerospace supply chain, gas turbine supply chain will stabilize anytime soon.
finding: RR expected the post-COVID V-shaped rebound to keep the gas-turbine supply chain unstable for years.

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: we expect large engine flying hours to grow between 120% to 130% of 2019 levels by the midterm.
finding: In 2023 RR planned on widebody flying hours of 120-130% of 2019; it later raised this to 130-140%.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: So the time-on-wing improvements, we are planning next 3, 4 years 40% improvement, right? All the engines will improve sort of varying degrees, not all the same, obviously. Most improvement will come from 97 and Trent 1000
finding: RR's initial durability target was 40% over three to four years, mostly on the XWB-97 and Trent 1000 (later raised to 80%).

speaker: Robert Watson, President Civil Aerospace
quote: with the V2500 with 2,000 regional aircraft in active service and more than 35 million to 40 million engine flying hours still ahead of us. And we also see an opportunity to continue to support the V2500 into the 2030s.

speaker: Robert Watson, President Civil Aerospace
quote: Over the medium term, OE deliveries will increase from 190 to between 300 and 350 a year. Major refurbishments grow from nearly 250 to between 700 and 750.
finding: RR planned a sharp widebody OE and overhaul ramp to 2027.

speaker: Robert Watson, President Civil Aerospace
quote: By midterm, we'll have halved the cost of a Trent XWB shop visit. In fact, at that point, the XWB will be the cheapest of the Trent's overhauls
finding: RR targets halving Trent XWB overhaul cost by the mid-term.

speaker: Robert Watson, President Civil Aerospace
quote: Of our total GBP 2.5 billion spend in the external supply chain this year, GBP 685 million is spent with this group. And since 2020, we've awarded GBP 3 billion worth of work to our high-performing suppliers.
finding: RR moves work from weak to strong suppliers to cut product cost.

speaker: Robert Watson, President Civil Aerospace
quote: around 60% of that large engine fleet in 2027 is XWB, so 84 and 97.
finding: RR's future aftermarket is concentrated on the sole-source Trent XWB.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: This is the same improvement that we have certified on the Trent 7000 blade, which we have already retrofitted to over 20% of the fleet. And we aim to double the time on wing of the Trent amongst over the next 2 to 3 years
finding: RR retrofitted its Trent 7000 durability fix first and gave a two-to-three-year horizon for the XWB-97 upgrade.

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: Of these, 262 were widebody engines, which included 53 spares. That supported increasing number of shop visits, that did as our fleet grows and total shop visits grew by 18% to 1,227. Of these, 368 were large engine refirms compared to 248 in 2022.
finding: RR's widebody deliveries and shop visits grew in 2023.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: This guidance assumes large engine flying hours at 100% to 110% of 2019 levels, reflecting yet to deliver 500 to 550 OE engines, of which around half will be widebody engines.
finding: RR's 2024 plan was for about 250-275 widebody engine deliveries.

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: We're looking at what's our make-buy strategy, what's our component strategy? Where should we be moving to dual sourcing?
finding: RR answered supplier stress by reviewing make-or-buy choices and dual sourcing.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: When you want more efficiency, it comes with higher temperature and so on, and therefore, cycle time is lower. So no, I think no engine we will produce Trent 700 cycle time.
finding: RR accepts that more fuel-efficient engines lose durability, so new engines will not match the Trent 700's life.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Our LTSA margins increased for all engine types, except the Trent 1000, which we expect to improve in the second half.
finding: The Trent 1000 was the one engine where RR could not yet raise service margins.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: We also invested to grow our capacity in Darby and Dahlewitz, which will allow us to deliver around 40% additional new engines per year from 2025 compared to 2023
finding: RR invested in OE capacity for about 40% more engines a year from 2025.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: This part will more than double the time-on-wing of the Trent 1000 engine and is already in service in 50% of the Trent 7000 fleet.
finding: RR proved the Trent 1000 HPT fix on the sister Trent 7000 first.

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: OE deliveries grew by 26% to 236. This was achieved despite the supply chain environment. Of the 236, 120 were large engines, of which 21 were spares.
finding: RR kept growing OE output through supply constraints in H1 2024.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: We are actively working to mitigate these headwinds, but we anticipate the supply chain to remain challenging for another 18 to 24 months.
finding: In mid-2024 RR expected supply chain strain into 2026.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Trent 1000 is our highest cost shop visits because of some sort of historic issues, frankly, but we are going to improve.
finding: The Trent 1000 installed base carries RR's costliest shop visits, a drag on margin and cash in 2024.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: We have invested to grow capacity in Derby, Dahlewitz and Singapore which will allow us to increase deliveries of new engines. And by the end of this year, have the capacity to deliver a 50% increase in shop visits as compared to 2023
finding: RR invested in new-engine and MRO capacity to support widebody share gains and rising shop visits.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: At the CMD, we set out our target of delivering a 40% increase in time on wing across our modern engines by the end of 2027. We now believe we can achieve double this time on the time on wing improvement within the same period
finding: RR doubled its time-on-wing target from 40% to 80% a little over a year after setting it, a change of position that shows the durability programme outperforming.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Our time on wing initiatives mean that shop visits will peak in 2026 before falling through 1,250 to 1,350 range in the midterm.
finding: RR plans for durability gains to cut shop visit volumes after 2026, lowering the cost of honouring its LTSAs.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Trent XWB-84 shop visit costs will halve versus 2019 with more than a 35% reduction already achieved by the end of last year.
finding: RR is well into its plan to halve Trent XWB-84 shop visit costs.

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: OE deliveries grew by 16% to 529. Of these, 278 were widebody engines, which included 221 installed engines, giving us a wide-body delivery share of more than 60% in 2024.
finding: RR took over 60% of widebody engine deliveries in 2024.

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: we increased Trent 1000 supply chain output by around 20% in 2024. We expect the supply chain to remain challenged for the next 12 to 18 months
finding: RR put a dedicated task force on Trent 1000 parts to cut groundings.

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: We expect large engine flying hours to grow to between 130% to 140% of 2019 levels by the midterm.
finding: RR's mid-term plan assumes strong widebody flying-hour growth.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Reliability of this engine is as good as the next. Our main issue has been time on wing. And we are effectively fixing it for good and we know it works.
finding: RR frames the Trent 1000 problem as time-on-wing, not reliability, and points to the Trent 7000 as proof the fix works.

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: In relation to what's driving that, I mean, it's very consistent with what we spoke about in the past, particularly parts supply availability, casting, forging.
finding: RR's supply chain problem centres on castings and forgings.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: For the Trent XWB-84, shop visit costs remain on track to fall by 50% between 2020 -- 2019 and the midterm.
finding: RR targets halving Trent XWB-84 shop visit cost as a core lever of aftermarket margin.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: In February, we set a target of improving the time on wing of our in-production engines by more than 80% by the end of 2027. As a result of the progress we made to date, more than half of the targeted improvement is not delivered or secured.
finding: RR treats durability as a funded programme with a hard target for in-production engines.

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: OE deliveries of 237 were broadly flat year-on-year. Of these, 122 were large engines, of which 23 were spares, as we continue to increase our
finding: RR held large engine output flat in H1 2025 under supply constraints and kept building spare engines for flexibility.

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: Shop visits, they grew to 696, an increase of 12% year-on-year. Of these, 217 were large engine refurbs. That compares to 195 last year.
finding: RR's shop visit throughput is rising as MRO capacity and parts supply improve.

speaker: Helen McCabe, CFO
quote: we expected the supply chain to remain challenging during 2025 and '26. That is still our view. The industry continues to see product cost inflation
finding: RR plans on a constrained, inflationary aerospace supply chain through 2026.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: In non-benign environments, we are going to double the time on wing. And in benign environments, we are going to increase time on wing by 50%. That is progressing, but that won't be completed before 2027.
finding: The Trent XWB-97 durability fix for harsh environments runs to 2027, so a problem remains on RR's newest widebody engine.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Trent 1000, what we call 2 upgrades, BoM B and BoM C, and we obviously did BoM B, which is more than doubling time on wing. By the end of this year, we will do BoM C.
finding: RR finishes the Trent 1000 fix in two steps (BoM B, then BoM C) to make the 787 engine competitive by the end of 2025.

speaker: Sebastian Resch, Civil Aerospace operations
quote: You might have read a Bloomberg article about short force, a recent article about short force in delivery on the narrowbody and long [indiscernible] engine. But the root cause of that article, casting of metal, right?
finding: RR attributes narrowbody engine delivery shortfalls to casting supply and cites its own in-house casting investment.

speaker: Sebastian Resch, Civil Aerospace operations
quote: So in general, because we have no narrowbody. We have some disadvantage on buying power. And we only can compensate that with consolidating our volume.
finding: RR concedes that having no narrowbody engine weakens its purchasing scale against narrowbody-heavy rivals.

speaker: Chris Cholerton, President Civil Aerospace
quote: And our ambition will be to approach the returns enjoyed by our competitors as our engines further mature.
finding: RR concedes rival engine makers earn higher returns than it does.

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: I never called duopoly very competitive place, but the economics books will disagree with you, I think. But -- and duopoly, it is. So -- and with [indiscernible], we can go in because of our technology and engineering and so on. But we are the probably only one who can go in.
finding: RR sees the narrowbody engine market as a profitable CFM-Pratt duopoly and itself as the only credible third entrant.

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: UltraFan is more efficient engine, as I said, than any other engine available in the market at this point in time. And the IPs we have on that on a geared structure is very favorable.
finding: In reply to a question on the two incumbents' different narrowbody technology routes, RR claims an efficiency lead and favourable geared-architecture IP for UltraFan.
trigger: CFM and Pratt & Whitney pursuing different next-generation narrowbody technologies
response: RR positions UltraFan and its geared IP as partner bait

speaker: M. Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO
quote: Our competition goes with long times, a lot longer than we put on LLPs. We go, here is the limit, and only when we understand operational with high fidelity, we sort of raised the limit, right?
finding: RR says it sets life-limited part limits more cautiously than competitors and raises them only after gathering data, a lever it is now using to cut XWB-84 refurbs.

speaker: John Rose, CEO
quote: We are involved in an unprecedented number of new programs, which the underpinning of our growth over the next decade and where we're saying that we are confident that the business can double organically as it has over the last decade.
finding: In 2010 RR framed its strategy as organic growth from an unprecedented number of new programmes, targeting a doubling of the business over the decade.

numbers.organic_growth_target: double the business over the decade to 2020

speaker: John Rose, CEO
quote: we have to ensure that we have the capacity in place to deliver that growth. That has to be done ahead of the revenue. And you have to put in place the total capacity and then occupy it.
finding: RR's principle is to build total capacity ahead of revenue and then fill it, accepting fixed-cost and cash drag in the ramp.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: we believe that revenues will double over the next decade from organic growth alone. This is a complex and long-term task. We are investing in new facilities, new technology and recruiting new people. It is also clear that we must focus on execution, cost, cash conversion and efficiency.
finding: The new CEO, Rishton (from April 2011), kept the inherited strategy and its organic-doubling target (persistence) but added a sharper focus on execution, cost and cash conversion.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: because of the nature of our aftermarket business, because it is so long-term contract based, it tends to be more stable... The beauty of our long-term contract model is that we're much more stable and we get paid on an hourly basis, not on shop visits.
finding: RR prices its aftermarket mainly as long-term contracts paid per flying hour (TotalCare) rather than per shop visit, and values the stability this gives over the time-and-material model.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: 4 or 5 years ago, if we were projecting forward to 2011, we wouldn't have envisaged anything like the quantity of Trent 700 engines going into production on the Airbus A330... we were in the market for lift... if some programs are delayed or some capacity has delayed then older programs turned to benefits.
finding: RR sees itself as selling into aggregate demand for lift: when new programmes (787, A350) slip, older platforms on which it is installed (A330 with the Trent 700) pick up the demand, cushioning the delay.

speaker: Andrew Shilston, Finance Director
quote: as the engine for the Boeing 787 goes into service, you've got more engineering time to address the engine for the Airbus A350. So when you look at it in aggregate, as the old programs mature you have more resource available for new.
finding: RR runs a roughly constant engineering pool, moving it from maturing programmes to new ones (Trent 1000 to XWB). Total R&D stays steady, which limits how many new engines it can develop at once.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: When I look at the other things that we invested our money in and our position on the widebody, for example, also across a broader spectrum. So if you take into account the Marine business and the Tognum acquisition, those kind of things, for me, it's a rational and sensible business decision.
finding: Rishton justified skipping the narrowbody re-engine as an opportunity-cost trade-off against widebody programmes and the Tognum acquisition.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: we need to address the financial returns that we're getting from our Energy business and we need to think carefully about how we can do that.
finding: Rishton flagged the Energy segment's returns as needing action, the start of a return-driven portfolio review that led to later exits.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: We continue to grow our installed base, a hugely valuable asset for the company, but based on the surprise in the value of our IAE holding, is not fully appreciated by everyone. And the provision of product-related services is essential for us and our customers.
finding: RR treats its installed base as its main value store and pointed to the IAE sale price as proof that the market undervalues installed-base aftermarket.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: A credit rating, a good investment credit rating is key where we have long contracts with governments and customers that are spending 20 years. People want to know that we're going to be around over that sort of period.
finding: RR keeps an investment-grade rating as a commercial necessity because customers sign 20-year contracts, so balance-sheet risk is capped to protect engine sales.

speaker: Mike Terrett, COO
quote: The XWB, we're building the first engines... that gives us an opportunity to build a platform for 25 years of production, and a further 25 years of aftermarket. That's a much better place to be than sitting on legacy products
finding: RR values a new engine programme as about 25 years of production plus a further 25 years of aftermarket, and prefers new platforms to legacy products.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: we are focused on 3 main areas: delivering the promises we've made; deciding where to grow, and just as importantly, where not to; and improving our financial performance... Where will we not be growing? Fuel cells.
finding: RR carried out its 'where not to grow' priority by ceding fuel cells to a partner (LG took majority control), showing willingness to exit sub-scale bets.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: it's quite clear if you look at the segment results and you look at them over a number of years that the financial performance there is unacceptable, so we need to address that.
finding: Rishton escalated his judgement of the Energy segment from 'disappointing' (2011) to 'unacceptable', a precursor to portfolio exits.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: I continue to be particularly pleased that we have focused on and continued to focus on our a TotalCare packages rather than time and materials... in terms of the performance that we've had versus what you're seeing with some people who are primarily on time and materials
finding: RR presented its TotalCare model as an advantage over rivals that rely on time-and-material, whose services revenue was weaker.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: Where we have chosen not to grow, as you know, we have sold our Tidal business and the majority stake in our fuel cells business. While these businesses may both prove to be successful, they did not play to our strengths.
finding: RR exits businesses that do not play to its core strengths even if they might succeed; fit with strengths is a test for investing.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: those that continue with TCA, those that switch to T&M, and that tends to be driven by how short they plan to keep their service in fleet. So we certainly look and seek to extend TCA contracts... by using our scale of economy to help make it cost effective and share some of that benefit with the customer.
finding: RR tries to renew TotalCare by sharing scale savings with airlines; airlines planning to retire fleets soon tend to switch to time-and-material.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: And I don't think you should assume 85% is a trend or something for the future.
finding: Rishton rejected the analyst's reading that 85% linked TotalCare capture would be a lasting trend.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: If I look at our turn rate across the group, for the sake of argument, it's around 3%. That is too low... what we're trying to balance there is delivery to customer and execution, where I do not want to fail and we will not fail, against the benefits of -- the financial benefits of releasing cash.
finding: RR puts on-time delivery to customers ahead of releasing cash from inventory, although it called its inventory turns (about 3, stated as 3%) too low.

speaker: Mark Morris, Finance Director/CFO
quote: In the aftermarket world and TCA capture, we would typically set the work scope. And we can decide when and where we're going to pull engines off. So it allows us to optimize the loading into the shops... some of that is shared. But net-net, it should help drive margins.
finding: Under TotalCare RR sets overhaul timing and work scope to optimise shop loading, shares part of the savings with customers, and expects net margin gains.

speaker: Colin Smith, Director of Engineering and Technology
quote: research and technology, which is the very long-term technology sometimes up to 25 years out. We try and be broadly consistent because we've got technology centers and universities working on this stuff, and you can't keep turning it on and off. And as new programs come in, you pull it off the shelf and implement it.
finding: RR keeps research and technology spending steady (up to 25 years out) regardless of the cycle, so technology is ready to take off the shelf when an airframer launches a programme.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: I think we've made a slower start on cost and cash than I would have hoped for... It actually goes to our competitors have an advantage if they have better cost, that means they can price more aggressively than we can. That means they can invest in more product than we can.
finding: Rishton admitted slow progress on cost and cash and tied unit cost to competitiveness: lower-cost rivals can price more aggressively and fund more products.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: as in all businesses, we'll continue to address portfolio issues as we see them and as opportunities arise. And I think the sale of our 50% holding in the RTM322 helicopter is just evidence of opportunistic in some ways and a view that, that wasn't something we wanted to invest in at this point in time.
finding: RR sold its 50% RTM322 helicopter-engine JV stake to its partner Turbomeca (p1114) rather than invest further: an opportunistic JV exit to the partner.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: So in broad terms, cost progression in Aerospace is virtually nothing, and we have to address that because it is our biggest cost base and our biggest issue.
finding: RR admitted almost no unit-cost progress in Aerospace in 2013; Civil, in a boom, resisted cost discipline.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: if we don't improve our cost of cash performance, we can't invest as much as we want in new products and do the things we want to do in terms of people, trading, infrastructure, products, all those kinds of things.
finding: RR's leadership tied new-product investment capacity directly to cost and cash performance: weak cash constrains new launches.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: Oil & Gas is a good business, as I've said, on a number of times, but it's small. We had a good market share. It's basically us and GE... Power Generation is much troublesome for us in terms of financials, where we are a tiny, tiny, tiny flare. We're looking at what we should or shouldn't do
finding: RR judged sub-scale positions (power generation) as candidates for exit while valuing niches where it shares a duopoly with GE (oil and gas).

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: So in simple terms, I'll put more inventory in to protect the customers; supply chain performance has improved, but it isn't yet at the point where we can reduce the inventory offering and still protect our customers, but we're getting closer to it.
finding: RR deliberately held extra inventory to protect on-time delivery to customers (persistence of customer-over-cash priority) until supply-chain reliability allows it to be reduced.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: what we have been doing which was not smart was allowing our costs to grow ahead of the volume increases. In some areas, that's inevitably the case... we don't need much of Singapore at the moment, going to build 50 engines there this year. But at some point in the foreseeable future, we've going to have one a day.
finding: RR admitted costs had grown ahead of volume, some of it unavoidably: Seletar built 50 engines in 2013 but was sized for about one a day.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: with shorter-cycle, longer-cycle, earlier cash generation, longer-cash generation, more capital intensive, less capital intensive. So there's a mix there that I think is important to get that balance right.
finding: RR's portfolio logic is to balance long-cycle, capital-intensive gas turbines with shorter-cycle businesses that generate cash sooner.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: one of the things that we're keen to do is to ensure that by lowering the cost of overhauls and so forth we can extend the life of those. But it's in our planning.
finding: RR cuts overhaul costs on ageing RB211 fleets to extend their service lives and slow retirements.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: in the future we're going to get extra benefits of volume, and when we start getting the capacity and the demand in balance, we get that as a windfall. But if we right-costed the business before we get there, then we're in great shape
finding: RR's approach was to right-size costs before volume arrives, so that later capacity utilisation gains come as a windfall.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: you've also got the business jet engines, which traditionally have higher-margin, and because they fly less hours in the aftermarket. So a logical business analysis says you get more on the OE.
finding: RR prices business-jet engines for higher OE margin because low utilisation limits their aftermarket, unlike widebody engines priced for aftermarket recovery.

doc: Special Call (sale of Energy business to Siemens)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: While it has excellent products, technology and people, it lacks scope and scale to compete effectively. ... The sale addresses one of our 4 Cs: concentration, where to grow and where not to
finding: RR exits businesses where it lacks the scale to compete, even with good technology, as with the Energy gas-turbine sale to Siemens.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: concentrate on what we're good at and where we add value; concentrate on supporting our customers through the life cycle of the product; invest in technology; concentrate on growth markets with barriers to entry
finding: RR's stated strategic rules are to focus on core competences, support products through life, keep investing in technology and stay in growth markets with high barriers to entry.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: barriers to entry in this market, very high; investment, high; time to earn cash, high. No surprises. Different in this one, shorter. And when I come to look around the industry, it comes as no particular surprise to me and, I suspect, nor to you that there are no pure-play civil businesses
finding: RR says civil gas turbines have very high entry barriers, high investment and a long time to cash, which is why it keeps shorter-cycle businesses alongside civil aerospace.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: And the bottom 3: wide-body gas turbines; narrow body; and medium speed recips.
finding: In 2014 RR's three strategic investment priorities were widebody gas turbines, a return to narrowbody, and medium-speed reciprocating engines.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: And the relationship revenue-wise from OE to aftermarket, again, as I think you're familiar with, is about 4:1, 4 for the aftermarket, 1 for OE. And thrust is not a bad proxy for revenue.
finding: RR estimates lifecycle aftermarket revenue at about 4 times OE revenue, and uses installed thrust as a proxy for aftermarket revenue.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: sometimes, some people I meet, they think we can stop and start and stop. You can't in this game. It is a constant requirement to remain what we term internally as being match fit. ... You don't lay them off and bring them back.
finding: RR will not stop and restart technology spending because its engineering capability, mainly people, cannot be laid off and rebuilt, so R&D continues through cycles.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: It's about 71% of the volume and about 50% of the value. ... Customer intimacy: If we're only talking about wide body, it's just part of it. If you're talking about the whole wide and narrow, it's -- you're much more into it with your customer.
finding: RR values narrowbody re-entry because it is about 71% of volume and 50% of value, and being in both segments deepens customer relationships and spreads technology.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: we see ourselves as a growth business, first and foremost. We see great opportunities, and they sit predominantly around our Trent programs at the moment.
finding: RR's CFO put organic growth through the Trent programmes first among its capital priorities.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: And of course, we're strongly focused on closing the margin gap with our competitors, as we have talked to you before.
finding: RR acknowledged a margin gap versus its competitors and made closing it an explicit goal.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: whenever we look at any form of investment and look at minimum requirements that we have an IRR that exceeds our WACC, of course, we expect it to be considerably higher than that. And WACC, I carry a number of about 9% around in my head, post tax.
finding: RR's investment hurdle is an IRR above its roughly 9% post-tax WACC, and in practice well above it.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: when we look at our capital allocation, we look at it sequentially, starting at the top, which is what is most dear to our heart, which is investing in our own business, organic growth; R&D, the lifeblood of what we do.
finding: RR allocates capital sequentially, starting with organic investment in R&D and capex, which it calls its lifeblood, before other uses.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: So when I talk about M&A, let me just be clear. It can also mean partnerships. It can mean joint ventures.
finding: RR treats partnerships and joint ventures as part of its disciplined M&A toolkit for gaining technology, products or routes to market.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: Return on invested capital to be greater than our WACC within 3 years and obviously, as a minimum, that the IRR would exceed WACC.
finding: RR's M&A and partnership criteria require ROIC above WACC within 3 years and IRR above WACC.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: 90% of our Trent fleet is now covered by TotalCare long-term service agreement-style contract
finding: About 90% of RR's Trent fleet was under TotalCare-style long-term service agreements in 2014.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: first-tier operators are typically contracting for between 10 and 15 years ... But then there's always a second-tier opportunity, and we're typically contracting for between 5 and 7 years for the second-tier operator
finding: RR's TotalCare contracts run 10-15 years with first operators and 5-7 years with second-tier operators.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: we have defined terms in our OE contracts, under which Rolls-Royce sells and the operator buys spare parts either from Rolls-Royce or from a Rolls-Royce-approved vendor.
finding: RR writes aftermarket parts control into OE sales contracts so operators buy spares from RR or RR-approved vendors, whether on TotalCare or time and material.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: TotalCare has become the model of choice for customers, and that's really because it underpins -- it transfers risk to Rolls-Royce because we guarantee the availability of the aircraft, and we also have very predictable costs for the airline
finding: RR's TotalCare transfers maintenance and availability risk from airlines to RR in exchange for a per-flying-hour fee.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: An engine, typically, around about 4,000 hours per year that we would expect to see on a wide-bodied aircraft. And we have arrangements and contractual thresholds in there for minimum utilization.
finding: RR prices TotalCare on about 4,000 flying hours a year per widebody engine and protects itself with minimum-utilisation clauses and repricing if usage changes.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: We have more data and information than anybody else. We have the scale of economies around us, the spare engines, the networks to sweat [ph] our assets properly and share some of those benefits with our customers to incentivize them to go down the TotalCare path.
finding: RR shares part of its data and scale advantages with airlines through pricing to steer them into TotalCare contracts.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: contractual aftermarket right exists to the extent there is a loss on the sale of original equipment because we don't always lose money when we sell original equipment. But when we do, it creates something called an aftermarket right
finding: RR sells some engines below cost and capitalises the OE loss as a contractual aftermarket right, since it expects to recover more than the loss from aftermarket spares.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: because it's a longer point in the cycle, there's an element of us trying to make sure we incentivize people to stay on so we can be something like reducing our margin as a way of making sure that we keep the fleet flying for longer.
finding: On ageing fleets such as the RB211, RR gives up margin to keep operators flying the aircraft longer, protecting aftermarket revenue.

speaker: Colin Smith, Engineering Director
quote: the R&T, research and technology programs, that we're doing for the big, big engines flow down to the small or the middle of the market engines as well, so there's no duplication
finding: RR's widebody research and technology is meant to flow down to a narrowbody engine, lowering the incremental cost of re-entering that market.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: I also said seeing no new major program which I, in some way, you could say, the narrow-body potentially is. ... So the challenge there is how much can we grow in the future, where you're spending that cash versus reducing the growth relative to the cash.
finding: RR recognises that a narrowbody launch would be a new major programme that delays the cash-conversion improvement, and frames it as a growth-versus-cash trade-off.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: But here we are today with 50% of the wide-body share and we've done that organically from about sort of 2%. So yes, you could do it. And sort of the question is, are you determined to do it? How long does it take?
finding: RR cites its organic climb from about 2% to 50% of widebody engines since 1990 as proof it can build share over decades by sustained investment, and applies the same patient view to narrowbody re-entry.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: this is a really competitive market, and the reason that we and the airlines like TotalCare is it aligns our interest and their interest together. ... I mean we both want to keep the wing -- the engine on wing for as long as possible.
finding: RR describes TotalCare as aligning its incentives with airlines on time on wing, and describes the aftermarket as competitive rather than locked in.

speaker: Tony Wood, President Aerospace
quote: So I think it's quite clear that there is risk transfer going on, as John has explained, on a TotalCare contract. And for that, we seek to generate a better margin
finding: RR prices TotalCare for a higher margin than time-and-material in return for taking the maintenance risk.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: is to make sure that you have firm relationship, a partnership with your critical suppliers where you both benefit rather than trying to push them underwater for a period of time just to get ahead of price now.
finding: RR prefers partnership with critical suppliers over short-term price squeezes, drawing on car-industry lessons.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: I think when we look to the life of our engine, we assume sort of 25 years. ... Our experience, generally, is that where we've got to the end of TotalCare, generally, they're renewed.
finding: RR assumes a 25-year engine life and usually renews TotalCare contracts at the end of the first 10-15 year term, on new terms.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: We currently expect new engine deliveries to level off around the 2018 time frame. This inflection point will start to see a greater weighting towards more aftermarket revenues from the larger installed base as we move into a period of harvest, which will drive up margins and improve cash conversion.
finding: RR's medium-term plan is a sow-then-harvest cycle: OE deliveries level off around 2018, after which aftermarket revenue from the larger installed base raises margins and cash conversion.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: Trent XWB and Trent 7000 are predominantly unlinked
finding: RR sells its new-generation engines (Trent XWB, Trent 7000) mainly on unlinked contracts, so OE losses are taken at delivery and the aftermarket is booked separately.

doc: Guidance/Update Call (trading statement and medium-term outlook)
speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: new programs, naturally, certainly at the front end, will depress margins because we're spending money on CapEx and R&D ... We get about 20% of the revenue on the OE, and it's much lower margin; 80% of the revenue, much higher margin on the aftermarket ... When see these opportunities, we'll continue to make those investments.
finding: RR will invest in new engine programmes despite near-term margin dilution because about 80% of lifecycle revenue, at much higher margin, comes from the aftermarket and only about 20% from OE.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: As the products mature, you've gone through parts of the launch pricing, you've gone through parts of the launch cost. As the volume increases, we utilize our capacity far more effectively. ... I used the term, inflection point, was 2018.
finding: RR expects civil margins to improve as programmes mature past launch pricing and launch costs and capacity utilisation rises with volume, with an inflection point around 2018.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: what we've always liked about the contract or TotalCare is that the economics sort of give a couple of benefits, both to us and, we believe, to our airlines. And looking at the penetration we have would suggest they agree with us.
finding: RR prefers power-by-the-hour TotalCare because airlines get predictable cost per flying hour and RR gets monthly cash instead of waiting years for time-and-material shop visits.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: Across the business, joint ventures in our industry are more prevalent than in many other industries and have been pretty successful with varying degree. So I'm not going to rule out doing joint ventures, but I don't want to go through the pain and grief that we went through with some of the joint ventures
finding: RR stays open to joint ventures, common in the engine industry, but is wary after painful experiences such as the long Tognum buy-out.
trigger: Analyst asked for assurance RR would not repeat a long-drawn JV like Tognum
response: Will not rule out JVs but wants to avoid the pain of past ones

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: within that affordability, we figure out whether we can do new programs. And then the question is does a program come along or not? Or do 2 programs come along and then we take the decision as to which ones we're going to be on or not.
finding: RR decides which new engine programmes to bid by fitting them within an engineering load and capacity budget of about 5% of sales for R&D; when two programmes arrive together it chooses between them rather than expanding.

speaker: Mark Morris, CFO
quote: But that is driven mainly by our load capacity balance. We can't just double the number of engineers and build aircraft engines.
finding: RR says its engineering headcount limits how many new engine programmes it can take on at once.

speaker: Mikael Makinen, President Marine
quote: you will actually not see, on a group level that we take some of the capital from air and put it into Marine. But it's not like in air, when I talk about billions of dollars to develop something new.
finding: Group capital allocation keeps the big development money in aerospace, where a new product costs billions, while non-aero adjacencies get small amounts that do not divert capital from air.

speaker: Mark Alflatt, Finance Director Marine
quote: He talked about the new engine that we just brought to market in the last month, 3 years to come to market, GBP 25 million. ... So 2 to 3 years is not uncommon compared to multi-years, if not more than a decade of the kind of product cycle, again, you're used to in the Aerospace sector.
finding: RR management frames aerospace engine development as a multi-year to decade-plus product cycle, in contrast to a 3-year, GBP 25m marine engine.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: we are just at the first few years of creating a 30-year business there... we're in a heavy investment phase of that. And that is clearly impacting margins and free cash flow, but I don't see that, at all, as a bad thing... making sure efforts to cut costs are not going to undermine the investment in our future.
finding: RR accepts lower margins and free cash flow during heavy launch investment and shields that investment from cost cutting.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: It gives us the ability to withstand our shocks and turbulences, which sometimes occur in our industry. But it also provides important confidence to our customers, who, remember, are buying products that will remain in service for decades and require decades of aftermarket support. They look very closely to our credit rating.
finding: RR defends a strong credit rating partly because airline customers buying decades of TotalCare support check its creditworthiness; the message was repeated in July.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: this is a long-term business. We invest for the long term, as we have done consistently for decades. Our products are mission-critical and take years to develop. As the manufacturers of original equipment, we are well placed to provide aftermarket services that make up 48% of our group revenue.
finding: RR describes itself as a long-term investor that uses OE positions to capture aftermarket services (48% of group revenue in 2014).

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: This is demonstrated, I think, quite clearly when we sold our stake in IAE, when, I know, many of you were surprised by the value we've realized for what was just one small component of the Civil aerospace business.
finding: RR cited the IAE stake sale price as evidence of the value of installed-base aftermarket rights.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: Commercially, we and our competitors recognize the requirement for both scale and breadth of portfolio. Scale is crucial to maintaining a strong balance sheet and protecting our investment-grade rating, which, as David has said, is essential comfort for customers who sign long-term service agreements with us.
finding: RR justified its conglomerate breadth and scale as needed for balance-sheet strength and an investment-grade rating that service customers require.

speaker: John Rishton, CEO
quote: For example, this has driven growth in Civil large engines, where in the 1980s we had a market share of less than 10%. We now have more than 50% of the wide-body engines on order.
finding: Over three decades RR's persistent wide-body strategy took it from under 10% to over 50% of wide-body engines on order.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: I think it's right in a more uncertain environment to set guidance in a way that's cautioned... to run it on a series of plans that allow you to make the upside if it comes through so you have the flexibility, but make sure that we're planning cautiously in the short term.
finding: RR's CFO plans cautiously in the short term while keeping flexibility for upside.

speaker: Ian Davis, Chairman
quote: Particularly if I call it David and Goliath, we're up against some very big beasts in not just the Aerospace industry, but in the Land & Sea business as well... So restructuring, yes, but growth is, to me, strategically much more important.
finding: RR's board saw itself as the smaller challenger to much larger rivals and put long-term growth ahead of restructuring.

speaker: Ian Davis, Chairman
quote: Warren will be focusing on the strategic development of the company and building the other aspects, not least around the services, which, as you know, Ben, is more than 50% of our revenues and value.
finding: RR's board put services, more than half of revenue and value, at the centre of strategy.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: It's around delivering improved engine costs and customer pricing. After we get through the launch phase, it's about getting the capacity utilization up... it's about the aftermarket margin that comes with a 50% installed base. We're still in the 30s in installed base at today, but we'll be up beyond 50% as we get through 2020.
finding: RR's margin plan relied on post-launch cost and price gains, better capacity utilisation and aftermarket margin as its wide-body installed-base share rose from the 30s to over 50% by 2020.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: it's taken us 30 years to get to this position. And we're within 5 years, really, of achieving it now... once we get to this kind of level of installed base market share in wide-bodies, we'll be in a very strong position to continue to drive profitability in the aftermarket
finding: RR's wide-body strategy took 30 years of share-building before reaching about 50% of the installed base, with aftermarket profit as the reward.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the product transition from the Trent 700 to the Trent 7000 as Airbus winds down the production of the current A330 where Trent 700 is one engine option in favor of the new A330neo where the Trent 7000 will enjoy an exclusive position... From a business perspective, this move to an exclusive position is positive
finding: RR values sole-source positions: it called its exclusive Trent 7000 slot on the A330neo positive despite the painful run-out of the competed Trent 700.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: partners again as: That's part of how we go about doing our business. It's broadly a good thing, and I actually don't see any reason for significant changes in that, in principle.
finding: RR's new CEO endorsed its risk- and revenue-sharing partnership model and saw no reason to change it.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And this is a very long-term business, and decisions that we make today, for instance, maintaining our investments in engineering and technology, and particularly at the R&D end of it, to produce technologies which we're going to be building upon in 10 and 15 years time. Of course, that is important.
finding: RR protects early-stage technology R&D even in a crisis, because it underpins engines launched 10-15 years later.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And in terms of the choices that one faces in the business as well, in terms of having to avoid, if possible, making bets. It'd be very easy to do custom engines for every airplane. But as David was just describing the discussion about 380, this is a dangerous thing to get sucked into from a business point of view.
finding: RR's CEO warned against bespoke engines for every airframe and avoided speculative bets, citing the A380neo.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the basic financial dynamics of the business are remarkably similar in terms of turnover R&D upfront that may go nowhere, a ton of product development cost built on R&D that has gone somewhere, followed by some revenue coming in when one sells products in the first place followed by a long tail
finding: RR's CEO likened jet engines to ARM's royalty model: upfront R&D and development followed by decades of tail revenue.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: We will take scenarios around that when coming up with our own pricing assumptions and evaluating the programs. All I was really saying is actually the evidence hasn't changed, but we are more cautious in that when we do our own evaluations.
finding: RR prices engine campaigns and programmes on assumptions more cautious than the historic ~25-year average engine life.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So we don't actually need to do anything right now other than enjoy the aftermarket revenue and work on making sure that we're earning that aftermarket revenue as efficiently as possible and maximizing the profit opportunity on that over the next several years, developing our technology and taking advantage of an opportunity if and when an opportunity arises.
finding: RR's narrow-body posture was harvest-plus-option: milk the V2500 aftermarket, keep developing technology, and commit only if and when a platform opportunity arises.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: In fact, we're on course to achieve a greater than 50% share of the installed base by the early 2020s... Some of the new engines that we're selling at the moment, pricing is lower than it could be. This is launch pricing, this is normal. This has happened with all the other engines that Rolls-Royce has introduced over many years.
finding: RR treats low launch pricing on new wide-body engines as normal, repeated practice for every new engine, accepted in exchange for building a >50% installed-base share.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We do expect this revenue to decline. We have no new opportunities for design -- getting design into new products. And we actually expect that revenue to decline as the existing products retire to about 1/3 of today's revenue over the next 5 years... this is very much an example of a business that we need to harvest.
finding: Where RR has lost its design positions (regional jets) it explicitly harvests the installed base rather than invest to re-enter.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the value is all about the installed base and it's about how we generate profit from that installed base... the revenue that we extract from that is about the volume of the installed base and the price that we're charging for the flying hour.
finding: RR's civil business model is explicitly installed-base driven: value comes from flying-hour pricing on a growing installed base, not from OE sales.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: Firstly, we have an outstanding opportunity with wide-body engines to transform our business into a true world leader with critical mass in both scale and financial success.
finding: RR's CFO framed wide-body engines as the core opportunity around which the group's scale and returns would be built.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: As you know, we believe the NPV of embedded cash flow is the most appropriate way of valuing our Civil Aerospace business
finding: RR evaluates its civil business on the NPV of embedded lifecycle cash flows rather than on near-term profit.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: The decisions we make as to how we prioritize and best make our discretionary investments, including investing cash in building out our installed base of large engines, and capturing that long-term aftermarket revenue stream are fundamental to the long-term shape and scale of this business
finding: RR treats cash spent building the large-engine installed base (OE losses) as discretionary investment for the aftermarket stream, central to its capital allocation.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: It requires us to have a clear view on our weighted average cost of capital, our return on capital employed for individual projects, and the risks of those projects... It is also essential that we impose greater discipline as to the hurdles we are seeking
finding: RR's new CFO committed to project-level return hurdles (WACC and ROCE, risk-adjusted) with tighter discipline for investment decisions.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: So don't think that in there, we've necessarily got a straight 25 years, which is the experience over the last 20 years of engine life. We actually model that in different ways. So we look at scenarios and we put risk factors in about that and take account of that when we look at the program cash flows.
finding: RR evaluates programme cash flows with risk-adjusted scenarios on engine life and utilisation rather than simply assuming the historic 25-year life.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: most of our engines are sold with a TotalCare agreement, the very, very significant majority of those... Our customers are prepared to pay for that arrangement... the customers appreciate is that we take that risk and they pay us a premium for taking that risk.
finding: Most RR large engines are sold with TotalCare, and RR says airlines pay a premium for RR carrying the maintenance risk.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Yes, the issue is that we're spreading that manufacturing cost over approximately the same value though, because the higher volume of engines are much lower cost engines. And when you're talking about spreading the fixed cost, you spread -- we're in the cost domain then rather than the volume domain and so, it comes to the same thing.
finding: RR's CEO argued that the higher volume of narrow-body engines gives no special fixed-cost advantage because they are much lower-value engines.
trigger: Analyst asked how RR squares operating gearing with focusing on lower-volume wide-bodies and not re-entering narrow-body
response: Argued value, not unit volume, drives cost absorption

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: our fixed cost base is simply too high. It makes us very sensitive to market changes, and that's not acceptable, and we are doing something about it.
finding: After the 2015 profit warnings RR's new CEO judged its fixed costs too high and too exposed to market shifts, and launched a transformation programme.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the famous TotalCare accounting complexity. Now, when I look at that, there's nothing intrinsically wrong with it, absolutely nothing, particularly in steady state. But clearly, when we move from one business model to another, it doesn't handle that transition very well.
finding: RR defended the TotalCare model but admitted its accounting masked the move from profitable old engines to loss-making new ones.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: installed thrust is a good proxy for aftermarket revenue potential. Installed thrust is all about volume, number of airplanes that are there and the price per flying hour. The price per flying hour increases with thrust because more thrust means more passengers means more value for our customers.
finding: RR values platforms by installed thrust because flying-hour prices scale with thrust, which favours large widebody engines.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: when we do our business cases, we're only taking into account the first part of the lifecycle of the engine when we're building our business cases.
finding: RR's engine business cases (for example a possible A380neo Trent) count only the first part of the engine lifecycle, which makes them conservative.
trigger: Analyst question on an A380neo with a new Trent
response: Business case unaffected by late-life service pricing because it counts only the early lifecycle

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the changes to OE profit recognition mean that the forecast of any engine build, as I've said, will be taken in the first year. And this underlines really the importance of our focus on improving our unit cost position for cash purposes, which will significantly reduce these cash losses over time.
finding: With OE losses recognised upfront under IFRS 15, RR stresses unit-cost reduction as the lever to cut new-engine cash losses.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We've been working with them as a risk- and revenue-sharing partner for many years. ... Our joint venture partner chose to exercise a put option. Absolutely, the timing was their choice, not ours. But directionally, this is quite a desirable thing as we can consolidate more of the high value that is there in both the OE and aftermarket.
finding: RR bought out its partner's stake in ITP, a long-time risk-and-revenue-sharing partner, to consolidate more OE and aftermarket value on the Trent 1000 and XWB.
trigger: RR's joint venture partner exercised a put option on its ITP stake
response: Acquire full control of ITP

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the way to mitigate the CARs effects is to get the cash losses out as quickly as we possibly can. But equally, managing the whole cash cycle is going to be very important here.
finding: RR's management priority on new engines is to eliminate OE cash losses as fast as possible and manage the full cash cycle.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Because the engines spend 25 years or so in active service, and we need to look after our customers and make money out of that throughout the 25 years.
finding: RR plans on engines earning money over about 25 years of service, which is the horizon for its lifecycle economics.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: I've seen lots and lots of companies wither on the vine through not embracing new technologies in time. I've also seen lots of companies wither on the vine because they enthusiastically invest in all sorts of fancy new technologies that no hope and the market doesn't want them just yet.
finding: RR's CEO sees technology timing as a two-sided risk, moving too late or investing before the market is ready, which implies a measured pace for UltraFan-type bets.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: we catch up in profit terms around the time of the second service on most engines. So the more mature the fleet, the higher cumulative profit should be recognizing and therefore, the higher the reported margins.
finding: RR's engine programme economics break even on a lifecycle basis around the second shop visit, so mature fleets drive margins.

speaker: Eric Schulz, President Civil Aerospace
quote: as we will reach 50% of market share in the future within the next 3 or 4 years, we should expect to have more aircraft parked because this is just a sign of maturity. And again, this is why it is very, very important for us to work on transitions, mainly with leasing companies
finding: RR expected to reach about 50% of the widebody engine market within 3-4 years and to protect it by working with lessors on transitions.

speaker: Eric Schulz, President Civil Aerospace
quote: Addressing the in-fleet issues is absolutely key to preserve our reputation and keep the customer with us, and that's a big, big focus for us.
finding: RR treats fast resolution of in-service engine problems as essential to keeping customers.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: The application of the new standard requires us to treat our contracts with airframes and airlines as independent, even though the economic substance of the overall transaction is to generate overall positive cash returns from the combined arrangement.
finding: RR prices engines as a combined OE-plus-aftermarket deal, accepting OE losses as long as the whole arrangement returns positive cash.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the further we push our overhauls by improving time on wing or the more we can take out our cost, actually the rest, revenue and profit, we book or it happens further out. But that's something we just have to accommodate. But it's still the right thing to do, from our point of view.
finding: RR pursues longer time on wing under its service contracts even though this defers reported revenue and profit, because it raises lifecycle value.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: record expenditure in R&D in 2016, even though times are tough, we recognize this is an engineering- and technology-led business. And it's very important that we spend that ... money, because that money is going into new products
finding: RR kept R&D at a record level in 2016 despite a profit collapse, protecting new-engine spending through a downturn.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: we value a very robust balance sheet with a healthy investment-grade rating. We believe this is commercially important when offering products and support contracts, so we'll be in operation for decades.
finding: RR protects its investment-grade rating because customers buying engines with decades-long support contracts need confidence in its balance sheet.

speaker: David Smith, CFO
quote: the important thing is to roll out the new engines with an exclusive position on the A330neo, for the Trent 7000 and on the A350 for the XWB. And that will significantly grow our installed base.
finding: RR's widebody strategy relies on sole-source positions (Trent 7000 on the A330neo, XWB on the A350) to build an installed base that produces aftermarket cash for decades.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we do need to start to tilt a little bit to the future, look ahead, to think about new disruptive technologies and ways in which we can improve the competitiveness of our business from a strategic point of view to disrupt and to win.
finding: In early 2017 RR began shifting emphasis from fixing operations towards disruptive future technologies to compete.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Our older engines, time and materials, these RB211 engines are being retired, and that's what's contributing the downward pressure. Those time and materials contracts are high margin. That's being offset by newer engines, and newer engines tend to be long-term service agreements
finding: RR's aftermarket mix is shifting from high-margin time-and-materials work on old RB211s to long-term TotalCare agreements on new engines.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: as we grow that with our new engines faster than the older engines that are retiring, we get a growth in the size of the overall fleet, and that's fueling our aftermarket growth.
finding: RR's business model accepts OE losses to grow the installed fleet, which drives aftermarket revenue.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we do sell our engines at a loss. So the cash margin per engine sold, an improvement of that cash margin, in other words a smaller loss, ultimately leading to breakeven for 1 or 2 of our engines, remains incredibly important.
finding: RR's civil cash model is OE loss plus aftermarket; the aim is a smaller OE loss and breakeven on only one or two engine types.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we can invest for the future and place some of the biggest stakes where we see opportunities for growing cash flows in the future in new engine programs. That disciplined capital allocation is very important: that we are sensible and disciplined around setting return on capital targets, cash return on capital targets over not short-term cycles but medium, long-term cycles, so 5-, 10-, 15-year cycles
finding: RR says new engine programmes are its biggest investment bets and should be judged against cash return-on-capital targets over 5-15 year cycles.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we believe that we have a design of gearbox that is going to be successful. But we're very, very early. We only just started testing it under power. And I would really hesitate for any of our spokespeople to comment on it's going to be glorious because we've got a program over the next several years of extensive testing.
finding: RR treats its UltraFan power gearbox as early-stage technology needing several years of testing before any claim of readiness, which argues against an early UltraFan launch commitment.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: particularly in the aftermarket cash margin because that's the big cash driver. And when you think about it, it's not hugely dissimilar from a subscription business
finding: RR's CFO describes the aftermarket cash margin as the main cash driver and likens the installed-base service model to a subscription business.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: it will be dependent on whether we can get a sensible business case on the individual project. And that depends on where Boeing end up with the specifications for their aircraft and the requirements for the engine and where we are with our architecture developments at the time.
finding: RR's go/no-go on a new airframe engine depends on a project-level business case, the airframer's specification and its own technology readiness.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We're developing those new architectures for new wide-body applications at the back end of the decade.
finding: In 2017 RR aimed its Advance and UltraFan architectures mainly at new widebody applications around the end of the decade.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Sometimes, in trying to achieve better performance, we bump into one of those boundaries, and that's what's happening with Trent 1000 at the moment.
finding: RR concedes that pushing for fuel-burn performance can push durability over the edge, as with the Trent 1000.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: it's almost a financial imperative for us to have this level of free cash flow, given our long-term investments that we have to make where we were developing engine programs for engines that may not be on the plane for another 10 or 15 years or so.
finding: RR frames about GBP 1bn of free cash flow as a financial imperative because it must fund engine programmes that may not fly for 10-15 years.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We have been working hard over many years to gain the design wins, and now we're delivering on those design wins and growing the size of our fleet.
finding: RR's model is to win airframe design slots, then earn from a growing fleet's flying hours (invoiced flying hours +12% in 2017).

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: one of the advantages that this means is that they're a risk and revenue-sharing partner for us. And we've been through a lot of the risks on XWB and the development that they've done on XWB. We're now coming into the revenue bit. And so this is a great opportunity to actually capture 100% of that revenue
finding: RR bought out ITP to capture 100% (from 50%) of its XWB risk-sharing revenue once development risk was past, buying back partner shares at the revenue stage.
trigger: ITP put option exercised
response: acquire full ownership of ITP

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We highlighted in 2016 a 7% compression of the deficit; and 37% in 2017, largely price driven rather than cost driven. Of course, we would rather it be more cost driven than price driven, but we will take the benefit.
finding: XWB-84 OE deficit reduction came mostly from higher prices as launch discounts rolled off, rather than lower cost.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: the Trent 900 has some temporary pricing impact that's dragging the gross margin down. And the Trent 700 has had a good year of sales as it enters its final 1 or 2 years of -- a couple of years of its OE experience
finding: RR discounts end-of-life OE (Trent 700) to place more engines before the programme becomes aftermarket-only, keeping the average OE loss at GBP 1.6m.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We've now moved 75% of the weighting of our management bonus schemes to cash flow, which I think is an encouraging sign.
finding: RR weighted 75% of management bonuses to cash flow, pushing management towards cash-conserving decisions.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: At the same time, of course, electrification is not going to hit widebody airplanes in the mainstream for many years. And so it's absolutely essential that we remain cutting-edge in terms of our gas turbine capability.
finding: RR judged that gas turbines would dominate widebodies for many years and kept investing to stay at the front in gas-turbine technology.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: TotalCare is the -- in a vast proportion -- a vast majority of the fleet. Well over 90% is on TotalCare. And that's the model of choice, and that's what customers prefer
finding: Over 90% of RR's widebody fleet was on TotalCare flying-hour contracts, the customer-preferred model.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we try to secure on a basic principle, more value to the customer means more money to Rolls-Royce. So the -- if it's a bigger thrust engine and I can lift more people into the air, then I pay more.
finding: RR prices engines and services on value to the customer: more thrust or payload means higher price.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: If I can do that and, at the same time, spend less on the fuel that is required to do it, then part of that value is actually just competed away. It's -- these newer engines are cleaner, they're more efficient, but they need to be in order to maintain our competitive position.
finding: RR accepts that much of a new engine's fuel-efficiency value is competed away to customers; efficiency gains keep share rather than raise price.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: starting at the preliminary design review rather than engine certification. So once we prove the economics of the engine, we start capitalizing it.
finding: RR capitalises engine R&D from preliminary design review, once it has proved the engine's economics, in line with MTU and Safran.

speaker: Ian Davis, Chairman
quote: I would draw attention to the fact that we have sustained investment in capital expenditure and R&D, notwithstanding short-term financial pressures. We are putting increased emphasis on strategic partnerships and collaborations. These collaborations range across electronics, composite materials, gearbox technology, digital technologies and services.
finding: RR's board kept technology investment going through short-term financial pressure and leaned more on partnerships, including for gearbox technology.

speaker: Paul Stein, CTO
quote: UltraFan, though, may be the last step using pure gas turbine technology before we need the electrification technology, I spoke of earlier, to drive down towards a 30% CO2 reduction
finding: RR regarded UltraFan as possibly the last pure gas-turbine step before electrification.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We're now going from the developing market share phase into the using market share phase, where we use that market share to generate returns and invest in new technology going forward.
finding: In 2018 RR moved from buying widebody share to harvesting it: using its installed base to generate returns rather than chase more share.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Now to make this business really work, we need to have an annuity type income. And so what's been developing over that period is the TotalCare packages evolved from few to most of them. And in fact, when we take orders today, about 99% plus go out with a TotalCare package.
finding: RR sells almost every new engine (over 99%) with a TotalCare flying-hour service contract, making aftermarket annuity income central to its pricing.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We understand on technology that we need to be using the world's best technology, but we can't necessarily own it all. We need to be quite selective in terms of what we own, what we produce, where the key intellectual property is ... where we need to do some partnering
finding: RR said it would own only key IP and partner for the rest, which makes partnerships on new engines consistent with its strategy.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: There'll be a lot around this presentation that we'll talk about the future and the good things that are going to happen but we shouldn't forget there is risk within our business. The Trent 1000, the Trent 900 is a very good example of the risk that is within our engines and their performance.
finding: RR's CFO named in-service durability (Trent 900/1000) as the main risk to its aftermarket cash model.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we have brought to the market 6 new civil aero engines during that period during the last 10 years. On average, Civil NPI has been around 50% of group R&D spend. We're unlikely to see that period of activity again over the next 10 years as we move into a service business after having been an R&D, an OE business
finding: In 2018 RR expected no comparable new-engine investment wave for about 10 years, moving from an R&D/OE business to a service business (civil NPI had been about 50% of group R&D).

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: The ambition, to decline to around 6% of sales as the pace of Civil NPI slows down. And then at some point, we will again move into an investment cycle, but that won't be in the next sort of 10 years.
finding: RR planned net R&D to fall to about 6% of sales and expected no new investment cycle for about a decade, a low appetite for new engine launches in 2018-2028.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Number one, customer confidence. We do have, as we showed on those previous charts, long-term investment cycles for our aerospace programs, multiyear service contracts. Our customers need to be confident they are investing in a strong and healthy business.
finding: RR prioritises a strong credit rating because airline customers signing multi-decade service contracts need confidence in its solvency, a constraint on balance-sheet risk.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: These are the 4 metrics against which we assess the credibility and the traction of each investment that's being put forward: internal rate of return, net present value, cash return on invested capital and also the maximum negative cash flow to the business.
finding: RR screens every investment on IRR, NPV, cash return on invested capital and maximum negative cash exposure, chaired by the CFO monthly.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We include within our investment proposals now mandatory minimum contingencies. There has been a, I would say, a streak of optimism in previous investments that have taken place, which have caught us out.
finding: RR admitted past investment optimism and now requires minimum contingencies and sensitivity tests in proposals.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: they must demonstrate a return 5% above our weighted average cost of capital of 10%, which is the group. So we're targeting a 15% cash return on invested capital for each investment.
finding: RR's hurdle for any investment, including new engines, is a 15% cash return on invested capital (group WACC 10% plus 5%).

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Rolls-Royce in the past has, I think, largely been a profit-driven business and has benefited from long-term contract accounting through using a profit measurement. But its cash flow is the best and key indicator of economic performance.
finding: In 2018 RR changed from accounting-profit targets to cash flow, tying incentives to cash flow per share and cash return on invested capital.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Typically, it costs us around GBP 1.5 billion, GBP 2 billion of R&D and CapEx for that engine program. We then have installed OE losses of around GBP 3.2 billion. So there's 2,000 engines at a GBP 1.6 million loss per engine ... over the next 25 years, we have around a GBP 10 billion aftermarket cash margin
finding: RR's model for a 2,000-engine programme: GBP 1.5-2bn R&D and capex, about GBP 3.2bn of OE losses, and about GBP 10bn of aftermarket cash margin over 25 years.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Cash flow per share, very simple terms, this is much more simple, this one. We are dividing underlying free cash flow by the number of shares.
finding: RR targeted over GBP 1 of free cash flow per share in 5-6 years from about 15p, while admitting it was 'just a PowerPoint'.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we tend to find that new engines, launch pricing tends to be less keen than a mature, a more mature engine. So the -- and the 7000 and the XWB-97 are the 2 most significant examples of that.
finding: RR's launch pricing on new engines (Trent 7000, XWB-97) is steeper than on mature ones, so new-engine OE losses are larger and fall over time.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: With Civil Aerospace, a longer-cycle business, 12.5% cost of capital seems more appropriate.
finding: RR uses a 12.5% cost of capital for Civil Aerospace (8% Power Systems, 6.5% Defence), so civil engine programmes face the highest hurdle.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: if that means developing an engine with a business plan that doesn't make sense according to the rigor that we are intending to treat these projects with, then we'll find other ways of doing it.
finding: RR would pursue a market (here business jets) only with engines that meet its investment hurdles, otherwise it would find other routes such as partnering.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: So first of all, a series of abnormal events, giving rise to a significant level of cost of a nature not normally expected. And most importantly, it's not reflected in the contract price, not included in the original long-term contracts.
finding: RR's long-term contract prices do not include costs of fleet-wide abnormal events, which it books as exceptional.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: ITP is a very important partner to Rolls-Royce. It has shares on all our key engine programs, particularly the newer engine programs and it has it where it has, for example, shares of around 10% or so on the XWB.
finding: RR spreads its engine programmes across risk-sharing partners such as ITP (about 10% of the XWB), which it brought fully in-house at end-2017.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: the improvement in the deficit still the majority is price driven rather than cost driven, but cost increasingly paying a contribution. So I would kind of think about sort of 70-30 in that mix
