finding: About 70% of the XWB-84 OE loss reduction came from price (launch-customer discounts rolling off) and about 30% from unit cost.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And our hook to maintain a claim on that profit pool is the knowledge that we have of our engines and the intellectual property that's embodied therein.
finding: RR protects its aftermarket share through engine knowledge and IP, and sees independent MROs and airlines competing for the same profit pool.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We've all got what you might call issues with our engines and our customers in terms of durability of components and reliability and so on. And I don't think -- I think all of us are pretty occupied with dealing with our own issues for now.
finding: RR said every engine maker had durability problems and none was about to service rivals' engines, so aftermarket entry against CFM was not a near-term option.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We have to generate a sensible, competitive amount of cash. So that we can reliably continue to invest in R&D at the sort of levels that we need to invest in. I don't anticipate any great kick-ups in investment in R&D after 2020. It's business as usual
finding: RR ruled out a big R&D step-up after 2020, suggesting no near-term launch of a large new engine programme beyond UltraFan technology.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And if you don't achieve a sufficient level of maturity, you lay yourselves open to all sorts of in-service issues, customer -- potential customer disruption, and that's not a good place to go from a risk and a commercial point of view.
finding: After the Trent 1000, RR would not put an immature engine into service, putting maturity ahead of winning a platform.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Just as a reminder, at the bottom here, at the bottom left-hand corner, 2018 is expected to be the peak year for R&D cash spend.
finding: RR called 2018 its peak R&D cash-spend year, signalling it planned no new large-engine development wave in the near term.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: So this balance effectively represents deferred revenue for Rolls-Royce, cash collected in advance of the shop visit. Cash receipts are higher than revenue and it's a core part of our business model, this particular mechanism.
finding: RR's business model collects flying-hour cash before shop-visit costs, funding operations from customers' prepayments.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We aspire over the midterm of 2.5x free cash flow dividend covered through the cycle. But we put -- we look at our shareholder payments in the context of our capital allocation priorities.
finding: RR's capital priorities put balance sheet first (single A rating), then organic technology investment, then a dividend 2.5x covered by FCF, then selective M&A.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: But we do know from bitter experience, that you need to do a huge amount of very rigorous testing work to ensure a certain level of maturity when the engine enters into service. And we simply couldn't find enough hours in the day, even if you threw many more bodies at it and much more money at it
finding: Trent 1000 lessons made RR refuse compressed development schedules: extra money could not buy the testing time needed for NMA maturity.
trigger: Boeing NMA schedule
response: withdrew rather than compress testing

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: It's certainly not our intention that the sort of Airbus-Rolls, GE-Boeing thing is accentuated. And to that end, it would have been very good to being able to participate in the NMA program.
finding: RR did not want to become an Airbus-only engine supplier and regretted missing NMA, but still would not compromise on maturity.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: So we're moving from a situation of multiple engines in a relatively small volume to essentially 2 engines and variant and 1 variant each thereof. And therefore, a higher volume of all of those engines
finding: RR planned to reach OE breakeven by consolidating onto two high-commonality engine families (XWB-84/97 and Trent 1000/7000), with XWB about half of 2019 shipments.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: And what we will be doing is building, I would say, more contingency into our estimates around contract margins going forward to protect us from those volatile swings.
finding: After the negative catch-ups, RR said it would build more contingency into long-term contract margin estimates, a more conservative approach to aftermarket accounting.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And it is a very long-cycle business. And the sums of money involved in investment programs are very large. So it's essential that we have a balanced portfolio from a financial point of view with shorter-cycle businesses and stronger, reliable cash flow.
finding: RR relies on Power Systems and Defence cash flows to underpin the very large, long-cycle investments in Civil Aerospace.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We have grown market share in all of these sectors over recent years and we spent about 2/3 of our R&D money on making sure that our existing product portfolio continues to be refreshed and maintains our competitiveness.
finding: About two-thirds of RR's R&D goes into refreshing existing products rather than new platforms.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Now for the time being, our senior managers are all incentivized around, and there is a serious emphasis on cash flow, but of course, that is balanced with profit.
finding: RR's management incentives put heavy weight on cash flow, which pushes the company towards cash-conserving choices.

speaker: Paul Stein, CTO
quote: UltraFan will be nearing the aerodynamic and thermal dynamic limits of pure gas turbines even though it will be powering aircraft for the next 40 years
finding: RR regarded UltraFan as close to the limit of gas-turbine efficiency, and as the engine architecture for about 40 years.

speaker: Ian Davis, Chairman
quote: After a period of heavy investment, we're focused on generating strong returns and the cash flow that will allow us to compete even more effectively in what continue to be attractive growth markets.
finding: RR's board presented 2019 as a harvest phase after heavy investment, with returns and cash coming before new commitments.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: It's very important with very long-term contracts that we continue to invest in technology for current products. That investment goes into things like optimizing the designs for cost reductions so that over time, we can make more profit out of selling the same things and importantly, out of improving the in-service performance, longer time on wing.
finding: Because of its long-term service contracts, RR puts R&D into cutting cost and extending time-on-wing on existing engines, which lifts profit on programmes it already sells.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: it's up to us and our customers and others in the ecosystem to lead rather than react to public opinion. ... But I think it's important as a business that we remember we have to generate the returns now in order to fund the R&D
finding: RR framed decarbonisation R&D as something it must fund out of current returns, tying new-technology investment to cash generation today.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: we highlighted 3 core drivers that between them would contribute GBP 1.75 billion of incremental cash flow to Rolls-Royce in the midterm. Those 3 core drivers are: first of all, reducing the loss on the engines -- on the unit loss on each engine that we sell in Civil Aerospace, wide-body engine deficit reduction; secondly, the improved aftermarket cash margin
finding: RR's mid-term cash plan rests on three levers: smaller OE losses per widebody engine, a better aftermarket cash margin, and lower R&D/capex/C&A as a share of sales, together worth GBP 1.75bn.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Important to note here that we are coming out of investment cycle. We've brought to the market 7 new engines, Civil Aerospace, over the last 10 years. There's been a 70% increase in our R&D, looking at the bottom right-hand corner there, in R&D since 2010. So the 6% midterm ambition is very much in line with industry peers.
finding: After seven new civil engines in a decade, RR planned to cut cash R&D to about 6% of sales, signalling reluctance to fund another big new-engine cycle soon.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Our capital allocation priorities remain unchanged, a strong balance sheet and improving our credit rating, as I just talked about earlier. Funding organic investments, Warren talked much about this, to drive growth and technology leadership
finding: RR ranked its capital priorities as balance sheet and rating first (aiming back to single A), then organic investment, then shareholder payments, with M&A last.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The Pearl 15 was the seventh new production engine in a decade. And I said on the wires call this morning, that is the richest period of new engine development for Rolls-Royce in its entire history. We don't have to develop those engines anymore.
finding: RR saw itself at the end of its richest new-engine development period, freeing resources for new technologies within a flat R&D budget rather than a new engine.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: But basically, we believe that we can approach this problem with the resources that we have within the R&D envelope that we currently have. I mean when I say within, it will fluctuate by perhaps GBP 100 million or so in either direction
finding: RR said it would fund electrification and new technology inside its existing R&D budget (plus or minus GBP 100m), not by raising R&D.
trigger: UTC-Raytheon merger rationale that scale is needed for electrification
response: fund within existing R&D envelope

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: those OE loss reduction on XWB, yes, it is a mixture of continued removal of launch discounts from the mix and ongoing cost reduction.
finding: RR's OE losses come partly from launch-customer discounts that roll off over time, alongside unit-cost reduction.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Whilst obviously in a competitive environment, one needs to respond to aggression with aggression, there are limits of commercial common sense. And so we won't always go there.
finding: RR meets aggressive pricing but only within 'commercial common sense' limits, judging deals against an expected business case across its portfolio.
trigger: GE aggressive pricing on 787; Boeing pressure on A330neo
response: selective price aggression

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: And we have a sort of expected business case. And we are taking some business way above that and some business way below that, and we look at it on a portfolio basis. And that applies to how we do Trent 1000 and how we sell 7000s on the A330neos at the moment as well.
finding: RR prices engine campaigns on a portfolio basis, accepting some deals well below its business case if the programme overall meets it.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The only thing that would destroy it is if we made our insurance contracts of the long-term service agreements so attractive, that it would wean people off time and materials. But you don't get something for nothing in this world. And if we made them so attractive, then they'd probably become less profitable for us.
finding: RR deliberately keeps time-and-materials aftermarket business on older engines rather than pricing LTSAs to capture it all.

doc: Special Call (Trading and Trent 1000 update), Nov 2019
speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: But an important distinction here is that going forward, new contracts that are outside that period of increased cash costs will be at a healthy margin, and we expect, therefore, the margin over time to start improving and then get back towards that sort of 20% or so
finding: RR expects to restore Trent 1000 aftermarket margins towards 20% by pricing new contracts outside the crisis window at healthy margins.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: in the R&D domain, that means effectively keeping our R&D flat as the sales grows. And within that fixed envelope, you can see here how we're tilting the amount of money spent towards future-looking technologies.
finding: Before COVID, RR already held R&D flat in absolute terms while moving the mix towards future technologies such as UltraFan and electrification.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: There are many of our customers who prefer to be paid at the shop visit rather than through the flying hour process. That has a higher yield per flying hour than had they just paid as the hours were generated
finding: RR charges a higher effective rate when customers pay at the shop visit rather than per flying hour, pricing the financing it provides.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: It's a reminder of our installed base. When you add up the Civil Aerospace installed base of 14,000 engines, the Power Systems installed base of 146,000 and then 16,000 in Defence, the 176,000 engines driving this service revenue.
finding: RR's strategy is to become a services business built on its installed base; services were 52% of group revenue in 2019.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the costs are dominated by the costs of those components and the cost of the components is dominated by the design of those components. We continue to spend engineering effort on modifying designs to take cost out, we take cost out on an annual basis.
finding: RR lowers OE unit losses mainly through design-to-cost engineering over a programme's life, not through volume.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: in the regional space, we see an opportunity for hybrid coming sooner than we do into the narrow-body space. So you have hybrid designs in the mid- to late 20s moving through to larger aeroplanes in the early to mid-30s.
finding: RR's timeline puts hybrid propulsion on regional aircraft in the late 2020s and on larger aircraft in the early-to-mid 2030s, with SAF-fuelled gas turbines for large aircraft.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: it's possible that we actually want to spend the money and have the components that improve the durability and the time on wing for service of and -- a given engine because we actually make more profit out of that, than we make from trying to squeeze a technical profit on the OE.
finding: RR will accept a permanent OE loss (for example on the XWB-97) if spending on durability raises lifetime aftermarket profit: it prices and designs for the life of the engine, not the OE sale.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: The cash is contractually ours and remains ours. Even if the airline stopped flying the planes forever. The cash is still our cash contractually.
finding: RR treats flight-hour cash received in advance as its own, non-refundable, which is how its LTSA model finances the business.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: this build of Trent 1000 engines will be a very good return on capital when we consider the cost that we're currently seeing for every day that an aircraft is on the ground.
finding: RR justifies spare engine capex by the compensation it pays airlines for each grounded aircraft, so customers' AOG costs fall on RR.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: at the larger end of the market, particularly for widebody long-haul flights, we don't yet see a viable technological pathway for fully electric flight.
finding: RR expects widebody long-haul aircraft to stay on gas turbines with lower-carbon fuels, with electrification limited to small aircraft.

speaker: Ian Davis, Chairman
quote: we're also very mindful of the need to protect Rolls-Royce's ability to innovate.
finding: Under shareholder pressure about losing large-engine design capability during COVID cuts, RR's board said it would protect innovation capacity.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: In reality, it's almost certainly the darkest hour for our whole company since the 1970s.
finding: RR's CEO called COVID its worst crisis since the 1970s insolvency, which explains the defensive, balance-sheet-first behaviour that followed.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Now we're not exposed to how full planes are. It's the flight that matters to us.
finding: RR's flight-hour pricing puts utilisation risk, not load-factor risk, on RR; its revenue follows flights, not passengers.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we get most benefit from owning the supply chain where our engineering and experience is a differentiating factor, especially where we have design and manufacture that are closely related. And we're reviewing our manufacturing activities to explore further outsourcing opportunity. And that would lower our capital intensity
finding: RR keeps in-house only the manufacturing tied to its engineering edge and outsources more to reduce capital intensity.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: how we collaborate with partners for the long term to reduce our future capital costs and risks.
finding: After COVID, RR said it wanted long-term partners to share the capital cost and risk of future programmes.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: The world is demanding cleaner energy, and we need to find the right approach that enables us to continue to lead the way in our markets without taking on unacceptable costs and risks.
finding: RR frames its technology leadership as limited by risk: it will lead only where costs and risks are acceptable.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we see a substantial opportunity for improvement in our aftermarket returns by extending the time on wing and working with MRO partners as our base of over 5,000 installed large engines grows.
finding: RR's civil returns strategy centres on time on wing and the annuity-like aftermarket from its installed base.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: it's not as important as perhaps it has been given that we're unlikely to see big new engine program orders over the next 2 or 3 years given the markets, but also given where we are in our engine program development at the moment.
finding: RR linked its credit rating to winning new engine programmes and expected no big new engine competitions for 2-3 years (to about 2023), so it deprioritised investment grade.
trigger: COVID market collapse
response: Downgraded urgency of investment grade

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: Our customers are committing to us when they place orders, making long-term commitments around engine programs that will be on their aircraft. So that's an important commitment that we're giving them, and our credit rating is an indication of the health of Rolls-Royce.
finding: RR sees its credit rating as part of what airframers and airlines weigh when choosing it for multi-decade engine commitments.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we are emerging from a period where we've spent a huge amount of investment on our Civil Aerospace business, created a portfolio of relatively new and new engines. Now is the time to capitalize on those new engines.
finding: RR's post-crisis capital allocation is to harvest recently launched civil engines and move investment to zero-carbon areas and other divisions.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: there is a limit to the amount that we can reasonably expect solely from our banks and the bond market without addressing the leverage as well.
finding: RR accepted equity dilution once debt capacity was used up, rather than risk its credit standing.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: A strong financial position does matter to our customers. In Civil Aerospace, airline customers signed multiyear service contracts with us. They want to know that we can be relied on as a long-term partner, and we'll live up to our side of the contract.
finding: RR sees balance sheet strength as a competitive asset because airlines buying multi-year service contracts need to trust it.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we're committed to long-term investment cycles in order to win positions on new programs. Our customers need to know that we are resilient enough to be able to invest in those products through the cycle.
finding: RR says winning new airframe positions requires showing airframers it can fund engine development through the cycle, which is why it wants investment grade.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: As our engine programs mature, the investment needs to reduce, of course, manufacturing efficiency improves, pricing increases, and the risk of in-service issues diminishes. And all of that creates a significant inflection in the financial performance.
finding: RR's model of an engine's life: early years carry high investment, low efficiency, low prices and in-service risk; maturity brings the payback. This is the lifecycle a new engine launch implies.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: once we achieve our aim of restoring financial returns and a more appropriate balance sheet, we'll be accelerating these aspects of our strategy, and you'll see substantial growth in that starting to happen by 2025.
finding: RR puts balance sheet repair ahead of new growth investment, and plans to accelerate growth programmes only after returns recover, around 2025.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: we came in with good momentum, having turned a bit of a corner as we emerged from a period of -- extended period, actually, of investments in new large civil engine programs to be looking forward to a period where we would see higher returns, reaping the returns from that investment on our large installed base and increased market share
finding: RR's pre-COVID plan was to harvest returns from its large installed base after a long new-engine investment phase that bought market share.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We're looking for a net cash positive of circa GBP 2 billion in the medium term. I think we had that view coming into this crisis ... It's driven by requirements to keep R&D going and that sort of thing.
finding: RR targets about GBP 2bn of net cash to fund continuous R&D through the cycle, which sets how much balance sheet it will risk on new engines.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: Time & Materials is more prevalent on the older programs than it is on the newer programs. And so you would expect to see in the long run Time & Materials declining slightly as a proportion.
finding: RR puts new engines almost entirely on long-term service agreements, so time-and-materials becomes a shrinking legacy stream.

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO
quote: We do not intend to remain in a net debt position. We're in a cyclical industry and need a strong balance sheet to be able to weather the storms without jeopardizing our commercial position or our through-cycle investments.
finding: RR's stated principle is a net cash balance sheet so that it can fund through-cycle engine investment in downturns.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: We're challenging ourselves to achieve better pricing and engineer greater efficiency to reduce per-unit cost and waste. It really is a fundamental transformation of the Civil Aerospace cost base.
finding: Besides cutting fixed costs, RR is pushing for better pricing and lower unit cost in civil, the levers that reduce its OE loss per engine.

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: the actions that we've taken to change our cost base and position for the recovery mean we're confident we'll be able to keep those costs low as volumes increase and that will deliver better cash margins in the future than we have achieved in the past.
finding: RR plans to keep costs down as volumes recover so that civil cash margins end up higher than before COVID.

speaker: Warren East, CEO

speaker: Warren East, CEO
quote: For journeys over 1,000 nautical miles, alternatives like electric solutions and hydrogen solutions become very challenging or even impossible.

speaker: Warren East, CEO

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO

speaker: Stephen Daintith, CFO

speaker: Warren East, CEO

speaker: Paul Stein, CTO

speaker: Warren East, CEO

speaker: Warren East, CEO

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO

speaker: Tufan Erginbilgic, CEO

finding: MS blended price targets are 991p bear (-20% vs 1240p), 1500p base (+21%) and 2058p bull (+66%).
implication: (inference) The asymmetric range (bull upside roughly three times bear downside) shows MS believes execution on the current franchise already drives most value; new-engine launches are not needed to reach the base case.

finding: In the base case MS values RR at 1334p on EV/EBIT, 1263p on P/E, 1299p on SOTP and 1702p on DCF; the 1500p blended target equals the simple average of the DCF (1702p) and SOTP (1299p) values, and the SOTP value equals the average of the EV/EBIT and P/E values.
implication: (inference) DCF is the most generous method (about 28-35% above the EV/EBIT and P/E values), so MS's long-dated cash-flow view of RR's installed base (aftermarket annuity) carries half the weight of the target.

finding: In the bear case MS's multiples give 751p (EV/EBIT) and 705p (P/E) but the DCF still gives 1253p, for a 991p blend; in the bull case EV/EBIT gives 1679p, P/E 1625p and DCF 2463p for a 2058p blend.
implication: (inference) Even MS's bear DCF (1253p) values RR above the 1240p share price; the bear downside comes from multiple compression (16x EV/EBIT, 20x P/E) rather than a collapse in long-run cash flow.

doc: Noealt Global Strategy Brief 2019: Global Commercial Aircraft Engine Manufacturers (Feb 2019)

doc: Noealt Global Strategy Brief 2019: Global Commercial Aircraft Engine Manufacturers (Feb 2019)

quote: AGI is a JV between Rolls Royce & Hispano-Suiza, a Safran group company, for manufacturing power transmissions for the UltraFan engine.

finding: RR hedges on hybrid-electric propulsion by partnering with Airbus and Siemens on E-Fan X, supplying the gas turbine and generator.

response: GE sole source

response: engine selection gated with the launch decision

finding: Boeing brought propulsion and nacelle integration work in-house (e.g., the MAX nacelle inlet) to capture value and IP around the engine, shrinking the scope left to engine and nacelle suppliers.
trigger: MAX nacelle inlet insourcing
response: Boeing takes propulsion integration in-house

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: But Rolls is very confident. And having been in the engine business myself, I mean, I understand how these things happen. And if they say they are confident, that they understand the root cause and have the fix in hand, then I believe them.
finding: Boeing's CEO publicly backed RR's root-cause claim after the 2010 test failure, showing that in 2010 the airframer still gave RR the benefit of the doubt on a technical problem.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: I think the -- especially on the heels of the GEnx and the Rolls engine being somewhat late on the 87, okay
finding: Boeing's CEO counted both 787 engines, RR's and GE's, as late: engine delay is part of how Boeing remembers the 787 and weighs engine risk.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: for me, the deciding item is the depth and length of their technical maturation program that they've had on this program, starting from the mid-'90s, that didn't exist to the same degree on the GEnx and the Trent offerings.
finding: Boeing judged the 787 Trent (and GEnx) to have had shallower technology maturation than CFM's LEAP and gave this as the deciding reason to trust LEAP on the MAX, so a long maturation record wins Boeing selections.
trigger: Boeing's choice of engine for the 737 MAX
response: Boeing favoured the engine with the longest technology maturation (CFM LEAP) over the approach taken on the Trent/GEnx

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: Now along with Aviall, you have to buy aftermarket product streams, and we continue to invest in different engines that -- maybe GE or Rolls or Pratt & Whitney no longer want to deal with. And it's been a very profitable business for us.
finding: Boeing (through Aviall) buys aftermarket product streams for engines that GE, Rolls-Royce or Pratt & Whitney may no longer want to support, and finds this very profitable, so engine makers sometimes give up tail-end aftermarket to others.

speaker: Randy Tinseth, VP Marketing, Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: So the question is, is it an all-new engine, which is expensive and challenging for us all, but it might be the right step forward as we look at not only at this airplane, but future applications? Or is it a derivative of things that we have on the table today?
finding: In 2016 Boeing left open whether its middle-of-market airplane needed an all-new engine (costly for everyone) or a derivative, a choice that decides how much engine makers must invest.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: On the defense services side, we announced exclusive aftermarket distribution agreements with GE Aviation and Rolls-Royce for engine spare parts that have a combined potential value of more than $10 billion over the life of the program.
finding: In 2017 RR (with GE) gave Boeing Global Services exclusive distribution of defence engine spare parts, a combined potential value above $10bn: RR shares aftermarket channels with an airframer.

speaker: Dennis Muilenburg, Chairman, President & CEO
quote: We still see that as a marketplace that's 4,000 to 5,000 airplanes. ... We don't see this as a technology push on engines or avionics or any of the internal systems in the airplane. Again, in large case, the ability to reuse or modify 787 systems or 737 systems or use existing engine technology packaged in a new way.
finding: By mid-2018 Boeing framed the NMA (4,000-5,000 aircraft market) as needing existing engine technology repackaged, not a new-engine push, a shift from its 2016 openness to an all-new engine.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO; Cai Von Rumohr (Cowen) question
quote: And I guess engine supplier decision is key. And what's your druthers: 1 or 2 suppliers? ... that goes through technology and obviously into the business case, into pricing, into engine technology and capabilities and efficiency and so on. ... So put more criteria in those gates based on lessons learned.
finding: Boeing evaluates engine technology, capability and efficiency inside pass/fail launch gates that it tightened after past programmes, and again declined to commit to one or two engine suppliers.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, President & CEO
quote: Yes. Well, engines always play into it. I don't think they're going to play into it anywhere near the extent to which they used to simply because the demands on that propulsion system in the next go around I don't think are going to be as significant.
finding: Boeing's CEO in 2021 expected engines to matter less in the next airplane's timing and differentiation, which weakens an engine maker's leverage from launching a new engine.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, President & CEO; Rob Spingarn (Credit Suisse) question
quote: and therefore, that the next plane would be conventionally powered? ... Yes, I believe that. Yes. And I'm on the record of saying that. Hydrogen power, I just believe, has a much longer time line than the time line that at least I've read like you did.
finding: Boeing expects its next airplane to use conventional (sustainable-fuel-capable) propulsion rather than hydrogen, so the next Boeing engine competition is among conventional turbofans.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, President & CEO
quote: Most often, when a new airplane is developed by either side, it is usually developed around a propulsion package that offers 15% to 20% improvement with respect to efficiency versus the one it's displacing. ... I don't believe the next generation of engine can deliver that kind of performance.
finding: Boeing's CEO repeated in April 2021 that next-generation engines will not deliver the historical 15-20% efficiency step, so Boeing values a new engine less and will look to the airframe and manufacturing for gains.

speaker: Dave Calhoun, President & CEO
quote: That will get solved when a couple of the important players made up of probably airplane guys like us, propulsion guys like GE and Pratt, Rolls decide on the spec that they want for sustainable aviation fuel
finding: Boeing's CEO names Rolls-Royce with GE and Pratt as the propulsion players that, with the airframers, will set the sustainable-fuel specification: RR is treated as one of the three incumbent engine makers.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, President & CEO
quote: And third is, when is the technology ready? And I would say the answer is not now on all 3 of those work streams. As you point out, engine technology is going to be important element of that.
finding: In May 2025 Boeing said the market, Boeing itself and the technology, engines included, were all not ready for a new airplane, so engine makers face no near-term Boeing launch.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, President & CEO
quote: If you talk to our airline customers today, I think universally, they would say, we still have work to do and the durability of the existing newer engines that are there. And we'd like to make sure that we don't see the type of durability issues in the future.
finding: Boeing says airlines' shared complaint is the durability of the latest engines and wants that avoided on the next airplane, so an engine maker's durability record becomes a selection criterion.

speaker: Kelly Ortberg, President & CEO
quote: we have to watch the continued demand on the engines in both the forward fit and the aftermarket and the durability upgrades that are going on in the market. So that'll be an area that we'll continue to work with GE and CFM on.
finding: Boeing's 2025 engine supply-chain concern (forward-fit plus aftermarket demand and durability upgrades) names only GE and CFM as the engine partners to work with; Rolls-Royce is not mentioned.

speaker: James Bell, CFO
quote: We powered up the auxiliary power unit. We've had the engine runs at both GE and Rolls.
finding: Rolls-Royce was one of two engine makers on the 787 from the start, and Boeing listed RR's and GE's engine runs among the milestones showing the programme was on track in 2006.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: The Rolls [Rolls-Royce] engine is something that we're working on. Rolls is confident that they can support our schedule with a hardware and a software fix.
finding: When RR's 787 engine hit a problem during certification in 2010, Boeing relied on RR's own hardware and software fix and on RR's assurance that it could still meet Boeing's schedule.

response: RR proposed a hardware and software fix to hold the airframer's schedule

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: Let me deal with the Rolls engine, Joe, first. The event that caused a re-submittal of some data and some modification of hardware and software was a non-contained test stand failure that I think we all know about.

response: modified hardware and software and resubmitted data to regulators instead of recertifying

finding: Despite its 2010 test-stand failure, the RR-powered 787 was ahead of the GE-powered version in flight testing by April 2011, so RR was the lead engine for the 787's certification.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, CEO Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: This week, we're going to park the last of the Rolls Royce 787 flight-test airplanes, and we're about 96% through with the flight-test program.
finding: By May 2011 the RR-powered 787 flight-test fleet had finished its dedicated testing, with the 787 flight-test programme about 96% complete.

finding: Both 787 engines, RR's included, held 330-minute ETOPS engine certification by May 2011, leaving only airplane-level ETOPS testing before service.

speaker: Jim McNerney, Chairman & CEO
quote: We are also in the final phases of ETOPS and F&R test for the Rolls-Royce engine and expect certification before the end of August.
finding: In July 2011 Boeing expected the RR-engined 787 to be certified by the end of August 2011, the certification that would allow first deliveries to launch customer ANA.

speaker: Nicole Piasecki, VP & GM Propulsion Systems Division, Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: And then of course our 2 new development programs, we've certified in the last 3 weeks, we have certified both the 787 powered by the Rolls engine, as well as the 747-8 Freighter powered by GENX.
finding: Boeing certified the RR-powered 787 in the three weeks before 13 September 2011, meeting the end-August target it gave in July; the page names no GE-powered 787 certification yet.

quote: recent press commentary that suggests some of the challenges with the Rolls Trent 1000? ... So gearbox, you saw was a very small number of airplanes. We've swapped 4 of the 5 out ... So 4 are back in the air. And round-trip, a little over a week, so pretty minor.

finding: The fix for the RR gearbox problem on 5 in-service ANA 787s was also applied to production gearboxes, and Boeing expected no delivery-schedule impact.
trigger: RR gearbox issue on ANA 787s
response: fixes on in-service aircraft plus production gearboxes
